text: In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice that I've been turning over in my mind ever since. "Whenever you feel like criticizing any one," he told me, "just remember that all the people in this world haven't had the advantages that you've had." He didn't say any more but we've always been unusually communicative in a reserved way, and I understood that he meant a great deal more than that. In consequence I'm inclined to reserve all judgments, a habit that has opened up many curious natures to me and also made me the victim of not a few veteran bores. The abnormal mind is quick to detect and attach itself to this quality when it appears in a normal person, and so it came about that in college I was unjustly accused of being a politician, because I was privy to the secret griefs of wild, unknown men. Most of the confidences were unsought—frequently I have feigned sleep, preoccupation, or a hostile levity when I realized by some unmistakable sign that an intimate revelation was quivering on the horizon--for the intimate revelations of young men or at least the terms in which they express them are usually plagiaristic and marred by obvious suppressions. Reserving judgments is a matter of infinite hope. I am still a little afraid of missing something if I forget that, as my father snobbishly suggested, and I snobbishly repeat, a sense of the fundamental decencies is parcelled out unequally at birth. And, after boasting this way of my tolerance, I come to the admission that it has a limit. Conduct may be founded on the hard rock or the wet marshes but after a certain point I don't care what it's founded on. When I came back from the East last autumn I felt that I wanted the world to be in uniform and at a sort of moral attention forever; I wanted no more riotous excursions with privileged glimpses into the human heart. Only Gatsby, the man who gives his name to this book, was exempt from my reaction—Gatsby who represented everything for which I have an unaffected scorn. If personality is an unbroken series of successful gestures, then there was something gorgeous about him, some heightened sensitivity to the promises of life, as if he were related to one of those intricate machines that register earthquakes ten thousand miles away. This responsiveness had nothing to do with that flabby impressionability which is dignified under the name of the "creative temperament"—it was an extraordinary gift for hope, a romantic readiness such as I have never found in any other person and which it is not likely I shall ever find again.

text: The laboratory was, as I have said, situated in a quiet street and flanked by a large garden. Its exterior presented a facade of severe and plain design, constructed of grey stone that had weathered to a sombre hue. The windows were high and narrow, fitted with heavy frames of oak, and protected by iron bars of antique pattern. A massive door of dark timber, studded with iron nails and furnished with a ponderous knocker, gave admission to the interior. Within, the appearance of the rooms was strange and impressive. The entrance hall was paved with black and white marble, and from it opened a series of apartments of various sizes, all filled with the apparatus of chemical research. In one corner stood a large furnace, with its complement of retorts, crucibles, and other vessels of porcelain and glass. Shelves laden with bottles and jars of drugs and chemicals extended from floor to ceiling, while the tables were crowded with microscopes, test-tubes, Bunsen burners, and all the paraphernalia of the experimentalist. The air was heavy with the odour of acids and ethers, and a faint, peculiar smell that seemed to emanate from the substances with which the Doctor was occupied. In the largest room, which served as the principal laboratory, there was a perpetual sound of bubbling and simmering, as of some mysterious decoration in preparation. The walls were lined with bookcases filled with ponderous volumes in dark bindings, and portfolios of anatomical drawings. A skeleton, suspended from a bracket, swayed gently in the draught from the door, and in a glass case were arranged various pathological specimens preserved in spirits. The whole place had an air of mystery and seclusion, and was pervaded by that atmosphere of concentrated thought and ceaseless activity which characterizes the workshop of a man devoted to scientific pursuits. The Doctor himself, when engaged in his investigations, moved about from apparatus to apparatus with the quiet precision of one to whom every movement has become habitual, his keen eyes noting every change and phenomenon with unwearied attention.

text: The midnight in Julien Sorel’s solitude in the seminary study in Verrières was dim—dim enough that the candlelight cast long shadows on the wooden walls and the sound of distant church bells (ringing the hour) blended with the faint rustle of his linen cassock, mixing with the dry, ink-stained scent of the Latin Bible in his hands. He sat on a hard oak chair (its back carved with a cross, the seat worn smooth from years of priests’ sitting), the open Bible resting on his knees (its pages marked with pencil notes: translations he’d memorized to impress Abbé Pirard) and a crumpled letter from Madame de Rênal hidden in his cassock pocket (her handwriting soft, words trembling with longing: “Come back to me, even for a moment”), his eyes fixed on the window, where the lights of Verrières flickered like tiny, unattainable stars—each one a symbol of the wealth and status he craved, yet was barred from by his peasant blood. The air smelled of candle wax (dripping down the candlestick) and old parchment (from the theological books stacked on the shelf), and his threadbare woolen socks—mended at the toes, too thin to keep out the cold—clung to his feet, a quiet reminder of the poverty he’d fought to escape, the shame of his father’s blacksmith shop, the way the townsfolk had laughed at him for “thinking too big.” He thought of the day he’d left home for the seminary—of the way his father had shoved him out the door, spitting “You’ll end up a beggar, not a priest,” of the way he’d walked with his head down, his Latin grammar book clutched to his chest, determined to prove everyone wrong, of the way Madame de Rênal had kissed him goodbye in the woods, her tears wetting his cheek, a moment of warmth in the cold of his ambition. He’d thought the seminary was a ladder then, he realized—not just a place to study God, but a way to climb, to shed his “peasant” skin, to become someone who didn’t have to bow to lords or beg for respect. But now, the Bible in his hands felt like a mask: not a book of faith, but a tool—something to recite, to memorize, to use to convince Abbé Pirard he was pious, when all he could think about was the way Madame de Rênal’s hands had felt in his, the way her voice had called his name, not as “Julien the peasant,” but as “my love.” A candle sputtered, its flame shrinking for a second before flaring up again, and he flinched, as if the light had exposed his thoughts. He closed the Bible, running his thumb over the pencil marks—proof of the hours he’d spent pretending to care about theology, when his heart was still in the de Rênal’s drawing room, where he’d felt like a man, not a nobody. He thought of what Abbé Pirard had said to him that afternoon, his voice sharp with suspicion, “Ambition is a sin, Julien. You must love God above all else.” He’d nodded then, his lips forming the words “Yes, Father,” but his mind had been elsewhere—on the way the de Rênal’s son had called him “Monsieur Julien,” on the way the servants had bowed to him, if only for a moment. But now, as he sat there, listening to the bells fade and the wind rattle the window, he wondered if it was worth it. Maybe the ladder was a lie, he thought—maybe no matter how much Latin he memorized, no matter how many prayers he said, he’d always be “the blacksmith’s son” to them, always be an outsider looking in.

text: "Oh, Miss Audry," sobbed Martha, "Mistress has been scolding me dreadfully because I scorched her lace. I did not mean to do it, I really did not. I was in such a hurry because she called me away from the laundry to help her dress, and I forgot that the iron was too hot." "I know you did not mean it, Martha," said Audry gently. "Do not cry. I will speak to mother about it. She will not be so angry when I tell her that it was an accident." Audry went to her mother and begged her to forgive Martha. At first Eleanor refused, but Audry pleaded so hard that at last she consented, though she grumbled a great deal about it. Aline, too, was kind to the servants, but in a different way from Audry. She was more impulsive, and would often stand up for them when they were unjustly accused. She had a quick temper, and if she saw any one being ill-treated, she would speak out boldly, regardless of consequences. One afternoon, Aline was in the kitchen watching the cook make cakes. Thomas came in with some vegetables, and he dropped one of the baskets, spilling the vegetables all over the floor. The cook began to scold him loudly. "It was not my fault," said Thomas angrily. "The basket handle broke." "You are a clumsy fool," shouted the cook. "You always make some excuse. I will tell Mistress about this, and she will have you turned out of the house." Aline could not bear to hear Thomas spoken to like that. "It was an accident," she said sharply. "There is no need to shout at him like that. If you had mended the basket handle when it was loose, this would not have happened." The cook was taken aback by Aline's words. She was not used to being spoken to in such a way by a young girl, but she knew that Aline was a favourite with Master Mowbray, so she did not dare to answer back. She just picked up the vegetables and went on with her work. Thomas thanked Aline for standing up for him, and from that day he was even more ready to do anything for her.

text: A doctor is a highly trained, compassionate medical professional who diagnoses, treats, and prevents illnesses, injuries, and diseases, dedicated to improving the health and well-being of their patients. Doctors undergo years of rigorous education and training, including a bachelor’s degree, four years of medical school, and a residency program (ranging from 3 to 7 years) in a specific medical specialty, such as internal medicine, pediatrics, surgery, obstetrics and gynecology, or psychiatry. This extensive training equips doctors with the knowledge and skills to assess patients’ symptoms, order diagnostic tests (such as blood tests, X-rays, MRIs, or CT scans), interpret test results, and develop personalized treatment plans, which may include medication, surgery, therapy, or lifestyle changes. Doctors work in a variety of settings, including hospitals, clinics, private practices, and research institutions. In hospitals, doctors work in teams with nurses, surgeons, specialists, and other medical staff to provide comprehensive care to patients, often working long hours (10 to 12 hours a day) to ensure that patients receive timely, quality care. In private practices, doctors focus on building long-term relationships with patients, providing routine check-ups, preventive care, and treatment for common illnesses. Specialized doctors, such as surgeons, focus on performing surgeries to treat injuries, diseases, or conditions, while psychiatrists diagnose and treat mental health disorders, such as depression, anxiety, and schizophrenia. Doctors must possess a range of skills, including strong analytical skills to diagnose complex conditions, excellent communication skills to explain medical information to patients and their families, empathy to understand patients’ concerns and fears, and the ability to work under pressure in emergency situations. They also need to stay updated on the latest medical research, treatments, and technologies to provide the best possible care to their patients. The role of a doctor is not just to treat illness but also to promote health and prevent disease through education and counseling. Doctors advise patients on healthy lifestyle choices, such as proper nutrition, regular exercise, and avoiding harmful habits like smoking or excessive drinking, to help them maintain good health and reduce the risk of chronic diseases. Despite the challenges of the profession—including long hours, high stress, and emotional demands—doctors find great fulfillment in helping patients recover from illness, relieve pain, and improve their quality of life. Doctors are essential to society, as they play a vital role in maintaining public health, responding to medical emergencies, and advancing medical research to find new treatments and cures for diseases. Whether treating a common cold, performing a life-saving surgery, or providing mental health support, doctors are dedicated professionals who work tirelessly to care for others and make a positive impact on the lives of their patients and communities.

text: So, we had our slices served out, as if we were two thousand troops on a forced march instead of a man and boy at home; and we took gulps of milk and water, with apologetic countenances, from a jug on the dresser. Mrs. Joe was a very clean housekeeper, but had an exquisite art of making her cleanliness more uncomfortable and unacceptable than dirt itself. Her voice was usually high - pitched and shrewish, and she had a habit of finding fault with everything and everybody. The servant took away the soup - tureen. "Good Heavens!" thought Madame Magloire; "they have emptied it to the last drop. The bishop will have a good night's rest, with all that soup. He will not even have the indigestion." At this moment, the bishop reflected that if he wished to talk with this man, he must not allow him to exhaust himself in eating. text:
In effect the Church—and then the Churches—said to the novel, the play, the romance, and the ballad: “We are too busy cutting each other’s throats and inventing newer theologies, to bother any more about artistic productions. In the meantime we will remove the benefit of clergy that used to shield those who could manipulate a pen. You may write and compose what lay fictions you like, but the rack, the faggot or the pillory will attend you if you publish anything that we don’t like.” And the novelist, always a timid creature and in England avid of social consideration, was quick to take the hint. So Don Quichotte de la Mancha, the only gentleman produced by the genius of Cervantes, and indeed by all the genius of that age, had to become a pitiable lunatic. Yet it is impossible that a man of the perspicacity of the writer of that work could not have seen that the Don, wiping curds from his benign and tranquil countenance, was godlike in comparison to the crooks and gross peasants—the cats and monkeys!—that surrounded him. Nevertheless the Don must go!

With those Spaniards, then, the novel approached some sort of rendering of life and that sort of rendering was soon enough to make its appearance in England. It crossed the Bay of Biscay and the Channel with a picaresque work of a prodigious popularity in its day—Guzman d’Alfarache or the Story of a Rogue. Less picaresque in the true sense of being the strung-together life of a picaro or professional thief—less picaresque than the immortal Lazarillo de Tormes and less achingly tragic as a presentation of the life of the brothel and wine-shop than Celestina, the work of Hermann Alemannos, whose name betrays his Teutonic origin, was much more suited to the Anglo-Saxon taste than either one of the other three Spanish books that I have selected for mention.

text: The winter night in Hazel Moran’s New York apartment was loud—loud enough that she could hear the clatter of a streetcar outside her window and the distant laughter of partygoers from the bar downstairs, but the noise felt like a wall, thick and empty, keeping the quiet in instead of out. She sat on a threadbare velvet sofa, a half-full glass of rye whiskey in her hand and a crumpled cigarette pack beside her, her eyes fixed on the flickering glow of the floor lamp, its shade stained with a ring from an old martini glass. The apartment smelled of cigarette smoke and perfume—she’d sprayed a dash of her favorite scent that evening, hoping it would mask the smell of last night’s leftover takeout—and a fur coat, borrowed from a man she’d met at a club last week, lay draped over the arm of the sofa, its fur matted from being tossed in the corner. She thought of the day she’d first moved to New York—of the way she’d stared up at the skyscrapers, her suitcase in hand, thinking “This is it. This is where I’ll be happy,” of the way she’d danced until dawn at a speakeasy, surrounded by men who called her “darling” and “baby” but never asked her name, of the way she’d woken up the next morning in a stranger’s bed, her head throbbing and her hope a little smaller. She’d built a life of sorts, she thought—nights at clubs, days sleeping off hangovers, a rotation of men who bought her drinks and took her to dinners but never stayed long enough to hear her talk about the farm she’d grown up on, the sister she’d lost to the flu, the things that actually mattered. The streetcar rumbled past, its bells jangling, and she took a sip of whiskey, the burn sharp on her tongue. She set the glass down, running a finger over the cigarette pack—she’d promised herself she’d quit, again, tomorrow, but tonight felt like a night for breaking promises. She thought of Eddie, the man who’d left her last month, who’d said “You’re too much, Hazel. Too loud, too needy, too everything.” She’d laughed when he’d said it, but later, in the dark, she’d cried, because she knew he was right—not that she was too much, but that she was too empty, filling herself up with noise and attention because she was scared of what she’d find if she stopped.

text: My godmother lived in a handsome house in the clean and ancient town of Bretton. Her husband's family had been residents there for generations, and bore, indeed, the name of their birthplace—Bretton of Bretton: whether by coincidence, or because some remote ancestor had been a personage of sufficient importance to leave his name to his neighbourhood, I know not. When I was a girl I went to Bretton about twice a year, and well I liked the visit. The house and its inmates specially suited me. The large peaceful rooms, the well-arranged furniture, the clear wide windows, the balcony outside, looking down on a fine antique street, where the sun seemed always to shine—for my visits were in summer, or at least in bright weather—the great chairs, the deep settees, the curious cabinets, the pictures, the books, gave me a pleasure mixed with respect. Mrs. Bretton was a kind-hearted woman; she had a calm temper, a placid manner; she was not easily fretted, nor often strictly angry; but she expected to be obeyed, and her will was law. She had, moreover, a certain cast of intellect which I have never seen otherwise than accompanied with particular traits of character; she was logical, just, sensible; she had an exact memory, and was truthful. Her son, John Graham Bretton, was a handsome, faithless-looking youth of sixteen. I say faithless-looking, because I never read honesty in his face; and yet he was not a bad lad; his faults were the faults of his age; he was proud, but not in a bad sense; he was rather exacting, but not malignant; he was selfish, but not deliberately; he was careless, but not heartless. He expected much, and he gave little; but his expectations were the result of an unconscious estimate of his own deserts, and his gifts were the overflow of a superabundant vitality. He did not know what it was to be poor in spirit, to be weak in body, to be sad in heart; he had always been surrounded by comforts, his physical health was perfect, his spirits were ever gay. He had a good talents, but they were not cultivated; he had a fine person, but it was not disciplined; he had a kind heart, but it was not tried. In short, he was a boy—a spoiled boy—a boy who had been too much indulged, and who thought too well of himself; but he was not a bad boy, and I liked him. He was the only son of his mother, and she was a widow.

text: "Twist it, an' you'll choke 'm plentee," said Manuel, and the stranger grunted a ready affirmative. Buck had accepted the rope with quiet dignity. To be sure, it was an unwonted performance: but he had learned to trust in men he knew, and to give them credit for a wisdom that outreached his own. But when the ends of the rope were placed in the stranger's hands, he growled menacingly. He had merely intimated his displeasure, in his pride believing that to intimate was to command. But to his surprise the rope tightened around his neck, shutting off his breath. In quick rage he sprang at the man, who met him halfway, grappled him close by the throat, and with a deft twist threw him over on his back. Then the rope tightened mercilessly, while Buck struggled in a fury, his tongue lolling out of his mouth and his great chest panting futilely. Never in all his life had he been so vilely treated, and never in all his life had he been so angry. But his strength ebbed, his eyes glazed, and he knew nothing when the train was flagged and the two men threw him into the baggage car. The next he knew, he was dimly aware that his tongue was hurting and that he was being jolted along in some kind of a conveyance. The hoarse shriek of a locomotive whistling a crossing told him where he was. He had travelled too often with the Judge not to know the sensation of riding in a baggage car. He opened his eyes, and into them came the unbridled anger of a kidnapped king. The man sprang for his throat, but Buck was too quick for him. His jaws closed on the hand, nor did they relax till his senses were choked out of him once more. "Yep, has fits," the man said, hiding his mangled hand from the baggageman, who had been attracted by the sounds of struggle. "I'm takin' 'm up for the boss to 'Frisco. A crack dog-doctor there thinks that he can cure 'm." Concerning that night's ride, the man spoke most eloquently for himself, in a little shed back of a saloon on the San Francisco water front. "All I get is fifty for it," he grumbled; "an' I wouldn't do it over for a thousand, cold cash." His hand was wrapped in a bloody handkerchief, and the right trouser leg was ripped from knee to ankle. "How much did the other mug get?" the saloon-keeper demanded. "A hundred," was the reply. "Wouldn't take a sou less, so help me."

text: A river is a natural, flowing body of water that moves continuously from higher elevations (such as mountains or hills) to lower elevations, eventually emptying into a lake, sea, or ocean. Rivers are vital to life on Earth, providing fresh water for drinking, irrigation, and industrial use, supporting diverse ecosystems, and shaping the landscape through erosion and deposition. Rivers vary in size, from small streams that are only a few meters wide to large rivers like the Amazon, which is over 6,400 kilometers (4,000 miles) long and carries more water than any other river in the world. The course of a river is divided into three main sections: the upper course (source), where the river originates from springs, melting snow, or glaciers, and flows rapidly through narrow valleys with steep banks; the middle course, where the river widens, slows down, and meanders (curves) through floodplains; and the lower course (mouth), where the river becomes wider still, flows slowly, and deposits sediment to form deltas or estuaries. Rivers are home to a wide variety of plants and animals, including fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals, as well as aquatic plants like algae, water lilies, and reeds. These ecosystems depend on the river’s flow, water quality, and surrounding habitat for survival. For example, fish rely on the river’s current to find food and reproduce, while birds use the river’s banks for nesting and feeding. Rivers have played a crucial role in human history and civilization, as many ancient civilizations, such as the Egyptian civilization along the Nile River and the Mesopotamian civilization between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, developed along riverbanks due to the fertile soil and access to water for agriculture. Today, rivers continue to be important for human societies, providing water for crops, generating hydroelectric power, facilitating transportation, and offering recreational activities like fishing, boating, and swimming. However, rivers face numerous threats, including pollution from industrial waste, agricultural runoff, and plastic waste, which contaminates the water and harms aquatic life. Deforestation along riverbanks increases erosion, leading to sedimentation that clogs the river and reduces water flow. Overuse of water for irrigation and industrial purposes also depletes river levels, threatening ecosystems and human communities that depend on the river for water. Conservation efforts are underway to protect rivers, including reducing pollution, restoring riverbanks, and implementing sustainable water management practices. By protecting rivers, we can ensure that they continue to provide fresh water, support ecosystems, and benefit human societies for generations to come. Rivers are a symbol of life and movement, a natural force that connects landscapes, supports biodiversity, and shapes the world we live in.

text: A volcano is a geological structure where molten rock, ash, gas, and other materials from deep inside the Earth erupt through the planet’s surface, creating mountains, craters, and vast landscapes over thousands or millions of years. Volcanoes form primarily along tectonic plate boundaries, where plates collide, separate, or slide past each other, allowing magma from the mantle to rise upward and accumulate beneath the crust. When pressure becomes too great, eruptions occur, releasing lava, volcanic ash, cinders, blocks, and toxic gases such as sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Volcanoes vary widely in shape and behavior: shield volcanoes have broad, gentle slopes formed by fluid lava flows, while stratovolcanoes are steep, conical, and often associated with explosive eruptions. Some volcanoes are active, meaning they have erupted recently or may erupt soon; others are dormant, having not erupted for a long time but still capable of activity; and extinct volcanoes are unlikely to erupt again. Eruptions can be slow and peaceful, with lava quietly flowing downhill, or sudden and violent, sending ash clouds kilometers into the sky and triggering pyroclastic flows that destroy everything in their path. Volcanic ash can travel globally, affecting weather, air travel, and sunlight absorption. Over time, volcanic activity creates new land, enriches soil with minerals, and forms islands, mountains, and plateaus. However, eruptions also pose severe hazards, including lava flows, ashfall, poisonous gases, mudflows called lahars, and volcanic tsunamis. Scientists monitor volcanoes using seismometers, gas sensors, thermal cameras, and satellite imagery to predict eruptions and protect nearby communities. Despite their destructive power, volcanoes are essential planetary processes that shape Earth’s surface, recycle materials, and support unique ecosystems adapted to extreme conditions. They also hold cultural and spiritual meaning in many societies, often featured in myths, legends, and religious beliefs as symbols of creation, destruction, and divine power.

text: "Ether," Mr. Tench muttered, finally remembering. He let his lower lip hang loose, feeling gloomy, and began counting the cases of Montezuma beer stacked on the quay. A hundred and forty cases, twelve bottles each. Twelve times a hundred and forty—he gathered another mouthful of spit—twelve times forty was four hundred and eighty. "My God, that's a lot," he said to himself in English. Twelve hundred plus four hundred and eighty was sixteen hundred and eighty bottles. He spat again and stared at a young girl standing at the bow of the General Obregon. Her slender figure stirred a faint interest in him. The women here were mostly fat, with brown eyes and invariably a gold tooth. A fresh, delicate girl like this was a rarity. "What did you say?" a voice asked softly in English. Mr. Tench spun round. "Are you English?" he asked in surprise, but when he saw the small, haggard face with a three-day growth of beard, he corrected himself. "Do you speak English?" The man nodded. "A little." He stood stiffly in the shade, a small attaché case in one hand and a novel tucked under his arm. There was a garish illustration of a love scene peeking out from between the pages. His round, goldfish-like eyes gave him an air of unstable cheerfulness, as if he had been celebrating his birthday alone. Mr. Tench cleared his throat. "What did I say?" He couldn't recall a word. "You said, 'My God, that's a lot.'" "What did I mean by that?" He glanced up at the unforgiving sky. A buzzard hovered motionless above, a silent observer. "Oh, I suppose I was talking about the girl. You don't see many pretty women here. One or two a year, perhaps." "She's too young." "Oh, I didn't mean anything by it," Mr. Tench said wearily. "Just looking. I've lived alone here for fifteen years." "In this town?" "Round about." They fell silent. Time dragged on, and the shadow of the customs house inched closer to the riverbank. The buzzard shifted its position slightly, like the black hand of an old clock. "Did you come on that ship?" Mr. Tench asked. "No." "Waiting to go on it?" The small man hesitated, then replied evasively, "Just watching. Do you think it will sail soon?" "It's bound for Veracruz," Mr. Tench said. "Sails in a few hours."

text: None of them knew the color of the sky. Their eyes glanced level, and were fastened upon the waves that swept toward them. These waves were of the hue of slate, save for the tops, which were of foaming white, and all of the men knew the colors of the sea. The horizon narrowed and widened, and dipped and rose, and at all times its edge was jagged with waves that seemed thrust up in points like rocks. Many a man ought to have a bath-tub larger than the boat which here rode upon the sea. These waves were most wrongfully and barbarously abrupt and tall, and each froth-top was a problem in small boat navigation. The cook squatted in the bottom and looked with both eyes at the six inches of gunwale which separated him from the ocean. His sleeves were rolled over his fat forearms, and the two flaps of his unbuttoned vest dangled as he bent to bail out the boat. Often he said: 'Gawd! That was a narrow clip.' As he remarked it he invariably gazed eastward over the broken sea. The oiler, steering with one of the two oars in the boat, sometimes raised himself suddenly to keep clear of water that swirled in over the stern. It was a thin little oar and it seemed often ready to snap. The correspondent, pulling at the other oar, watched the waves and wondered why he was there. The injured captain, lying in the bow, was at this time buried in that profound dejection and indifference which comes, temporarily at least, to even the bravest and most enduring when, willy nilly, the firm fails, the army loses, the ship goes down. The mind of the master of a vessel is rooted deep in the timbers of her, though he command for a day or a decade, and this captain had on him the stern impression of a scene in the greys of dawn of seven turned faces, and later a stump of a top-mast with a white ball on it that slashed to and fro at the waves, went low and lower, and down. Thereafter there was something strange in his voice. Although steady, it was deep with mourning, and of a quality beyond oration or tears.

text: “My boy,” said the landlord, “you’ll have the nightmare to a dead sartainty.” “Landlord,” I whispered, “that aint the harpooneer is it?” “Oh, no,” said he, looking a sort of diabolically funny, “the harpooneer is a dark complexioned chap. He never eats dumplings, he don’t—he eats nothing but steaks, and he likes ’em rare.” “The devil he does,” says I. “Where is that harpooneer? Is he here?” “He’ll be here afore long,” was the answer. I could not help it, but I began to feel suspicious of this “dark complexioned” harpooneer. At any rate, I made up my mind that if it so turned out that we should sleep together, he must undress and get into bed before I did. Supper over, the company went back to the bar-room, when, knowing not what else to do with myself, I resolved to spend the rest of the evening as a looker on. Presently a rioting noise was heard without. Starting up, the landlord cried, “That’s the Grampus’s crew. I seed her reported in the offing this morning; a three years’ voyage, and a full ship. Hurrah, boys; now we’ll have the latest news from the Feegees.” A tramping of sea boots was heard in the entry; the door was flung open, and in rolled a wild set of mariners enough. Enveloped in their shaggy watch coats, and with their heads muffled in woollen comforters, all bedarned and ragged, and their beards stiff with icicles, they seemed an eruption of bears from Labrador. They had just landed from their boat, and this was the first house they entered. No wonder, then, that they made a straight wake for the whale’s mouth—the bar—when the wrinkled little old Jonah, there officiating, soon poured them out brimmers all round. One complained of a bad cold in his head, upon which Jonah mixed him a pitch-like potion of gin and molasses, which he swore was a sovereign cure for all colds and catarrhs whatsoever, never mind of how long standing, or whether caught off the coast of Labrador, or on the weather side of an ice-island.

text: Now in getting under weigh, the station generally occupied by the pilot is the forward part of the ship. And here Bildad, who, with Peleg, be it known, in addition to his other officers, was one of the licensed pilots of the port—he being suspected to have got himself made a pilot in order to save the Nantucket pilot-fee to all the ships he was concerned in, for he never piloted any other craft—Bildad, I say, might now be seen actively engaged in looking over the bows for the approaching anchor, and at intervals singing what seemed a dismal stave of psalmody, to cheer the hands at the windlass, who roared forth some sort of a chorus about the girls in Booble Alley, with hearty good will. Nevertheless, not three days previous, Bildad had told them that no profane songs would be allowed on board the Pequod, particularly in getting under weigh; and Charity, his sister, had placed a small choice copy of Watts in each seaman’s berth. Meantime, overseeing the other part of the ship, Captain Peleg ripped and swore astern in the most frightful manner. I almost thought he would sink the ship before the anchor could be got up; involuntarily I paused on my handspike, and told Queequeg to do the same, thinking of the perils we both ran, in starting on the voyage with such a devil for a pilot. I was comforting myself, however, with the thought that in pious Bildad might be found some salvation, spite of his seven hundred and seventy-seventh lay; when I felt a sudden sharp poke in my rear, and turning round, was horrified at the apparition of Captain Peleg in the act of withdrawing his leg from my immediate vicinity. That was my first kick. “Is that the way they heave in the marchant service?” he roared. “Spring, thou sheep-head; spring, and break thy backbone! Why don’t ye spring, I say, all of ye—spring! Quohog! spring, thou chap with the red whiskers; spring there, Scotch-cap; spring, thou green pants. Spring, I say, all of ye, and spring your eyes out!” And so saying, he moved along the windlass, here and there using his leg very freely, while imperturbable Bildad kept leading off with his psalmody. Thinks I, Captain Peleg must have been drinking something to-day.

text:
PYOTR SEMYONITCH, the bank manager, together with the book-keeper, his assistant, and two members of the board, were taken in the night to prison. The day after the upheaval the merchant Avdeyev, who was one of the committee of auditors, was sitting with his friends in the shop saying:
“So it is God’s will, it seems. There is no escaping your fate. Here to-day we are eating caviare and to-morrow, for aught we know, it will be prison, beggary, or maybe death. Anything may happen. Take Pyotr Semyonitch, for instance. . . .”
He spoke, screwing up his drunken eyes, while his friends went on drinking, eating caviare, and listening. Having described the disgrace and helplessness of Pyotr Semyonitch, who only the day before had been powerful and respected by all, Avdeyev went on with a sigh:
“The tears of the mouse come back to the cat. Serve them right, the scoundrels! They could steal, the rooks, so let them answer for it!”
“You’d better look out, Ivan Danilitch, that you don’t catch it too!” one of his friends observed.
“What has it to do with me?”
“Why, they were stealing, and what were you auditors thinking about? I’ll be bound, you signed the audit.”
“It’s all very well to talk!” laughed Avdeyev: “Signed it, indeed! They used to bring the accounts to my shop and I signed them. As though I understood! Give me anything you like, I’ll scrawl my name to it. If you were to write that I murdered someone I’d sign my name to it. I haven’t time to go into it; besides, I can’t see without my spectacles.”
After discussing the failure of the bank and the fate of Pyotr Semyonitch, Avdeyev and his friends went to eat pie at the house of a friend whose wife was celebrating her name-day. At the name-day party everyone was discussing the bank failure. Avdeyev was more excited than anyone, and declared that he had long foreseen the crash and knew two years before that things were not quite right at the bank. While they were eating pie he described a dozen illegal operations which had come to his knowledge.
“If you knew, why did you not give information?” asked an officer who was present.
“I wasn’t the only one: the whole town knew of it,” laughed Avdeyev. “Besides, I haven’t the time to hang about the law courts, damn them!”
He had a nap after the pie and then had dinner, then had another nap, then went to the evening service at the church of which he was a warden; after the service he went back to the name-day party and played preference till midnight. Everything seemed satisfactory.
But when Avdeyev hurried home after midnight the cook, who opened the door to him, looked pale, and was trembling so violently that she could not utter a word. His wife, Elizaveta Trofimovna, a flabby, overfed woman, with her grey hair hanging loose, was sitting on the sofa in the drawing-room quivering all over, and vacantly rolling her eyes as though she were drunk. Her elder son, Vassily, a high-school boy, pale too, and extremely agitated, was fussing round her with a glass of water.
“What’s the matter?” asked Avdeyev, and looked angrily sideways at the stove (his family was constantly being upset by the fumes from it).
“The examining magistrate has just been with the police,” answered Vassily; “they’ve made a search.”
Avdeyev looked round him. The cupboards, the chests, the tables—everything bore traces of the recent search. For a minute Avdeyev stood motionless as though petrified, unable to understand; then his whole inside quivered and seemed to grow heavy, his left leg went numb, and, unable to endure his trembling, he lay down flat on the sofa. He felt his inside heaving and his rebellious left leg tapping against the back of the sofa.
In the course of two or three minutes he recalled the whole of his past, but could not remember any crime deserving of the attention of the police.
“It’s all nonsense,” he said, getting up. “They must have slandered me. To-morrow I must lodge a complaint of their having dared to do such a thing.”
Next morning after a sleepless night Avdeyev, as usual, went to his shop. His customers brought him the news that during the night the public prosecutor had sent the deputy manager and the head-clerk to prison as well. This news did not disturb Avdeyev. He was convinced that he had been slandered, and that if he were to lodge a complaint to-day the examining magistrate would get into trouble for the search of the night before.
Between nine and ten o’clock he hurried to the town hall to see the secretary, who was the only educated man in the town council.
“Vladimir Stepanitch, what’s this new fashion?” he said, bending down to the secretary’s ear. “People have been stealing, but how do I come in? What has it to do with me? My dear fellow,” he whispered, “there has been a search at my house last night! Upon my word! Have they gone crazy? Why touch me?”
“Because one shouldn’t be a sheep,” the secretary answered calmly. “Before you sign you ought to look.”

text: We could never go back again, that much was certain. The past was still too close to us. And the things we tried hard to forget and put behind us would come creeping back into our minds, unbidden, and that sense of fear, that strange uneasiness, the suspicion that was gone with the wind, would become tangible again, like a living thing, as real as the chairs and the table in this room. His patience was amazing. He never complained, never uttered a word of regret, even when he thought of the past, and I was sure he thought of it often, though he would not admit it to me. How could he hide it from me? Sometimes he would sit for hours, lost in thought, his face expressionless, as if a mask had fallen over it, hiding all his emotions. At other times, he would chain-smoke, one cigarette after another, the ash falling unnoticed on the floor. And then there were the times when he would talk, talk rapidly and nervously, about nothing in particular, as if trying to drive away some inner demon. I had read somewhere that every couple who has been through a great ordeal comes out of it stronger and more noble, and that they should be grateful for the trial by fire that has made them what they are. There was some truth in that, I supposed, but we had had our fill of drama and excitement. I would have given anything for a quiet, uneventful life, a life without fear or suspicion. Happiness, I had learned, was not a possession to be prized, it was a state of mind, a mood. We were happy, in a way, but there was always a shadow hanging over us, a sense of foreboding that we could not shake off. We lived in a small inn, a dull and uninteresting place, but it suited us well. The food was bad, the service was indifferent, but we did not care. We had each other, and that was all that mattered. We avoided the big hotels, for we knew that we would meet people there who knew us, who would ask questions and make comments that we did not want to hear. We preferred the anonymity of the small inn, the simplicity of our life there.

text: The autumn night in Ifemelu’s Brooklyn apartment by the window was crisp—crisp enough that the air carried the faint smell of roasted chestnuts from the street vendor below and the distant honk of a yellow taxi, mixing with the soft hum of her neighbor’s jazz radio. She sat on a mismatched armchair (thrifted from a Queens store, its upholstery faded to a warm beige), a silver laptop in her hands (open to her blog “Raceteenth or Various Observations About American Blacks (Those Formerly Known as Negroes) by a Non-American Black”) and a mug of hibiscus tea beside her, her eyes fixed on the skyline, where the Empire State Building glowed red against the dark, like a lone candle in the night. The apartment smelled of jollof rice (she’d cooked a pot that evening, the spicy aroma clinging to her clothes) and sandalwood (a candle she’d brought from Lagos, its wick short from use), and a Ankara-print scarf—gifted by her mother before she left Nigeria—lay draped over the laptop, its bright patterns a stark contrast to the muted room. She thought of the day she’d arrived in New York—of the way the customs officer had stared at her passport, his eyebrow raised like he didn’t believe she belonged, of the way her cousin Dike had picked her up from the airport, chattering about his new job at a tech startup, of the way she’d walked down Broadway that first night, feeling both invisible and hypervisible, like her skin color was a sign that said “foreigner, outsider, not one of us.” She’d built a life here, she thought—written her blog that people read, made friends with fellow Nigerians and Americans alike, learned to navigate the subway and the unspoken rules of “polite” racism—but there were nights like this, when the jazz from next door sounded too foreign, when the hibiscus tea tasted less like home than she remembered, when she missed the sound of her father’s laughter and the way her mother sang hymns while cooking. A gust of wind rattled the window, and her scarf slipped off the laptop. She set the computer down, reaching to tuck the scarf around her neck—its fabric soft against her skin, a reminder of the markets in Lagos, of the women selling Ankara prints from wooden stalls, of the way her mother had said “Never forget where you come from, Ifemelu. Your roots are your strength.” She thought of Blaine, her American boyfriend, of the way he’d argued with her about her blog, saying “You’re too harsh on this country. It’s not all racism,” of the way he’d held her when she’d cried after a stranger called her “exotic” on the street, like she was a plant, not a person. She loved him, but he didn’t understand—not really, not the way someone who’d grown up in a country where your race didn’t define every interaction could understand.

It was easy enough out there, yet even in imagination his skin was wet and his mouth was dry. Even if the man slept, there was the dog. He must risk letting out the sheep. He covered the blade of the axe and went in a circuit to the sheep, and got over the yard on the side opposite to the hut. They rushed from him and huddled together, leaving him, although stooping, exposed. He had calculated for this, but not for the effect upon himself. Could they in the hut see him, he would be no match for the dog even with the axe. Heedlessly, fear-driven, he rushed to where he could see the door, regardless of exposing himself. Nothing counted now, but that the dog or the old man should not steal upon him unawares.

The door was still closed. No call for “Warder!” came from it, though he stood there a conspicuous object. While he watched he saw an ewe lamb make for the hut’s shelter. He stooped, still watching, and listened, but could hear nothing. He crept forward and loosened the hurdles. Never were they noisier, he was sure. He knew that the sheep would not go through while he was there. He crept away, but although the leader noted the freed exit, he and those he led were creatures of habit. None were hungry, and they were unused to feeding at night, though in the morning came man and dog never so early they were waiting.

Round the yard and past the gateway he drove them again and again. He began to feel impotently frenzied in the fear that the extraordinary lightness meant that daylight must be near. Every moment he persuaded himself that he could see more plainly. He held out his one hand and was convinced.

He straightened himself, rushed among them, caught one, and ran it kicking through the opening. It came back the moment he freed it. However it served his purpose, for as he crouched there, baffled, he unexpectedly saw them file out. Then they rushed through in an impatient struggling crowd, each fearing to be last with this invader.

When he “barrowed” out the first, he had kept his eyes on the hut, and had seen an old ewe and lamb run to it and bunt the closed door. But if there was any movement inside, the noise of the nearer sheep killed it.

text: The streets around Barchester Cathedral were narrow and winding, paved with cobblestones that glistened with the morning rain, reflecting the gray sky above. On either side stood tall, old houses with gabled roofs and leaded windows, their walls covered in ivy that had grown thick and untrimmed over the years. A few small shops lined the way—an apothecary with jars of colored liquids in the window, a baker's with the smell of warm bread drifting out, and a bookseller's whose door was propped open, revealing shelves crammed with leather-bound volumes. At the end of the street, the cathedral loomed, its great stone tower rising high above the rooftops, its stained-glass windows dulled by the overcast sky. A group of choristers in white surplices hurried past, their voices blending with the sound of a bell tolling from the tower. Near the cathedral gate, an old beggar sat on a stone step, wrapped in a tattered cloak, holding out a tin cup that clinked softly when a coin was dropped in. A gentle breeze stirred, carrying the scent of incense from the cathedral's open doors and the faint smell of wet earth from the churchyard nearby. A woman pushing a pram walked slowly, pausing to look at the flowers displayed outside a florist's shop—bunches of daffodils and tulips, their bright yellow and pink petals standing out against the gray day. A black cat slunk along the wall, its fur matted with rain, and disappeared into an alleyway. As the morning wore on, the rain stopped, and a pale sun broke through the clouds, casting weak light on the cobblestones. The choristers returned, laughing and chatting, and the beggar tucked his cup into his cloak, standing up to stretch his legs. The shops grew busier, with customers coming and going, and the sound of voices—soft and cheerful—filled the air. It was a street of quiet charm, where the old and the everyday blended together, as they had for centuries in the shadow of the cathedral.

text: Greek moussaka is a quintessential layered casserole, a dish that embodies comfort with every rich, hearty bite. Its most iconic feature is a goldenbrown top crust—formed by a thick layer of béchamel sauce that bakes to a subtle crunch—with edges that turn slightly crispy and bubbly, inviting you to dig in. The magic of moussaka lies in its distinct, flavorful layers, each prepared to perfection:  First, tender ground meat traditionally lamb for deep, gamey richness, or beef for a milder twist is cooked with diced tomatoes, finely chopped onions, and a blend of Greek spices oregano, cinnamon, and a pinch of cloves until it forms a savory, brown filling—juicy but not greasy, with tomatoes breaking down to add depth.  Next, slices of eggplant: peeled and cut into thick rounds, then roasting until soft and creamy roasting removes their bitter sap and concentrates their earthy flavor. These slices often have a subtle purpletinged edge, adding a pop of color against the meat and sauce.  Binding it all together is a thick, luxuriously creamy béchamel sauce—made with butter, flour, milk, and a whisper of nutmeg—poured over the layers to create a smooth, white blanket that turns golden in the oven. Visually, moussaka is undeniably hearty and indulgent: the deep brown meat layer peeks through gaps in the eggplant, the purpletinged eggplant adds warmth, and the goldenbrown béchamel top glistens, making it a showstopper on any dinner table. When sliced, the layers hold together beautifully, forming a cohesive dish that’s as satisfying to look at as it is to eat. Tastewise, it’s a symphony of comforting flavors:  The seasoned meat delivers bold savory notes, with cinnamon adding a subtle warmth that sets Greek moussaka apart.  The eggplant brings an earthy depth, its soft texture blending seamlessly with the meat.  The béchamel is rich and creamy, with a hint of nutmeg that adds a delicate nutty undertone—cutting through the meat’s savoriness and balancing the dish’s richness. Every bite feels like a hug, making it the ultimate comforting meal. Culturally, moussaka is a cornerstone of Greek home cooking. It’s the kind of dish prepared for family dinners, holiday feasts like Easter or Christmas, or to welcome guests—slowcooked with love and served in generous portions. It’s often paired with a simple side salad dressed with olive oil and lemon to cut through its richness, letting the casserole’s flavors shine. Its preparation relies on five intentional steps, each critical to building its signature layers and flavor: 1. Roasting: Eggplant slices are tossed in olive oil, spread on a baking sheet, and roasted until soft and golden. This step eliminates bitterness and ensures the eggplant doesn’t turn mushy in the casserole. 2. Browning: Ground meat is cooked in a skillet until browned, then onions are added and sautéed until soft. Tomatoes, spices, and a splash of broth are stirred in, and the mixture simmers until thick—creating a flavorful base layer. 3. Making: The béchamel sauce is made by melting butter, whisking in flour to form a roux, then slowly adding milk while stirring constantly. A pinch of nutmeg and salt are added, and the sauce is cooked until it thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon. 4. Layering: In a baking dish, a thin layer of meat is spread first, followed by overlapping eggplant slices, then a pour of béchamel. This sequence is repeated ending with a thick layer of béchamel to build the casserole’s height and texture. 5. Baking: The moussaka is baked in a preheated oven until the top is goldenbrown and the sauce is bubbly about 3040 minutes. It’s left to rest for 10 minutes after baking—this helps the layers set, making it easier to slice into cohesive pieces.

“You, no doubt, know more than I can gather from the bald, rather cryptic message that I have brought you. I mean that it conveys to you much more,” I said, bewildered at the discovery that Angela, the Little Countess, and the girl criminal were one and the same. But I kept my own counsel and allowed him to know nothing.

“Yes, much. I know exactly what she means.” Then he eagerly inquired about her and the circumstances in which we had met. To all his questions I replied quite frankly. So dejected and despairing was the young fellow that I felt sorry for him. Surely he could not be acting!

I knew that I was Cupid’s messenger, yet the whole circumstances were so romantic and mysterious that I felt an intense interest in them all. The one thing that really puzzled me most was the reason Lady Kingscliffe had preserved the secret of the girl’s identity.

The young man Owen had sunk into a chair, and was sitting with his eyes fixed across the room, seeing nothing.

“I am absolutely forbidden to write to her, eh?” he asked, utterly crushed.

“That was the message I was to deliver to you. She dare not write—and she will be in peril if you send her a letter. She said that you would quite understand.”

“Understand?” he cried suddenly, his eyes gleaming. “Understand? Yes, I understand. I—I understand—only—too—well,” he added, with the bitterness of despair in his voice. “Forgive me, Mr. Hipwell,” he craved next second. “I—I’m much obliged to you for troubling to come here. If you knew—knew what all this means to both of us—if you knew the truth, you would understand.”

“But can’t you tell me? I’m so completely in the dark,” I said, absolutely mystified and full of eagerness to obtain a clue to the mystery.

“No,” he replied in a low voice. “I have to respect the wishes of Lisely.” Then after a pause, he muttered to himself:

“So she is in Italy! Why, in heaven’s name, did she venture there? It was foolish—very foolish and dangerous! But I suppose there is some motive for it. There is always a motive in a woman’s fancies.”

“Remember,” I said, “that in sending you that message she is acting against her will.”

“I know. I pity her. Poor Lisely! She is acting under compulsion. Some people are born to despair. We are of those. And she is in Rome! I wonder why? I was there with her a year ago when—when I thought—I believed—I dreamed——”

He clenched his fists fiercely and, springing from his chair, crossed to the window.

“Forgive me, Mr. Hipwell,” he said again.

text: The midnight wind whipped through the open window of Sal Paradise's beat-up Ford, carrying the smell of diesel from the passing trucks and the faint, burnt scent of coffee from the gas station down the road. He pulled over to the gravel lot, killing the engine, and leaned back against the steering wheel—his neck ached from driving for six hours straight, his jeans stiff with road dust, and his pocket empty except for a crumpled dollar bill and a half-smoked pack of cigarettes. He paused, watching a semi-truck rumble past, its headlights cutting through the dark like two bright knives. For a second, he wondered where it was going—New York? California? Somewhere he'd never heard of? He thought of Dean Moriarty, his friend who'd left Denver last month with nothing but a backpack and a dream, and felt a twist in his stomach. Dean talked about 'finding the truth on the road,' but all Sal felt lately was lost. Lost in the miles, lost in the noise, lost in the way every town looked the same—same gas stations, same diners, same people staring at him like he didn't belong. He got out of the car, his boots crunching on the gravel, and walked toward the gas station. The door jingled when he pushed it open, and the cashier—a old man with a gray beard—looked up from his newspaper. 'Coffee?' he said, nodding toward a pot on the counter. Sal nodded, sliding his dollar across the table. 'Black, please.' The man poured the coffee, its steam fogging his glasses, and set it down. 'You headed somewhere?' he asked. Sal shrugged. 'Nowhere specific,' he said. 'Just... on the road.' He sat in a booth by the window, sipping the coffee—it was bitter, too hot, but it woke him up. Outside, a family pulled in in a station wagon, their kids yelling in the backseat. Sal watched them, their laughter loud and warm, and felt a pang in his chest. He hadn't talked to his mother in months, hadn't had a real home since he left Boston. Was this what he wanted? To keep driving, keep moving, never staying long enough to care about anyone? The old man finished his newspaper and stood up, stretching. 'Last call for coffee,' he said. 'I'm closing up.' Sal nodded, draining his cup. He walked back to his car, the night air cold on his face, and slid into the driver's seat. He turned the key, and the engine sputtered to life. For a second, he thought about driving back to Boston, about calling his mother, about settling down. But then he saw the highway ahead, dark and endless, and something in his chest loosened. He pulled out of the lot, merging into the stream of trucks. The radio played a country song, static cutting through the lyrics, but he didn't turn it off. He thought of Dean, of the letters he'd written—'The road's where the soul is, Sal'—and smiled. Maybe Dean was right. Maybe the truth wasn't in a place. Maybe it was in the driving, in the looking, in the way the wind felt when you rolled down the window and let it hit your face.

text: The little town of Verrières can pass for one of the prettiest in Franche - Comté. Its white houses with their pointed red - tiled roofs stretch along the slope of a hill, whose slightest undulations are marked by groups of vigorous chestnuts. The Doubs flows to within some hundred feet above its fortifications, which were built long ago by the Spaniards, and are now in ruins. Verrières is sheltered on the north by a high mountain which is one of the branches of the Jura. The jagged peaks of the Verra are covered with snow from the beginning of the October frosts. A torrent which rushes down from the mountains traverses Verrières before throwing itself into the Doubs, and supplies the motive power for a great number of saw mills. The industry is very simple, and secures a certain prosperity to the majority of the inhabitants who are more peasant than bourgeois. It is not, however, the wood saws which have enriched this little town. It is the manufacture of painted tiles, called Mulhouse tiles, that is responsible for that general affluence which has caused the façades of nearly all the houses in Verrières to be rebuilt since the fall of Napoleon. One has scarcely entered the town, before one is stunned by the din of a strident machine of terrifying aspect. Twenty heavy hammers which fall with a noise that makes the paved floor tremble, are lifted up by a wheel set in motion by the torrent. Each of these hammers manufactures every day I don't know how many thousands of nails. The little pieces of iron which are rapidly transformed into nails by these enormous hammers, are put in position by fresh pretty young girls. This labour so rough at first sight is one of the industries which most surprises the traveller who penetrates for the first time the mountains which separate France and Helvetia. If when he enters Verrières, the traveller asks who owns this fine nail factory which deafens everybody who goes up the Grande - Rue, he is answered in a drawling tone " Eh! it belongs to M. the Mayor."

Every time Dymov, Kiruha and Styopka pulled out the net they could be seen fumbling about in the mud in it, putting some things into the pail and throwing other things away; sometimes they passed something that was in the net from hand to hand, examined it inquisitively, then threw that, too, away.
“What is it?” they shouted to them from the bank.“It’s full!” he shouted, breathing hard. “Give us another!”
Yegorushka looked into the pail: it was full. A young pike poked its ugly nose out of the water, and there were swarms of crayfish and little fish round about it. Yegorushka put his hand down to the bottom and stirred up the water; the pike vanished under the crayfish and a perch and a tench swam to the surface instead of it. Vassya, too, looked into the pail. His eyes grew moist and his face looked as caressing as before when he saw the fox. He took something out of the pail, put it to his mouth and began chewing it.
“Mates,” said Styopka in amazement, “Vassya is eating a live gudgeon! Phoo!”
“It’s not a gudgeon, but a minnow,” Vassya answered calmly, still munching.
He took a fish’s tail out of his mouth, looked at it caressingly, and put it back again. While he was chewing and crunching with his teeth it seemed to Yegorushka that he saw before him something not human. Vassya’s swollen chin, his lustreless eyes, his extraordinary sharp sight, the fish’s tail in his mouth, and the caressing friendliness with which he crunched the gudgeon made him like an animal.
Yegorushka felt dreary beside him. And the fishing was over, too. He walked about beside the waggons, thought a little, and, feeling bored, strolled off to the village.
Not long afterwards he was standing in the church, and with his forehead leaning on somebody’s back, listened to the singing of the choir. The service was drawing to a close. Yegorushka did not understand church singing and did not care for it. He listened a little, yawned, and began looking at the backs and heads before him. In one head, red and wet from his recent bathe, he recognized Emelyan. The back of his head had been cropped in a straight line higher than is usual; the hair in front had been cut unbecomingly high, and Emelyan’s ears stood out like two dock leaves, and seemed to feel themselves out of place. Looking at the back of his head and his ears, Yegorushka, for some reason, thought that Emelyan was probably very unhappy. He remembered the way he conducted with his hands, his husky voice, his timid air when he was bathing, and felt intense pity for him. He longed to say something friendly to him.

text:
By the time the thirty years or so that stretched between 1790 and 1820 had impinged on the world it had gradually become evident, on the Continent at least, that so many differing codes of morality could synchronize in the same era, in the same nation and even in the same small community—it had become so evident that if Simeon Stylites and Oliver Cromwell were saints, Jesus Christ and Gautama Buddha and several Chinese philosophers were very good men, that the Novel, if it was at all to express its day, must express itself through figures less amateurishly blacked than Uriah Heep and less sedulously whited than the Cherryble brothers.

Changes in literary methods are brought about very slowly and permeate more slowly still into the taste of the more or less unlettered classes who make up the bulk of the desirable readers for an author. As a rule the process begins with the younger writers who find tiresome or ludicrous the accepted work of their day; a little later the more experienced of readers, tiring in their turn of accepted methods in the works they consume, turn with relief to the younger writers, the professorial and established critics still thundering violently against the younger schools. For, everywhere but in England, schools establish themselves as soon as restlessnesses betray themselves in artistic circles. The more experienced readers, in spite of the critics, spreading abroad amongst the larger classes of the relatively unlettered the taste for the newer modes, at first that larger class become converts and then the professional critics whose bread and butter depends on their following the public taste. So a school is established and for a time holds its own. Then it gives place to other modes.

That is the quite invariable process with all the products and all the methods, of all the arts. But naturally, as the arts grow older, their practitioners have a better chance of evolving newer and sounder methods, for the number of their predecessors has inevitably increased. Bunyan must evolve his method for himself; Defoe could study Bunyan; Richardson, Bunyan and Defoe; Diderot, Richardson and his predecessors; Stendhal could draw on the experience of four generations; Flaubert on that of five; Conrad on that of six.

Bracknell had spent months hunting him, only to lose his trail in the northern woods. The fugitive leaned against the doorframe, his cane tapping the floor. “You’re not here for me. Not with that look in your eye. You’re chasing someone.” He nodded at the journal in Bracknell’s hand. “Her, isn’t it? Elizabeth Black.” Bracknell’s hand tightened around his pistol. “How do you know her name?” “Thomas told me.” Kuna Dick’s smile faded. “We served together, back before I became a ‘fugitive.’ Funny how the army calls you a traitor when you refuse to let them hang an innocent man.” He stepped aside, gesturing to the small room behind him. “Come in. We shouldn’t talk out here. The French scouts downstairs have ears like foxes.” Bracknell hesitated, then stepped inside. The room was sparse—just a cot, a small table, and a window covered by a tattered blanket. Kuna Dick closed the door, then lowered himself onto the cot with a wince. “Got shot in the leg three days ago,” he explained, nodding at his splint. “French patrol. They were hunting Thomas. Said he’d stolen plans for Fort Williams. Thomas found me hiding in an old trapper’s cabin, gave me these supplies before he left to find Elizabeth.” Bracknell pulled out the letter from Thomas and the journal. “He wrote that Elizabeth has the real plans. That the French are going to attack Fort Williams at dawn.”

text: People whose attention has never been specially called to the raison d'être of house-furnishing sometimes conclude that because a thing is unusual it is artistic, or rather that through some occult process the most ordinary things become artistic by being used in an unusual manner; while others, warned by the visible results of this theory of furnishing, infer that everything artistic is unpractical. In the Anglo-Saxon mind beauty is not spontaneously born of material wants, as it is with the Latin races. We have to make things beautiful; they do not grow so of themselves. The necessity of making this effort has caused many people to put aside the whole problem of beauty and fitness in household decoration as something mysterious and incomprehensible to the uninitiated. The architect and decorator are often aware that they are regarded by their clients as the possessors of some strange craft like black magic or astrology. This fatalistic attitude has complicated the simple and intelligible process of house-furnishing, and has produced much of the discomfort which causes so many rooms to be shunned by everybody in the house, in spite (or rather because) of all the money and ingenuity expended on their arrangement. Yet to penetrate the mystery of house-furnishing it is only necessary to analyze one satisfactory room and to notice wherein its charm lies. To the fastidious eye it will, of course, be found in fitness of proportion, in the proper use of each moulding and in the harmony of all the decorative processes; and even to those who think themselves indifferent to such detail, much of the sense of restfulness and comfort produced by certain rooms depends on the due adjustment of their fundamental parts. Different rooms minister to different wants and while a room may be made very livable without satisfying any but the material requirements of its inmates it is evident that the perfect room should combine these qualities with what corresponds to them in a higher order of needs. At present, however, the subject deals only with the material livableness of a room, and this will generally be found to consist in the position of the doors and fireplace, the accessibility of the windows, the arrangement of the furniture, the privacy of the room and the absence of the superfluous.

"Why have you so many clocks in your room?"

"I mend clocks," he answered. "I take the work up between times, on holidays, or when I can't sleep."

"So if my watch goes wrong I can bring it to you to be repaired?" Anna Akimovna asked, laughing.

"To be sure, I will do it with pleasure," said Pimenov, and there was an expression of tender devotion in his face, when, not herself knowing why, she unfastened her magnificent watch from its chain and handed it to him; he looked at it in silence and gave it back. "To be sure, I will do it with pleasure," he repeated. "I don't mend watches now. My eyes are weak, and the doctors have forbidden me to do fine work. But for you I can make an exception."

"Doctors talk nonsense," said the accountant. They all laughed. "Don't you believe them," he went on, flattered by the laughing; "last year a tooth flew out of a cylinder and hit old Kalmykov such a crack on the head that you could see his brains, and the doctor said he would die; but he is alive and working to this day, only he has taken to stammering since that mishap."

"Doctors do talk nonsense, they do, but not so much," sighed Auntie. "Pyotr Andreyitch, poor dear, lost his sight. Just like you, he used to work day in day out at the factory near the hot furnace, and he went blind. The eyes don't like heat. But what are we talking about?" she said, rousing herself. "Come and have a drink. My best wishes for Christmas, my dears. I never drink with any one else, but I drink with you, sinful woman as I am. Please God!"

Anna Akimovna fancied that after yesterday Pimenov despised her as a philanthropist, but was fascinated by her as a woman. She looked at him and thought that he behaved very charmingly and was nicely dressed. It is true that the sleeves of his coat were not quite long enough, and the coat itself seemed short-waisted, and his trousers were not wide and fashionable, but his tie was tied carelessly and with taste and was not as gaudy as the others'. And he seemed to be a good-natured man, for he ate submissively whatever Auntie put on his plate. She remembered how black he had been the day before, and how sleepy, and the thought of it for some reason touched her.

text: Such enormous masses of material could well explain the rosy and other curious lights that are from time to time observed. But cosmic dust is not the only matter in the air that could occasion the phenomena; the atmosphere is constantly filled with innumerable forms caught up by currents and carried to inconceivable heights, and thus to great distances, to be precipitated to the earth in hail, snow, or rain. Near St. Domingo, Darwin tells us, the atmosphere became thick and hazy from the impalpable fine dust that actually injured their astronomical instruments. 'The morning before we anchored at Porto Praya,' he says, 'I collected a little packet of this brown-colored dust, which appeared to have been filtered from the wind by the gauze of the vane at the masthead. Mr. Lyell has also given me four packets of dust which fell on a vessel a few hundred miles northward of these islands. Professor Ehrenberg finds that this dust consists in great part of infusoria with siliceous shields, and of the siliceous tissue of plants. In five little packets which I sent him, he has ascertained no less than sixty-seven different organic forms. The infusoria, with the exception of two marine species, are all inhabitants of fresh water. I have found no less than fifteen different accounts of dust having fallen on vessels when far out in the Atlantic. From the direction of the wind whenever it has fallen, and from its having always fallen during those months when the harmattan is known to raise clouds of dust high into the atmosphere, we may feel sure that it all comes from Africa. It is, however, a very singular fact, that, although Professor Ehrenberg knows many species of infusoria peculiar to Africa, he finds none of them in the dust which I sent him; on the other hand, he finds in it two species which hitherto he knows as living only in South America. The dust falls in such quantities as to dirty every thing on board, and to hurt people's eyes; vessels even have run ashore, owing to the obscurity of the atmosphere. It has often fallen on ships when more than a thousand miles from the coast of Africa, and at points sixteen hundred miles distant in a north and south direction. In some dust which was collected on a vessel three hundred miles from the land, I found particles of stone, above the thousandth of an inch square, mixed with finer matter. After this fact, one need not be surprised at the diffusion of the far lighter and smaller sporules of cryptogamic plants.'

There, take this copper-pump, and hail ’em through it. Tell ’em to avast dreaming of their lasses. Tell ’em it’s the resurrection; they must kiss their last, and come to judgment. That’s the way—that’s it; thy throat ain’t spoiled with eating Amsterdam butter. FRENCH SAILOR. Hist, boys! let’s have a jig or two before we ride to anchor in Blanket Bay. What say ye? There comes the other watch. Stand by all legs! Pip! little Pip! hurrah with your tambourine! PIP. (Sulky and sleepy.) Don’t know where it is. FRENCH SAILOR. Beat thy belly, then, and wag thy ears. Jig it, men, I say; merry’s the word; hurrah! Damn me, won’t you dance? Form, now, Indian-file, and gallop into the double-shuffle? Throw yourselves! Legs! legs! ICELAND SAILOR. text: Japanese sushi, particularly nigiri—its most iconic style—is a masterclass in precision and freshness, defined by small, intentional details that elevate simple ingredients. Each piece starts with small, perfectly formed ovalshaped mounds of vinegared rice: the rice is cooked to a tender yet firm texture, then seasoned to be slightly sticky so it holds its shape without being gluey and coated in a light mixture of rice vinegar, sugar, and salt, giving it a subtle glossy sheen that catches the light. Topped on these rice mounds is the star: fresh raw fish, sliced with meticulous care to showcase its natural quality. Popular choices include:  Tuna maguro: a deep, vibrant deep red with a dense, firm texture that offers a meaty bite.  Salmon sake: a soft pale pink with marbled fat, making it rich and fatty meltinyourmouth creamy when fresh.  Shrimp ebi: translucent white when raw, or gently poached until it turns a delicate pink—tender and sweet, with a subtle brininess. The fish is sliced thin just thick enough to feel substantial, thin enough to pair harmoniously with the rice and placed neatly on top of the rice mound. Some nigiri gets a finishing touch: a tiny dot of wasabi freshly grated for brightness, not harshness between the rice and fish, or a light brush of soy sauce on the fish to avoid oversaturating the rice. Visually, nigiri is understated yet elegant: the vivid colors of the fish pop against the pale rice, and the clean, simple presentation lets the ingredients’ quality shine. Tastewise, it’s a study in clean and delicate flavors—no heavy sauces to overpower the core components. The rice is subtly sweet from sugar and tangy from vinegar, balancing the fish’s natural savory notes: tuna is deeply rich, salmon is luxuriously creamy, and shrimp is mild and sweet. Wasabi adds a quick, sharp, spicy kick that cuts through richness, while a dip in lowsodium soy sauce amplifies the fish’s brininess—all coming together in a bitesized burst of harmony. Culturally, sushimaking is revered as an art form. Chefs itamae train for years—often a decade or more—to master three core skills: perfectly seasoning the rice too much vinegar makes it tart, too little makes it bland, precisely slicing the fish each cut must match the fish’s texture to maximize tenderness, and expertly shaping the rice each mound must be uniform in size and stickiness. This dedication to craft reflects Japan’s culinary philosophy of “respect for ingredients.” Unlike many dishes, nigiri requires no cooking for raw fish—its magic lies in freshness above all. The seasoning, slicing, and shaping steps are intentional, designed to highlight the fish’s natural flavor and the rice’s balanced tanginess. Every bite is a celebration of simplicity done right—proof that when ingredients are exceptional, less is always more.
