text: The winter night in Luzhen was wrapped in snow, cold and quiet, except for the faint crackle of firecrackers from distant families celebrating the Blessing Festival. I sat alone at a wooden table in the hotel, a cup of rice wine in front of me, its warmth barely cutting through the chill that seeped in through the broken windowpanes. The oil lamp on the table flickered, casting a dim light over the rough walls, where a few tattered posters of old operas were pasted crookedly. I thought of Xianglin’s Wife. Of the way she’d stood in this very hotel months ago, her hair half-white, her hands chapped and rough from years of hard work, asking me in a trembling voice, “Do you think… there really is a Hell after death?” I’d hesitated then, fumbling for words, not daring to tell her the truth I suspected—that there was no Hell, but also no comfort for the suffering she’d endured. Now, I learned she was dead—frozen to death on the eve of the Blessing Festival, her body found in the snow outside the town, still clutching a handful of broken joss sticks. The firecrackers sounded louder, closer now, as families set off more to pray for good fortune. I took a sip of rice wine, but it tasted bitter. I thought of how she’d been married off by her brother, how her first husband died of illness, how her son was eaten by a wolf, how she’d been driven out of the Lu family’s house like a stray dog after her second husband passed away. The people of Luzhen had pitied her at first, then grown tired of her stories of suffering, then mocked her, calling her “unlucky” and refusing to let her touch the ritual utensils during the festivals. A breeze blew through the window, carrying a flake of snow that landed on my hand. I thought of her eyes—once bright, then dimmed by sorrow, then hollow with fear of Hell. She’d tried so hard to fit in, to earn a place in this cold town, to find even a little warmth. But the world had given her nothing but cold shoulders and cruel words. And I—what had I done? I’d avoided her, hesitated to answer her questions, let her walk away into the cold alone. I looked at the empty chair across the table, as if she might still be sitting there, waiting for my answer. The oil lamp sputtered, and for a second, I thought I saw her shadow on the wall—thin, hunched, like a withered leaf. I shook my head, telling myself it was just the light playing tricks. But the guilt stayed, heavy in my chest. The firecrackers continued, echoing through the snow-covered streets. The Blessing Festival—supposed to be a time of hope and new beginnings. text: If it were possible for human beings to penetrate to the abyssal depths of the ocean, finny torch-bearers would be found from the very surface to nearly four miles beneath it; existing in many cases under conditions almost incomprehensible when the enormous attendant pressure is considered. While it is extremely difficult to tell the exact depth from which a fish is taken by the dredge, sufficient data has been secured for naturalists to assume, though there is great difference of opinion, that, to a greater or less degree, the forms of certain depths have certain peculiarities. These are often seen in the organs of vision, which have been modified in many ways by the lack of light. Thus the eyes of forms that are found living five or six hundred feet below the surface are often extremely large, as in Beryx (Plate XVIII., Fig. 1), as if to absorb the faintest beams of sunlight that may penetrate this distance. As we descend to twelve hundred feet, the eyes seem to grow larger; and beyond this, large and small eyed fishes are found indiscriminately. The former evidently use these organs; while those with small eyes are provided with remarkable organs of touch,—long feelers which can be thrown forward, or moved to a more or less extent, and used as the blind man uses his cane. An[92] interesting, indeed remarkable, example of this is seen in the fish Bathypterus longipes, Günther found at a depth varying from one-half to three-quarters of a mile from the surface in the Atlantic. The eyes are extremely small, apparently useless; but the blind man's cane is here, as the pectoral fins are modified to serve as feelers, two rays almost as long as the entire fish extending from the back of the head. As the fish swims freely, the fins are trailed behind; but, does it approach a prospective victim, the articulation of these wonderful feelers enables them to be thrown forward as a cane in advance of the fish. They are divided at the tip, and form a delicate sense-organ with which to explore the depths of this abyssal world. Upon the ventral fins, there are two similar rays, that serve a like purpose. Many fishes having remarkable feelers have quite recently been discovered, and among them Eustomias obscurus (Plate XIX.), a fish found at a depth of twenty-seven hundred meters, which has a long tentacle dependent from the lower jaw.

text: The late autumn wind rattled the fire escape outside the apartment window, carrying the smell of burnt leaves and the distant honk of a taxi. Holly Golightly knelt on the floor, her bare knees pressed into a pile of crumpled silk scarves, as she stuffed a handful of costume jewelry into an old leather suitcase—she'd talked about moving to Brazil for a week, but the suitcase was still half-empty, and the tickets on the table were unopened. The air smelled of cigarette smoke and the sweet, cloying scent of gardenias from a wilted bouquet on the windowsill, mixing with the cold draft that slipped through the cracked window frame. She paused, holding a pearl necklace up to the light, and stared at her reflection in the dusty mirror above the dresser. Her hair was messy, her lipstick smudged, and there was a faint smudge of ink on her wrist from a letter she'd started but never finished. 'I don't want to belong to anyone,' she'd told me once, 'not even to myself.' But right now, she looked like someone who was scared of being alone, scared that the freedom she talked about so loudly would turn into something empty. A cat jumped onto the suitcase, purring, and she laughed, a sharp, brittle sound that didn't reach her eyes. She stroked its fur, her fingers trembling a little, and said, 'You're the only one who doesn't ask me to be something I'm not, Cat.' The cat blinked, and she put the necklace back into the suitcase, closing it with a snap. She walked to the window, pressing her palm against the cold glass, and looked down at the street—people hurried past, their coats pulled tight against the wind, and a vendor sold hot dogs from a cart, the steam curling up into the gray sky. She'd always said she wanted to be like the people in Tiffany's, 'calm and safe, like nothing bad could ever happen to them.' But she was nothing like that. She was like the wind, she thought—here one minute, gone the next, never staying long enough to get attached. The wind picked up again, and she shivered, pulling a fur stole around her shoulders. She picked up the suitcase, but then set it down again, staring at the unopened tickets. Maybe tomorrow, she thought. Maybe tomorrow she'd pack the rest of her things, maybe she'd buy a new bouquet of gardenias, maybe she'd stop talking about freedom and start living it. But today, she'd stay. Today, she'd sit on the floor with the cat, and smoke a cigarette, and pretend that the empty spaces in the suitcase didn't scare her. Today, that was enough.

text: The boy with fair hair lowered himself down the last few feet of rock and began to pick his way toward the lagoon. Though he had taken off his school sweater and trailed it now from one hand, his grey shirt stuck to him and his hair was plastered to his forehead. He was clambering heavily among the creepers and broken trunks when a bird, a vision of red and yellow, flashed upwards with a witch-like cry; and this cry was echoed by another. 'Hi!' it said. 'Wait a minute!' The undergrowth at the side of the scar was shaken and a multitude of raindrops fell pattering. 'Wait a minute,' the voice said. 'I got caught up.' The fair boy stopped and jerked his stockings with an automatic gesture that made the jungle seem for a moment like the Home Counties. The voice spoke again. 'I can't hardly move with all these creeper things.' The owner of the voice came backing out of the undergrowth so that twigs scratched on a greasy wind-breaker. The naked crooks of his knees were plump, caught and scratched by thorns. He bent down, removed the thorns carefully, and turned around. He was shorter than the fair boy and very fat. He came forward, searching out safe lodgments for his feet, and then looked up through thick spectacles. 'Where's the man with the megaphone?' The fair boy shook his head. 'This is an island. At least I think it's an island. That's a reef out in the sea. Perhaps there aren't any grownups anywhere.' The fat boy looked startled. 'There was that pilot. But he wasn't in the passenger cabin, he was up in front.' The fair boy was peering at the reef through screwed-up eyes. 'All them other kids,' the fat boy went on. 'Some of them must have got out. They must have, mustn't they?' The fair boy began to pick his way as casually as possible toward the water. He tried to be offhand and not too obviously uninterested, but the fat boy hurried after him. 'Aren't there any grownups at all?' 'I don't think so.' The fair boy said this solemnly; but then the delight of a realized ambition overcame him. In the middle of the scar he stood on his head and grinned at the reversed fat boy. 'No grownups!'

text: The winter sun climbed slowly over the snow-capped Alps, casting a pale, icy light over the white lawns of the sanatorium. Hans stood on the frost-covered terrace, his hands tucked into the pockets of his thick woolen coat, watching the other patients trudge along the path below—some leaning on canes, their shoulders hunched against the cold, others walking in slow pairs, their voices muffled by scarves wrapped tight around their faces. A thin layer of frost covered the railing in front of him, and when he touched it with his finger, it left a tiny, melting streak of water. The air smelled of pine and wood smoke from the sanatorium's fireplaces, sharp and clean against the faint, medicinal scent of iodine that lingered in the corridors inside. A nurse in a starched white uniform walked past, carrying a tray of steaming cups, and nodded at him—her smile small, professional, like she'd seen too many faces fade into the mountain mist. Hans nodded back, his eyes drifting to the mountains in the distance, their peaks sharp against the pale blue sky. They looked permanent, unchanging, nothing like the fragile bodies of the people around him—bodies that coughed, that weakened, that measured time in days spent in bed and temperatures taken at dawn. He thought of his cousin Joachim, who'd arrived at the sanatorium a year ago, full of plans to return to the army, to live a life of action. Now Joachim walked with a shuffle, his cheeks flushed with the faint fever that never quite went away, and talked only of the next 'cure'—the next round of treatments, the next trip to the solarium, the next small hope that kept him going. Hans had come for a three-week visit; now three months had passed, and the line between 'visitor' and 'patient' felt thinner every day. Time here was strange, he thought. It didn't move like it did in the lowlands—no rush, no deadlines, no sense of progress. It just hung in the air, like the frost on the terrace, melting slowly, almost imperceptibly. A bell rang from inside the sanatorium, sharp and clear, signaling the start of morning treatments. The patients below began to turn back, their steps even slower than before, as if the cold had seeped into their bones. Hans lingered, watching a single bird—small, brown, resilient—hop across the snow, pecking at something hidden beneath the drifts. It reminded him of the sparrows in his hometown, the ones that nested in the eaves of his family's house, that didn't care about snow or sickness or the slow drag of time. For a second, he felt a flicker of something like hope—a small, bright thing, easily lost if he didn't hold onto it. He pulled his coat tighter around him, his breath forming small clouds in the cold air, and turned to walk inside. The corridor was warm, the air thick with the smell of soup and iodine, and he could hear the soft murmur of voices from the common room. Today would be like yesterday, he thought—treatments, meals, quiet conversations about weather and health.

“You might have hurt your head very badly!” remarked an elderly, well-preserved woman who sat on my left. She was very handsomely dressed and extremely refined.

text: The spring sun warmed the windowsill of Carol Kennicott's house, where a pot of lilacs bloomed in soft purple—their scent thick, sweet, so strong it seeped through the open window and mixed with the smell of freshly baked pie from Mrs. Bogart next door. Carol sat at her oak table, her fingers tracing the edges of a crumpled sketch: a plan to widen Main Street, to add a small park where the old livery stable stood, to paint the storefronts in brighter colors. The paper was smudged with coffee stains, its lines faded—she'd drawn it three years ago, when she first moved to Gopher Prairie, full of hope that she could 'wake up this sleepy town.' She paused, setting the sketch down, and looked at the photograph on the table: her and Will, on their wedding day, her in a white dress, him in a dark suit, both smiling like they thought the world was made of sunshine and clover. Back then, Will had laughed at her plans but said 'Whatever makes you happy, Carol.' Now, he just sighed and said 'You're too busy trying to fix things that aren't broken.' The townsfolk felt the same—Mrs. Bogart called her 'fancy,' Mr. Garrick the banker said she was 'wasting time on nonsense,' even the children stared when she walked down Main Street in her city dresses. A knock on the door made her jump. She smoothed her skirt—still a little too tailored for the town's taste—and opened it. It was Mrs. Bogart, holding a tin pie plate. 'Smelled your coffee,' she said, pushing the plate into Carol's hands. 'Thought you might want a slice of rhubarb pie. My Harold says it's the best I've ever made.' Carol smiled, thanking her, but the smile felt tight. She knew Mrs. Bogart meant well—but the pie, the friendly chats, the way everyone knew everyone's business… it all felt like a soft cage, wrapping around her, keeping her from breathing. She closed the door, setting the pie on the counter, and walked back to the window. The lilacs swayed in the breeze, their petals falling like tiny purple tears. She thought of her old life in St. Paul—her job at the library, her friends who talked about books and art, the way the streets were full of people with 'big ideas.' Here, the biggest idea was whether the church supper would have enough potato salad. She'd tried to fight it, at first—hosted book clubs, pushed the town council to fix the park, even taught the girls' club how to paint. But slowly, she'd felt herself fading, like the lines on her sketch. She picked up the sketch again, folding it carefully and tucking it into the drawer with her old city dresses. Maybe Will was right. Maybe some things didn't need fixing. Maybe she should just accept it— the pie, the lilacs, the quiet days where nothing ever changed. But then she looked at the lilacs again, their purple petals bright against the gray house, and felt a spark in her chest. She'd moved here to be happy, yes—but happy didn't mean giving up who she was.

text: Such, then, was the person that I saw seated on the transom when I followed Captain Peleg down into the cabin. The space between the decks was small; and there, bolt-upright, sat old Bildad, who always sat so, and never leaned, and this to save his coat tails. His broad-brim was placed beside him; his legs were stiffly crossed; his drab vesture was buttoned up to his chin; and spectacles on nose, he seemed absorbed in reading from a ponderous volume. “Bildad,” cried Captain Peleg, “at it again, Bildad, eh? Ye have been studying those Scriptures, now, for the last thirty years, to my certain knowledge. How far ye got, Bildad?” As if long habituated to such profane talk from his old shipmate, Bildad, without noticing his present irreverence, quietly looked up, and seeing me, glanced again inquiringly towards Peleg. “He says he’s our man, Bildad,” said Peleg, “he wants to ship.” “Dost thee?” said Bildad, in a hollow tone, and turning round to me. “I dost,” said I unconsciously, he was so intense a Quaker. “What do ye think of him, Bildad?” said Peleg. “He’ll do,” said Bildad, eyeing me, and then went on spelling away at his book in a mumbling tone quite audible. I thought him the queerest old Quaker I ever saw, especially as Peleg, his friend and old shipmate, seemed such a blusterer. But I said nothing, only looking round me sharply. Peleg now threw open a chest, and drawing forth the ship’s articles, placed pen and ink before him, and seated himself at a little table. I began to think it was high time to settle with myself at what terms I would be willing to engage for the voyage. I was already aware that in the whaling business they paid no wages; but all hands, including the captain, received certain shares of the profits called lays, and that these lays were proportioned to the degree of importance pertaining to the respective duties of the ship’s company. I was also aware that being a green hand at whaling, my own lay would not be very large; but considering that I was used to the sea, could steer a ship, splice a rope, and all that, I made no doubt that from all I had heard I should be offered at least the 275th lay—that is, the 275th part of the clear net proceeds of the voyage, whatever that might eventually amount to. And though the 275th lay was what they call a rather long lay, yet it was better than nothing; and if we had a lucky voyage, might pretty nearly pay for the clothing I would wear out on it, not to speak of my three years’ beef and board, for which I would not have to pay one stiver.

Kashtanka jumped back, squatted on all four paws, and craning her nose towards the cat, went off into loud, shrill barks; meanwhile the gander came up behind and gave her a painful peck in the back. Kashtanka leapt up and dashed at the gander.
“What’s this?” They heard a loud angry voice, and the stranger came into the room in his dressing-gown, with a cigar between his teeth. “What’s the meaning of this? To your places!”

“All right, all right,” said his master, yawning. “You must live in peace and friendship.” He stroked Kashtanka and went on: “And you, redhair, don’t be frightened. . . . They are capital company, they won’t annoy you. Stay, what are we to call you? You can’t go on without a name, my dear.”

text: A somewhat similar fog appeared in the United States, a portion of Europe, and Africa in August, 1831. The daylight was perceptibly diminished, while at night a conspicuous phosphorescent light was emitted. A remarkable luminous fog occurred in Switzerland in 1859. M. L. F. Wartmann of Geneva states that the strange light was observed on five successive nights, and apparently proceeded from a heavy dry fog that hung over Geneva during the time. The light was so brilliant that this gentleman distinguished the smallest objects upon his table with perfect ease, no other light being in the apartment. The light caused general comment in the places in which it appeared, and a traveller between Geneva and Annemassi stated that he readily found the road by its means. Dr. Verdeil of Lausanne describes a fog which diffused so much light that distant objects were perfectly visible at night. Among the phenomena which attended the eruption of Vesuvius in 1794 was one which did not tend to allay the fears of the people. During the day a fine dust filled the air about Naples, which was not particularly noticeable; but as night came on, it emitted a pale though distinct phosphorescent light. An English gentleman sailing near Torre del Greco noticed that where the dust collected upon his hat it was luminous, and no little consternation was caused among the superstitious sailors by the occurrence. Luminous dust-showers have been noticed in several localities; and the peculiar glows that were seen in this country a few years ago were accredited by many to them, the supposition being that dust, perhaps from volcanic eruptions, was floating about in the upper strata of the atmosphere. Many other explanations were given, and the literature upon the subject is extremely voluminous and interesting. The amount of material floating about in the upper regions of the air is perhaps little realized by my young readers, and some reference to the phenomenon may be of interest. Professor Nordenskjöld has for many years been a close observer of dust of all kinds that has fallen upon the earth in rain or snow; and it was his good fortune, during the expedition of the 'Vega,' to prove beyond a doubt the presence of cosmic dust. For many years we have been assured by astronomers that the earth was being bombarded, as it were, continually, by innumerable meteors. The moment they enter our domain, we observe the spectacle of their ignition. In a moment they are reduced to ashes, and the fine impalpable dust drops slowly, an invisible shower, upon the earth. When such showers are intensified, it is not impossible that some outward and visible phenomena may be the result.

The candle on the rickety table flickered, casting long, wavering shadows across the bare walls of the attic. Sydney Carton leaned back in his wooden chair, his head in his hands, the smell of brandy and ink hanging thick in the cold night air. Outside, the streets of Paris were quiet—but he could feel the tension, like electricity in the wind, the quiet rumble of a storm that would soon break. He had spent the evening in a tavern, drinking to forget, to drown out the voice in his head that whispered of wasted potential, of a life half-lived. But the alcohol had only sharpened the ache, the sense that he was nothing but a shadow, a pale reflection of what he might have been.

He thought of Lucie Manette, her face soft and kind, her voice like a melody that lingered in his memory. He had seen her earlier that day, walking with her husband, Charles Darnay, their hands clasped, their eyes full of love. The sight had pierced his heart—not with jealousy, but with a deep, abiding sorrow. He loved her, had loved her from the moment they met, but he had never dared to tell her, never dared to hope that someone like her could ever see anything in someone like him. "I am a disappointed drudge," he muttered to himself, his voice thick with self-loathing. "I care for no man on earth, and no man on earth cares for me."

But as he spoke the words, something shifted inside him. He thought of Lucie's smile, of the way she had looked at him with compassion, not judgment, when he had stumbled into her father's house drunk and disheveled. He thought of her children, small and innocent, and of the danger that loomed over them all—the revolution that was gathering strength, the guillotine that waited for nobles and their allies alike. Charles Darnay, with his noble blood, was in mortal danger. And Lucie—she would be destroyed if anything happened to him.

A fire ignited in his chest, a resolve he had never felt before. He stood up, his legs unsteady but his mind clear. He would not let her suffer. He would not let the life she had built be torn apart. He walked to the window, pushed it open, and felt the cold night air on his face. Below, a dog barked in the distance, and a clock struck midnight. "It is a far, far better thing that I do, than I have ever done," he said softly, the words hanging in the air like a promise. "It is a far, far better rest that I go to, than I have ever known.

text: When she opened her eyes in the morning it was because a young housemaid had come into her room to light the fire and was kneeling on the hearth-rug raking out the cinders noisily. Mary lay and watched her for a few moments and then began to look about the room. She had never seen a room at all like it and thought it curious and gloomy. The walls were covered with tapestry with a forest scene embroidered on it. There were fantastic, dark trees and weeping willows with trailing branches, and among them stood figures of men and women in queer, rich costumes, and in the distance could be seen the turrets of a castle. There was a fireplace with a curious, high, carved mantel, and on the mantel was a portrait of a stiff, plain little girl who seemed to stare at her. The windows were set in deep, thick walls and there were heavy, purple draperies which could be drawn to cover them completely. The room was furnished with dark, heavy oak furniture, massive and richly carved. Mary thought it must be a hundred years old. When the housemaid had made the fire she came up to the bed. 'It's a wild morning,' she said. 'Th' wind's howling across th' moor. It's fit to blow the hair off your head.' 'What is that noise?' Mary asked. She could hear a distant, roaring sound. 'That's th' wind wuthering round th' house,' answered the maid. 'It sounds like th' sea. We're near th' sea here, though you can't see it from th' house. On a night like this it sounds as if all th' waves were beating on th' cliffs.' Mary felt a strange thrill. She had never heard the wind make such a sound before. The moor seemed a wild, desolate place, but there was something exciting about its very wildness. After the maid had gone, Mary got up and went to the window. She drew back the heavy draperies and looked out. She saw a great, purple moor stretching away to the horizon, with no trees and no houses, only here and there a few stunted bushes that the wind had twisted into strange shapes. The sky was low and gray, and the wind was driving clouds of rain across the landscape. It was the bleakest view she had ever seen, and yet there was a certain savage beauty about it that fascinated her.

text: That whale of Stubb’s, so dearly purchased, was duly brought to the Pequod’s side, where all those cutting and hoisting operations previously detailed, were regularly gone through, even to the baling of the Heidelburgh Tun, or Case. While some were occupied with this latter duty, others were employed in dragging away the larger tubs, so soon as filled with the sperm; and when the proper time arrived, this same sperm was carefully manipulated ere going to the try-works, of which anon. It had cooled and crystallized to such a degree, that when, with several others, I sat down before a large Constantine’s bath of it, I found it strangely concreted into lumps, here and there rolling about in the liquid part. It was our business to squeeze these lumps back into fluid. A sweet and unctuous duty! No wonder that in old times this sperm was such a favourite cosmetic. Such a clearer! such a sweetener! such a softener! such a delicious molifier! After having my hands in it for only a few minutes, my fingers felt like eels, and began, as it were, to serpentine and spiralise. As I sat there at my ease, cross-legged on the deck; after the bitter exertion at the windlass; under a blue tranquil sky; the ship under indolent sail, and gliding so serenely along; as I bathed my hands among those soft, gentle globules of infiltrated tissues, woven almost within the hour; as they richly broke to my fingers, and discharged all their opulence, like fully ripe grapes their wine; as I snuffed up that uncontaminated aroma,—literally and truly, like the smell of spring violets; I declare to you, that for the time I lived as in a musky meadow; I forgot all about our horrible oath; in that inexpressible sperm, I washed my hands and my heart of it; I almost began to credit the old Paracelsan superstition that sperm is of rare virtue in allaying the heat of anger; while bathing in that bath, I felt divinely free from all ill-will, or petulance, or malice, of any sort whatsoever.

text: The afternoon sun slanted through the oak trees, casting long, dappled shadows across the yard where Sethe stood, her hands clasped loosely at her waist. The air was thick with the sweet, cloying scent of honeysuckle climbing the fence, a scent that carried her back to Sweet Home—the plantation where she had been born, where she had loved and lost, where the scars on her back had been carved like a map of suffering. She closed her eyes, and for a moment, she could feel the weight of the chains, the sting of the whip, the cold fear in her bones as she ran north, toward freedom, toward the daughter she had risked everything to save. When she opened her eyes, the yard was still there—quiet, green, safe—but the ghosts lingered, as they always did. She thought of Beloved, her baby girl, the one she had killed to keep from the slave catchers, the one who had returned to her as a woman, pale and strange, with eyes that held all the pain of the grave. 'I'm sorry,' she whispered, her voice cracking. 'I'm so sorry I couldn't protect you better.' She had thought freedom would heal her, would erase the past, but the past was a ghost that refused to be laid to rest, a shadow that followed her everywhere she went. A movement at the door caught her eye—Beloved, standing in the doorway, her dress white as a sheet, her hair falling in loose curls around her shoulders. Sethe's heart skipped a beat, a mixture of joy and terror flooding through her. She had dreamed of this moment, of her daughter's forgiveness, but she had also feared it—feared the anger, the accusation, the truth of what she had done. 'Sethe,' Beloved said, her voice soft, almost childlike. She took a step forward, her bare feet touching the warm grass. Sethe reached out, her hands trembling, and Beloved took them, her fingers cold but gentle. For a moment, they stood there, silent, the only sounds the rustle of leaves and the distant chirp of a bird. Sethe could feel the weight of the years melting away, the pain easing, if only for a moment. She thought of the love she had for Beloved, a love so fierce it had driven her to madness, to murder, to a lifetime of guilt. She thought of the way Beloved had clung to her, the way she had needed her, and she knew that somehow, they would heal—together. Beloved leaned forward, pressing her forehead against Sethe's. 'I know,' she said. 'I know you loved me.' Sethe's tears began to fall, hot and unbidden, as she pulled Beloved close, holding her as if she would never let go. The honeysuckle scent wrapped around them, sweet and comforting, a reminder that even in the darkest of times, there was love, there was hope, there was a chance to be whole again.

text: The summer night over the Sahara was quiet, so quiet that you could hear the stars breathe—faint, distant hums that hung in the air like forgotten songs. He’d drawn it last night, while the prince talked about his planet—about the volcanoes he cleaned every day, about the baobabs he pulled up before they split the earth, about how his rose was “the only one of her kind in all the world.” He thought of the prince’s laugh, light and clear, like the tinkle of a bell in an empty room. How the boy had pointed to a star and said, “That’s where my rose is. Even if you can’t see her, she’s there—and that makes all the stars shine brighter.” At the time, the pilot had smiled, thinking it was just a child’s fancy. Now, he looked up at the sky, and every star seemed to wink at him, as if holding a secret only he and the prince knew. The sand was still warm from the day’s sun, and he wiggled his toes in it, feeling its grit between his fingers. He thought of the adults he’d met—businessmen who counted stars like they were coins, kings who ruled over empty deserts, lamplighters who lit lamps for no one. They’d all talked about “important things,” but none of them had talked about roses. None of them had talked about how a single flower could make a planet feel like home. A breeze blew past, carrying the smell of distant sand dunes and the faint rustle of his tent. He folded the sketch carefully, tucking it into the breast pocket of his jacket—close to his heart, like he was keeping a piece of the prince safe.

He had been cowardly, had even been afraid of the moon, had openly expressed thoughts and feelings such as he had not expected in himself before; for instance, the thought that the paltry people who philosophized were really dissatisfied. The hospital porters came, took him by his arms and legs, and carried him away to the chapel.

“Maple walnut and strawberry,” said Isabel without an instant’s hesitation. “Thank you, you dear Person,” she added with a smile rather like melted ice cream, sweet, but lacking vigor.

When her father returned her mother helped herself and her husband to a little less than a third of the cream apiece and handed Isa the box, because she preferred it thus. Seated on the upper step under the brilliant summer stars, taking heaped spoonfuls of the delicious cream for which Ebers was famous for miles, and licking the top of each spoonful into a cone to get the full flavor, a mannerless way of eating that the night and out-of-doors allowed, Isabel began to feel comforted. The strawberry ice cream was dotted with seeds to prove that fruit, not flavoring gave it its flavor; the maple walnut was as strong of maple syrup taste as a Vermont sugar camp vat.

Isabel licked her spoon blissfully, if inelegantly, since no one could see her, and felt that life still held a great deal to enjoy. As to her father, who had taken the walk to get the cream for her when he was surely tired, how could she express the flavor of his love for his girl?

“Father, you blessing, my throat does feel scrumptious after that cream, and I hope some day, I’ll have a big, hard thing to do for you and mother, just to show you!” Isabel said at last, getting up from the step with a contentedly-weary yawn, and going over to kiss her best-beloveds good-night.

The first thing in the morning, while Isa was still at breakfast, there appeared Mark in a state of great excitement.

“Well, what do you suppose!” he burst forth at once. “Oh, good morning, Mrs. Lindsay! I forgot. But what do you suppose, honest?”

“What are we to suppose about, Mark?” hinted Mrs. Lindsay.

“I’d say about ’most anything,” returned Mark. “Things are happening in all directions. You couldn’t guess this; you didn’t know about it, I suppose. Say, Isa, you know Kathie Stevens’ coins?”

“’Course,” said Isa, leaning forward breathlessly.

“Gone!” cried Mark.

“Gone?” echoed Isabel. “Where? How do you mean gone?”

text: Entering that gable-ended Spouter-Inn, you found yourself in a wide, low, straggling entry with old-fashioned wainscots, reminding one of the bulwarks of some condemned old craft. On one side hung a very large oilpainting so thoroughly besmoked, and every way defaced, that in the unequal crosslights by which you viewed it, it was only by diligent study and a series of systematic visits to it, and careful inquiry of the neighbors, that you could any way arrive at an understanding of its purpose. Such unaccountable masses of shades and shadows, that at first you almost thought some ambitious young artist, in the time of the New England hags, had endeavored to delineate chaos bewitched. But by dint of much and earnest contemplation, and oft repeated ponderings, and especially by throwing open the little window towards the back of the entry, you at last come to the conclusion that such an idea, however wild, might not be altogether unwarranted. But what most puzzled and confounded you was a long, limber, portentous, black mass of something hovering in the centre of the picture over three blue, dim, perpendicular lines floating in a nameless yeast. A boggy, soggy, squitchy picture truly, enough to drive a nervous man distracted. Yet was there a sort of indefinite, half-attained, unimaginable sublimity about it that fairly froze you to it, till you involuntarily took an oath with yourself to find out what that marvellous painting meant. Ever and anon a bright, but, alas, deceptive idea would dart you through.—It’s the Black Sea in a midnight gale.—It’s the unnatural combat of the four primal elements.—It’s a blasted heath.—It’s a Hyperborean winter scene.—It’s the breaking-up of the icebound stream of Time. text: The autumn night in Celie’s cabin on the Georgia farm was crisp—crisp enough that she’d pulled a patchwork quilt over her lap, its squares stitched from old dresses and flour sacks, each one holding a memory. She sat on a rickety wooden chair by the window, a crumpled letter in her hands and a half-burned tallow candle on the sill beside her, her eyes fixed on the words she’d written to Nettie, smudged with tears, the ink running in places where her hand had shaken. The cabin smelled of wood smoke and baked sweet potatoes—she’d put a pot in the fireplace earlier, hoping the warmth would chase away the chill—and a shelf above the table held a jar of peaches she’d canned that summer, their syrup glinting in the candlelight.  She thought of the day Nettie had left—of the way she’d hugged Celie tight, her suitcase in one hand, saying “I’ll write every week, Celie. You’ll see,” of the way the dust had kicked up behind the wagon as it pulled away, of the way Celie had stood in the yard until the wagon was nothing but a dot on the horizon, her throat too tight to cry. Those letters had stopped coming months ago, but Celie kept writing anyway, pouring every thought, every hurt, every hope onto the page. It was the only thing that made her feel like she was still alive, like her voice mattered.  The wind whistled through the cracks in the cabin walls, and the candle flame flickered, casting shadows on the wall where she’d tacked up Nettie’s last letter. She traced the edge of the crumpled paper with her finger, remembering the way Nettie’s handwriting had slanted, the way she’d dotted her i’s with little circles. “You’re not just a wife, Celie,” Nettie had written. “You’re not just a mother. You’re *you*—and that’s enough.” Celie hadn’t believed it then. How could she, when all she’d ever been told was that she was ugly, that she was useless, that her only purpose was to work and obey? But lately, when she looked at the quilt in her lap, at the peaches in the jar, at the letters she kept writing, she wondered if Nettie had been right.  She picked up a pencil from the table, sharpening it with a knife she kept in her apron pocket. She’d write another letter tonight, she decided. She’d tell Nettie about the sweet potatoes, about the way the cotton fields looked at sunset, about the cat that had kittens in the barn. She’d tell her she missed her, that she hoped she was safe, that she still believed they’d see each other again.  The candle sputtered, and Celie leaned forward to trim the wick. Outside, an owl hooted, and the moon peeked through the clouds, turning the cotton fields silver. For a moment, she didn’t think about Mister’s cruelty, or the hard work, or the letters that never came back. She just thought about Nettie’s voice, about the way her hands felt when she wrote, about the quiet hope that maybe—just maybe—someone would hear her.  And that, she thought, was enough.

text: After college, I moved to Boston for graduate school, the unspoken motive being that I wanted to experience Sabrina’s New England for myself. I visited Salem during my first October in the area. Many friends warned me to be careful and told me that I was walking into a Halloween tourism nightmare. I was willing to take the risk, if only to see trees ablaze with reds and oranges in the town that Sabrina and her aunts spoke about so often.When I got there, the scent of cinnamon seemed to be everywhere. Buses crowded with tourists moved through the narrow streets, always with a boisterous announcer at the front. The speakers shouted out gruesome details about the Salem Witch Trials, turning heads as they drove by. Usually sleepy during the off-season, the town’s storefronts drew in crowds by the dozens and before long, everyone on the street had either a tiny witch hat or a flowing black cloak.My stomach was uneasy with it all as I took in the sight of trash scattered across the historic cemetery, visitors wandering off the designated paths and onto graves. I was a part of it too, showing up the weekend before Halloween with romantic notions of strolling through the town’s old side streets to take pictures of the architecture and foliage. I didn’t know how to appreciate the cobblestoned streets and historical sites without thinking about the women who lost their lives there.In Boston, a similar disillusionment descended. The city’s past stung my fantasies with its racism and segregation and its patriotism built on the backs of others. No American town is untouched by these issues, but the letdown in Boston felt something akin to making pancakes with my mother for the first time. The city’s middle was too raw, its shell too charred in comparison to the image that I had dreamed up from *Sabrina* episodes.

“How nasty,” I whispered, “how nasty!”

The grown-ups would take it and eat it, eat it alive with its eyes, its teeth, its legs! While it squeaked and tried to bite their lips. . . .
I frowned, but . . . but why did my teeth move as though I were munching? The creature was loathsome, disgusting, terrible, but I ate it, ate it greedily, afraid of distinguishing its taste or smell. text: The winter night in Minnie Babbitt’s kitchen at her Zenith home was still—still enough that she could hear the tick of the mantel clock above the stove and the distant rumble of her husband George’s car pulling into the garage. She sat on a wooden chair pulled up to the table, an unfinished embroidery hoop in her hands (blue thread half-wound around the needle, a pattern of daisies half-stitched) and a chipped enamel mug of lukewarm coffee beside her, her eyes fixed on the steam curling from the mug, its thin wisp fading into the cool air. The kitchen smelled of baked bread (she’d made a loaf that afternoon, now wrapped in a checkered cloth on the counter) and soap (the sink still held a basin of soapy water from washing dinner dishes), and a woolen apron—frayed at the hem, its pockets stuffed with safety pins and a scrap of fabric—hung from a hook on the wall, just beside the stove. She thought of the day she’d moved into this house with George—of the way he’d carried the box of her mother’s china into the kitchen, grinning and saying “No more renting, Minnie. This is ours,” of the way she’d run her hand over the kitchen table, imagining the meals they’d cook, the children they’d feed, of the way he’d kissed her then, warm and eager, not like the quick, distracted pecks he gave her now, when he was rushing to read the newspaper or take a call from his office. They’d had a good life, she told herself—two children grown and married, a comfortable house, a husband who never missed a bill—but there were quiet hours, like this one, when she felt like a ghost in her own home, like the things she cared about (the embroidery, the way the light hit the table at dusk, the stories she used to tell the kids) didn’t matter to anyone but her. The clock ticked louder, and the coffee mug grew colder. She set the embroidery hoop down, running a finger over the half-stitched daisies—she’d started the pattern months ago, but never had time to finish, not with cleaning, cooking, mending George’s socks, answering the phone. She thought of her sister Clara, who’d moved to Chicago years ago, who wrote letters about working in a dress shop, about going to the movies with friends, about “living for herself” instead of “living for everyone else.” Minnie had envied her, at first—envied the way Clara sounded free, unburdened—but then she’d remind herself that Clara was alone, no husband, no children, no house to call her own. Stability, she’d tell herself, was better than freedom. But sometimes, when the house was quiet and George was in his study, she wondered if that was true.

text: Mount Fuji, located on the Japanese island of Honshu, is an active stratovolcano and the highest mountain in Japan, standing at an elevation of 3776 meters and widely recognized as a global symbol of natural beauty, serenity, and Japanese cultural identity. Formed over hundreds of thousands of years through repeated volcanic eruptions, Mount Fuji features a near-perfect symmetrical conical shape capped with snow for more than five months each year, creating a breathtaking visual landmark visible from Tokyo, Yokohama, and surrounding regions on clear days. The mountain is surrounded by the Fuji‑Hakone‑Izu National Park, a protected area encompassing five beautiful lakes known as the Fuji Five Lakes: Kawaguchi, Yamanaka, Saiko, Shoji, and Motosu, which reflect the mountain’s iconic silhouette and enhance its scenic grandeur. Mount Fuji last erupted in 1707 during the Edo period, an event known as the Hoei eruption, which deposited volcanic ash across much of central Japan and altered the surrounding landscape permanently. Despite being classified as active, volcanic activity has remained minimal for centuries, leading to its safe status as a major tourist destination and pilgrimage site. Each year, between July and August, hundreds of thousands of hikers and pilgrims ascend the mountain along four main official trails: Yoshida, Subashiri, Gotemba, and Fujinomiya, with most climbers starting at night to reach the summit in time for the spectacular sunrise view known as Goraiko. The trails pass through ten distinct stations, with the fifth station serving as the primary starting point for most hikers, offering parking, facilities, shops, and panoramic viewpoints. At the summit, visitors find a crater measuring approximately 800 meters in diameter, multiple weather stations, religious shrines, and panoramic vistas stretching across the Japanese Alps, Pacific coast, and surrounding plains. Mount Fuji holds profound religious significance in Japanese spirituality, particularly within Shinto and Buddhist traditions, revered as a sacred, divine mountain embodying purity, transcendence, and spiritual renewal. For centuries, it has been a central site for pilgrimage, meditation, mountain worship, and ritual purification, with numerous shrines and temples located at its base and along climbing routes. The mountain’s timeless beauty has inspired countless works of art, literature, poetry, theater, and ukiyo‑e woodblock prints, most famously the Thirty‑Six Views of Mount Fuji series by Katsushika Hokusai, which remains internationally renowned and has shaped global perceptions of Japanese aesthetics. In 2013, Mount Fuji was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognized for its exceptional natural beauty, cultural importance, spiritual significance, and artistic inspiration spanning centuries. Beyond climbing and sightseeing, the Mount Fuji region offers a wealth of recreational activities including boating on the Fuji Five Lakes, hot spring bathing known as onsen, cycling, camping, skiing in winter, and photography during cherry blossom and autumn foliage seasons. The area’s natural environment supports diverse alpine and temperate vegetation, including vibrant moss, resilient pine trees, alpine flowers, and colorful autumn leaves that change with the seasons. The iconic snow cap, clear blue skies, reflective lakes, and perfectly shaped cone combine to create one of the most photographed and recognizable natural landscapes in the world. Environmental conservation efforts focus on protecting the mountain’s delicate ecosystem, reducing litter left by hikers, preserving water quality in the lakes, managing tourism impact, and monitoring volcanic activity for safety. Mount Fuji represents harmony between nature and culture, serving as a powerful national symbol that evokes pride, tranquility, and aesthetic appreciation in Japanese society. Its universal appeal draws visitors from every continent, all seeking to experience its majestic presence, witness its iconic beauty, and partake in the spiritual and recreational traditions surrounding it. Whether viewed from a distance, reflected in a calm lake, or experienced up close during a climb, Mount Fuji continues to inspire awe and reverence as a masterpiece of natural architecture and a living cultural treasure.

text: A painting is a timeless form of visual art that involves applying paint, pigment, color, or other mediums to a solid surface called a canvas, paper, or wall, using a variety of tools such as brushes, palette knives, or even fingers. Paintings have been a fundamental part of human culture and expression for thousands of years, dating back to prehistoric cave paintings in Lascaux, France, and Altamira, Spain, which depicted animals and hunting scenes with primitive pigments made from clay and charcoal. Throughout history, different art movements have emerged, each with its own distinct style, techniques, and philosophical underpinnings that reflect the social, political, and cultural context of the time. These movements include the Renaissance with its focus on realism, perspective, and humanism; the Impressionist movement characterized by loose brushstrokes, vibrant colors, and depictions of light and movement; the Surrealist movement that explored the subconscious mind with dreamlike, irrational imagery; and the Abstract Expressionist movement that emphasized emotional expression through non-representational forms and bold color fields. A painting can convey a wide range of emotions, ideas, and narratives, from the serene beauty of a landscape bathed in golden sunlight to the raw intensity of a political statement or the tender intimacy of a portrait capturing a fleeting moment. The choice of medium is crucial in painting, with artists using oils for rich textures and slow drying times, acrylics for versatility and quick drying, watercolors for their transparent and luminous qualities, or gouache for opaque and vibrant finishes. Museums, galleries, and private collections around the world house priceless works of art, attracting art enthusiasts, historians, and researchers who come to admire the skill, creativity, and cultural significance of these paintings. Appreciating a painting often requires looking closely at the details, understanding the artist’s intent, and considering the historical background that influenced its creation, making it not just a visual delight but also a window into the human experience and imagination.

text: The moon was a pale, thin crescent in the black sky over Paris, its light barely touching the rooftops as Sydney Carton leaned against the window of his shabby attic, a half-empty bottle of wine in his hand. The air smelled of smoke and the faint stench of the streets below, of the candle wax that dripped slowly onto the rickety table beside him, of the musty paper of the legal documents he had abandoned hours ago. The room was silent save for the distant cry of a watchman and the soft rustle of the wind through the cracks in the walls—a silence that pressed in on him, heavy with the weight of his own wasted potential. He thought of Lucie Manette, of her gentle smile, of the way her eyes had looked at him with kindness, not contempt, when he had confessed his worthlessness to her. She had seen something in him that he could not see himself—a spark of goodness buried beneath years of apathy and self-loathing. 'I wish you could be better,' she had said, her voice soft, and those words had haunted him ever since. Better than what? He wondered. Better than a drunkard who wasted his brilliant mind on trivial cases, better than a man who had nothing to live for but the next bottle of wine? He took a swig of wine, wincing at its bitterness, and looked out at the city. Paris was a powder keg, he knew—rumors of revolution were everywhere, whispers of storming the Bastille, of bloodshed and vengeance against the aristocracy. He had no stake in it, no reason to care. Let the world burn, he thought. What did it matter to him? But then he thought of Lucie and her husband Darnay, of their innocent child, and a sharp pain pierced his chest. He could not let harm come to them. Not while he still breathed. What was a life like his worth, anyway? A life of empty promises and unfulfilled dreams, of nights spent drowning in regret. He had always been in Darnay's shadow—Darnay, who was honest and brave and loved by Lucie, while he was nothing but a disappointment. But what if he could change that? What if he could give his life for someone else, for someone who mattered? For the first time in years, a flicker of hope stirred in him—not hope for himself, but hope that he could do something meaningful, something that would make Lucie's faith in him not be in vain. He set the bottle down, his hands surprisingly steady, and walked to the table.

text:
A strange rumour!
Dr. Andrey Yefimitch Ragin is a strange man in his way. They say that when he was young he was very religious, and prepared himself for a clerical career, and that when he had finished his studies at the high school in 1863 he intended to enter a theological academy, but that his father, a surgeon and doctor of medicine, jeered at him and declared point-blank that he would disown him if he became a priest. How far this is true I don’t know, but Andrey Yefimitch himself has more than once confessed that he has never had a natural bent for medicine or science in general.
However that may have been, when he finished his studies in the medical faculty he did not enter the priesthood. He showed no special devoutness, and was no more like a priest at the beginning of his medical career than he is now.
His exterior is heavy—coarse like a peasant’s, his face, his beard, his flat hair, and his coarse, clumsy figure, suggest an overfed, intemperate, and harsh innkeeper on the highroad. His face is surly-looking and covered with blue veins, his eyes are little and his nose is red. With his height and broad shoulders he has huge hands and feet; one would think that a blow from his fist would knock the life out of anyone, but his step is soft, and his walk is cautious and insinuating; when he meets anyone in a narrow passage he is always the first to stop and make way, and to say, not in a bass, as one would expect, but in a high, soft tenor: “I beg your pardon!” He has a little swelling on his neck which prevents him from wearing stiff starched collars, and so he always goes about in soft linen or cotton shirts. Altogether he does not dress like a doctor. He wears the same suit for ten years, and the new clothes, which he usually buys at a Jewish shop, look as shabby and crumpled on him as his old ones; he sees patients and dines and pays visits all in the same coat; but this is not due to niggardliness, but to complete carelessness about his appearance.

In most other parts of the ocean, however, where these fish do not so largely abound, their wondrous voracity can be at times considerably diminished, by vigorously stirring them up with sharp whaling-spades, a procedure notwithstanding, which, in some instances, only seems to tickle them into still greater activity. But it was not thus in the present case with the Pequod’s sharks; though, to be sure, any man unaccustomed to such sights, to have looked over her side that night, would have almost thought the whole round sea was one huge cheese, and those sharks the maggots in it. Nevertheless, upon Stubb setting the anchor-watch after his supper was concluded; and when, accordingly, Queequeg and a forecastle seaman came on deck, no small excitement was created among the sharks; for immediately suspending the cutting stages over the side, and lowering three lanterns, so that they cast long gleams of light over the turbid sea, these two mariners, darting their long whaling-spades, kept up an incessant murdering of the sharks,* by striking the keen steel deep into their skulls, seemingly their only vital part. But in the foamy confusion of their mixed and struggling hosts, the marksmen could not always hit their mark; and this brought about new revelations of the incredible ferocity of the foe. They viciously snapped, not only at each other’s disembowelments, but like flexible bows, bent round, and bit their own; till those entrails seemed swallowed over and over again by the same mouth, to be oppositely voided by the gaping wound. Nor was this all. It was unsafe to meddle with the corpses and ghosts of these creatures. A sort of generic or Pantheistic vitality seemed to lurk in their very joints and bones, after what might be called the individual life had departed. Killed and hoisted on deck for the sake of his skin, one of these sharks almost took poor Queequeg’s hand off, when he tried to shut down the dead lid of his murderous jaw.

Well, for the future, when you cook another whale-steak for my private table here, the capstan, I’ll tell you what to do so as not to spoil it by overdoing. Hold the steak in one hand, and show a live coal to it with the other; that done, dish it; d’ye hear? And now to-morrow, cook, when we are cutting in the fish, be sure you stand by to get the tips of his fins; have them put in pickle. As for the ends of the flukes, have them soused, cook. I’m bressed if he ain’t more of shark dan Massa Shark hisself,” muttered the old man, limping away; with which sage ejaculation he went to his hammock.

text: We drove on through the streets of Monte Carlo, past the Casino, and along the sea - front. The sun was shining, and the sea was a deep blue. There were yachts in the harbor, and people strolling along the promenade. It was a gay and festive scene, but I did not see it. I was thinking of Maxim de Winter, and of the look in his eyes when he had smiled at me. Mrs. Van Hopper was talking, as usual, about herself. She was telling me about the people she had met in Monte Carlo, and the parties she had been to. I listened to her with half an ear, nodding and making the appropriate responses at the right times, but my mind was elsewhere. Suddenly, Mrs. Van Hopper stopped speaking. I looked up and saw that we had stopped outside a large house on the outskirts of Monte Carlo. It was a magnificent house, built in the style of the Italian Renaissance, with tall columns and a large portico. There were gardens in front of the house, and a driveway that led up to the main entrance. "Where are we?" I asked. "This is the house of Maxim de Winter," Mrs. Van Hopper said. "He has invited us to lunch." I felt a sudden thrill of excitement run through me. I had not expected to see Maxim again so soon, and I was not sure how I would behave in his presence. I had never been to a house like this before, and I was afraid that I would make a fool of myself. "Come on," Mrs. Van Hopper said. "Don't look so nervous. You will be all right." She got out of the car, and I followed her. We walked up the driveway to the main entrance, and Mrs. Van Hopper rang the bell. A butler answered the door, and he showed us into a large hall. The hall was decorated with paintings and sculptures, and there was a grand staircase at the far end.

text: As Queequeg and I are now fairly embarked in this business of whaling; and as this business of whaling has somehow come to be regarded among landsmen as a rather unpoetical and disreputable pursuit; therefore, I am all anxiety to convince ye, ye landsmen, of the injustice hereby done to us hunters of whales. In the first place, it may be deemed almost superfluous to establish the fact, that among people at large, the business of whaling is not accounted on a level with what are called the liberal professions. If a stranger were introduced into any miscellaneous metropolitan society, it would but slightly advance the general opinion of his merits, were he presented to the company as a harpooneer, say; and if in emulation of the naval officers he should append the initials S.W.F. (Sperm Whale Fishery) to his visiting card, such a procedure would be deemed pre-eminently presuming and ridiculous. Doubtless one leading reason why the world declines honoring us whalemen, is this: they think that, at best, our vocation amounts to a butchering sort of business; and that when actively engaged therein, we are surrounded by all manner of defilements. Butchers we are, that is true. But butchers, also, and butchers of the bloodiest badge have been all Martial Commanders whom the world invariably delights to honor. And as for the matter of the alleged uncleanliness of our business, ye shall soon be initiated into certain facts hitherto pretty generally unknown, and which, upon the whole, will triumphantly plant the sperm whale-ship at least among the cleanliest things of this tidy earth. But even granting the charge in question to be true; what disordered slippery decks of a whale-ship are comparable to the unspeakable carrion of those battle-fields from which so many soldiers return to drink in all ladies’ plaudits? And if the idea of peril so much enhances the popular conceit of the soldier’s profession; let me assure ye that many a veteran who has freely marched up to a battery, would quickly recoil at the apparition of the sperm whale’s vast tail, fanning into eddies the air over his head. For what are the comprehensible terrors of man compared with the interlinked terrors and wonders of God!

text: It was with some difficulty that he found the way to his own house, which he approached with silent awe, expecting every moment to hear the shrill voice of Dame Van Winkle. Rip called him by name, but the cur snarled, showed his teeth, and passed on. This was an unkind cut indeed. “My very dog,” sighed poor Rip, “has forgotten me!” He entered the house, which, to tell the truth, Dame Van Winkle had always kept in neat order. It was empty, forlorn, and apparently abandoned. This desolateness overcame all his connubial fears—he called loudly for his wife and children—the lonely chambers rang for a moment with his voice, and then all again was silence. He now hurried forth, and hastened to his old resort, the village inn—but it too was gone. A large rickety wooden building stood in its place, with great gaping windows, some of them broken and mended with old hats and petticoats, and over the door was painted, “The Union Hotel, by Jonathan Doolittle.” Instead of the great tree that used to shelter the quiet little Dutch inn of yore, there now was reared a tall, naked pole, with something on the top that looked like a red nightcap, and from it was fluttering a flag, on which was a singular assemblage of stars and stripes;—all this was strange and incomprehensible. He recognised on the sign, however, the ruby face of King George, under which he had smoked so many a peaceful pipe; but even this was singularly metamorphosed. The red coat was changed for one of blue and buff, a sword was held in the hand instead of a sceptre, the head was decorated with a cocked hat, and underneath was painted in large characters, “General Washington.”

text: Now this ambergris is a very curious substance, and so important as an article of commerce, that in 1791 a certain Nantucket-born Captain Coffin was examined at the bar of the English House of Commons on that subject. For at that time, and indeed until a comparatively late day, the precise origin of ambergris remained, like amber itself, a problem to the learned. Though the word ambergris is but the French compound for grey amber, yet the two substances are quite distinct. For amber, though at times found on the sea-coast, is also dug up in some far inland soils, whereas ambergris is never found except upon the sea. Besides, amber is a hard, transparent, brittle, odorless substance, used for mouth-pieces to pipes, for beads and ornaments; but ambergris is soft, waxy, and so highly fragrant and spicy, that it is largely used in perfumery, in pastiles, precious candles, hair-powders, and pomatum. The Turks use it in cooking, and also carry it to Mecca, for the same purpose that frankincense is carried to St. Peter’s in Rome. Some wine merchants drop a few grains into claret, to flavor it. Who would think, then, that such fine ladies and gentlemen should regale themselves with an essence found in the inglorious bowels of a sick whale! Yet so it is. By some, ambergris is supposed to be the cause, and by others the effect, of the dyspepsia in the whale. How to cure such a dyspepsia it were hard to say, unless by administering three or four boat loads of Brandreth’s pills, and then running out of harm’s way, as laborers do in blasting rocks. I have forgotten to say that there were found in this ambergris, certain hard, round, bony plates, which at first Stubb thought might be sailors’ trowsers buttons; but it afterwards turned out that they were nothing more than pieces of small squid bones embalmed in that manner.

The reading and writing classes, however, were a great success. By the autumn almost every animal on the farm was literate in some degree. The pigs were far and away the most literate. They had already learned to read and write fairly well from the books. The dogs learned to read fairly well, but were interested only in the Seven Commandments. Muriel, the goat, could read somewhat better than the dogs, and sometimes used to read to the others in the evenings from scraps of newspaper which she found on the rubbish - heap. Benjamin could read as well as any pig, but never exercised his faculty. So far as he knew, he said, there was nothing worth reading. Clover learned the whole alphabet, but could not put words together. Boxer could never get beyond the letter D. He would trace out A, B, C, D, in the dust with his great hoof, and then would stand staring at the letters with his ears back, sometimes shaking his forelock, trying with all his might to remember what came next, but never succeeding. On several occasions, indeed, he did learn E, F, G, H, but by the time he knew them, he had forgotten A, B, C, D. Finally he decided to be content with the first four letters, and used to write them out once or twice every day to refresh his memory. text: “A nice spot,” cried Flask; “just let me prick him there once.” “Avast!” cried Starbuck, “there’s no need of that!” But humane Starbuck was too late. At the instant of the dart an ulcerous jet shot from this cruel wound, and goaded by it into more than sufferable anguish, the whale now spouting thick blood, with swift fury blindly darted at the craft, bespattering them and their glorying crews all over with showers of gore, capsizing Flask’s boat and marring the bows. It was his death stroke. For, by this time, so spent was he by loss of blood, that he helplessly rolled away from the wreck he had made; lay panting on his side, impotently flapped with his stumped fin, then over and over slowly revolved like a waning world; turned up the white secrets of his belly; lay like a log, and died. It was most piteous, that last expiring spout. As when by unseen hands the water is gradually drawn off from some mighty fountain, and with half-stifled melancholy gurglings the spray-column lowers and lowers to the ground—so the last long dying spout of the whale. Soon, while the crews were awaiting the arrival of the ship, the body showed symptoms of sinking with all its treasures unrifled. Immediately, by Starbuck’s orders, lines were secured to it at different points, so that ere long every boat was a buoy; the sunken whale being suspended a few inches beneath them by the cords. By very heedful management, when the ship drew nigh, the whale was transferred to her side, and was strongly secured there by the stiffest fluke-chains, for it was plain that unless artificially upheld, the body would at once sink to the bottom. It so chanced that almost upon first cutting into him with the spade, the entire length of a corroded harpoon was found imbedded in his flesh, on the lower part of the bunch before described. But as the stumps of harpoons are frequently found in the dead bodies of captured whales, with the flesh perfectly healed around them, and no prominence of any kind to denote their place; therefore, there must needs have been some other unknown reason in the present case fully to account for the ulceration alluded to. But still more curious was the fact of a lance-head of stone being found in him, not far from the buried iron, the flesh perfectly firm about it. Who had darted that stone lance? And when? It might have been darted by some Nor’ West Indian long before America was discovered.

text: The autumn sun filtered through the golden leaves of the birch trees, dappling the ground with light and shadow. Pierre Bezukhov walked slowly through the woods of his country estate, his hands stuffed in the pockets of his loose coat, his mind far from the grand parties and political talks of Moscow. He kicked at a fallen branch, watching it skitter across the path. For months, he'd felt adrift—unhappy in his marriage, bored by his wealth, unsure of why he was alive. The war had come and gone, taking friends and changing the world, but it had left him with more questions than answers. 'What is the point of it all?' he muttered, stopping to lean against a tree. The bark was rough against his shoulder, a sharp contrast to the soft silk of his shirts back in the city. He thought of his estate, his horses, his fine wines—all the things people envied, yet none of them brought him peace. A bird chirped overhead, and Pierre looked up. It was a small sparrow, hopping from branch to branch, busy with its own little life—finding food, building a nest, surviving. For a moment, he felt a twinge of envy. The sparrow had a purpose, even if it was simple. He continued walking, his boots crunching on the dry leaves. Up ahead, he saw an old peasant woman bending over a patch of potatoes, her hands calloused from work. She didn't look up when he passed, just kept digging, her movements steady and sure. 'Does she know something I don't?' Pierre wondered. She had no wealth, no title, no grand plans—but she seemed content, rooted in the earth, in the work of feeding herself and her family. He sat down on a fallen log, closing his eyes. The air smelled of pine and damp soil. He thought of the war, of the men he'd seen die, of the way life could end so suddenly. And then he thought of the sparrow, of the peasant woman—of how they lived, not for themselves alone, but for something smaller, something real. 'Maybe it's not about being great,' he said aloud, opening his eyes. 'Maybe it's about being good—about caring for the people around you, about doing small things with honesty.' The sun dipped lower, painting the sky pink and orange. Pierre stood up, feeling lighter than he had in months. He still didn't have all the answers, but he had a direction—a sense that life's meaning wasn't found in palaces or parties, but in the quiet, ordinary moments of love and work. He turned toward the house, his steps faster now, his mind clear. For the first time in years, he didn't feel lost. He felt like he was finally starting to find his way.

text: Next morning, Monday, after disposing of the embalmed head to a barber, for a block, I settled my own and comrade’s bill; using, however, my comrade’s money. The grinning landlord, as well as the boarders, seemed amazingly tickled at the sudden friendship which had sprung up between me and Queequeg—especially as Peter Coffin’s cock and bull stories about him had previously so much alarmed me concerning the very person whom I now companied with. We borrowed a wheelbarrow, and embarking our things, including my own poor carpet-bag, and Queequeg’s canvas sack and hammock, away we went down to “the Moss,” the little Nantucket packet schooner moored at the wharf. As we were going along the people stared; not at Queequeg so much—for they were used to seeing cannibals like him in their streets,—but at seeing him and me upon such confidential terms. But we heeded them not, going along wheeling the barrow by turns, and Queequeg now and then stopping to adjust the sheath on his harpoon barbs. I asked him why he carried such a troublesome thing with him ashore, and whether all whaling ships did not find their own harpoons. To this, in substance, he replied, that though what I hinted was true enough, yet he had a particular affection for his own harpoon, because it was of assured stuff, well tried in many a mortal combat, and deeply intimate with the hearts of whales. In short, like many inland reapers and mowers, who go into the farmers’ meadows armed with their own scythes—though in no wise obliged to furnish them—even so, Queequeg, for his own private reasons, preferred his own harpoon. Shifting the barrow from my hand to his, he told me a funny story about the first wheelbarrow he had ever seen. It was in Sag Harbor. The owners of his ship, it seems, had lent him one, in which to carry his heavy chest to his boarding house. Not to seem ignorant about the thing—though in truth he was entirely so, concerning the precise way in which to manage the barrow—Queequeg puts his chest upon it; lashes it fast; and then shoulders the barrow and marches up the wharf. “Why,” said I, “Queequeg, you might have known better than that, one would think. Didn’t the people laugh?”

text: Mr. Erskine was counsel for the defendants; Lord Ellenborough was the judge. In the course of the defence, the witty Erskine went on to illustrate his position, by alluding to a recent crim. con. case, wherein a gentleman, after in vain trying to bridle his wife’s viciousness, had at last abandoned her upon the seas of life; but in the course of years, repenting of that step, he instituted an action to recover possession of her. Erskine was on the other side; and he then supported it by saying, that though the gentleman had originally harpooned the lady, and had once had her fast, and only by reason of the great stress of her plunging viciousness, had at last abandoned her; yet abandon her he did, so that she became a loose-fish; and therefore when a subsequent gentleman re-harpooned her, the lady then became that subsequent gentleman’s property, along with whatever harpoon might have been found sticking in her. Now in the present case Erskine contended that the examples of the whale and the lady were reciprocally illustrative of each other. These pleadings, and the counter pleadings, being duly heard, the very learned judge in set terms decided, to wit,—That as for the boat, he awarded it to the plaintiffs, because they had merely abandoned it to save their lives; but that with regard to the controverted whale, harpoons, and line, they belonged to the defendants; the whale, because it was a Loose-Fish at the time of the final capture; and the harpoons and line because when the fish made off with them, it (the fish) acquired a property in those articles; and hence anybody who afterwards took the fish had a right to them. Now the defendants afterwards took the fish; ergo, the aforesaid articles were theirs.

text: The next thing I remember is, waking up with a feeling as if I had had a frightful nightmare, and seeing before me a terrible red glare, crossed with thick black bars. I heard voices, too, speaking with a hollow sound, and as if muffled by a rush of wind or water: agitation, uncertainty, and an all - predominating sense of terror confused my faculties. Ere long, I became aware that some one was handling me; lifting me up and supporting me in a sitting posture, and that more tenderly than I had ever been raised or upheld before. I rested my head against a pillow or an arm, and felt easy. In five minutes more the cloud of bewilderment dissolved: I knew quite well that I was in my own bed, and that the red glare was the nursery fire. It was night: a candle burnt on the table; Bessie stood at the bed - foot with a basin in her hand, and a gentleman sat in a chair near my pillow, leaning over me. I felt an inexpressible relief, a soothing conviction of protection and security, when I knew that there was a stranger in the room, an individual not belonging to Gateshead, and not related to Mrs. Reed. Turning from Bessie (though her presence was far less obnoxious to me than that of Abbot, for instance, would have been), I scrutinised the face of the gentleman: I knew him; it was Mr. Lloyd, an apothecary, sometimes called in by Mrs. Reed when the servants were ailing: for herself and the children she employed a physician. "Well, who am I?" he asked. I pronounced his name, offering him at the same time my hand: he took it, smiling and saying, "We shall do very well by - and - by." Then he laid me down, and addressing Bessie, charged her to be very careful that I was not disturbed during the night. Having given some further directions, and intimates that he should call again the next day, he departed; to my grief: I felt so sheltered and befriended while he sat in the chair near my pillow; and as he closed the door after him, all the room darkened and my heart again sank: inexpressible sadness weighed it down. "Do you feel as if you should sleep, miss?" asked Bessie, rather softly. Scarcely dared I answer her; for I feared the next sentence might be rough. "I will try." "Would you like to drink, or could you eat anything?" "No, thank you, Bessie." "Then I think I shall go to bed, for it is past twelve o'clock; but you may call me if you want anything in the night."
