text: The rain beat against the windowpanes of Thornfield Hall, its rhythm slow and relentless, matching the weight in Jane Eyre's chest. She stood by the casement, her hands folded tightly at her waist, staring out at the dark gardens where the roses bent under the downpour—their petals clinging to their stems, stubborn even in the storm. "I will not be broken," she whispered, her voice barely audible over the rain. Memories of Lowood School flooded back: the cold dormitories, the thin porridge, Miss Scatcherd's sharp words that had cut deeper than any frost. She'd learned then to hold fast to herself, to wrap her pride around her like a cloak when the world tried to tear her down. A floorboard creaked in the hallway, and Jane tensed—half-expecting Mrs. Fairfax's soft knock, half-dreading the quiet reminder of her place here: a governess, hired to teach a child, nothing more. But no knock came. The house was still, save for the rain and the distant hoot of an owl. She turned from the window, her eyes falling on the small book she'd left on her desk—Paradise Lost, its pages worn from repeated reading. She'd found solace in its words, in the idea that even in suffering, there was a chance to choose one's path. "I am not an angel," she said aloud, as if arguing with an unseen critic. "I cannot live without my soul." The thought of Mr. Rochester crossed her mind—his deep voice, his sharp eyes that seemed to see past her plain dress to the fire beneath. But she pushed the thought away. To rely on his regard would be to give up the very thing she'd fought for: her independence. She'd rather walk back to Lowood, to hunger and cold, than be someone's possession, someone's pretty toy to be set aside when the novelty faded. She stepped to the mirror, her reflection pale but steady. The girl who'd cowered at Gateshead was gone—replaced by a woman who knew her worth, who refused to be diminished. "You have a heart and a mind of your own," she told her reflection. "Use them." The rain slowed, and a faint streak of moonlight broke through the clouds, casting a silver line across the floor. Jane took a deep breath, feeling the tension in her shoulders ease. Whatever the future held—whether Thornfield, or something unknown—she would face it as herself: unyielding, unapologetic, and free. She picked up her book, opening it to her favorite passage, and settled into her chair. The night was still long, but for the first time in weeks, Jane Eyre did not feel alone. She felt strong—strong enough to hold onto her soul, no matter what the world threw at her.

text: The dawn in Santiago’s skiff on the Gulf Stream was pale—pale enough that the first light seeped over the horizon in soft gray streaks and the sound of the ocean lapping against the hull blended with the faint creak of the mast, mixing with the bitter smell of cold coffee from the tin can at his feet. He sat on the weathered wooden deck (his hands calloused and stained from the fishing line, his shirt stiff with salt), the heavy line tight in his right hand (wrapped around his palm to keep it from cutting, the way he’d done for forty years) and a crust of hard bread in his left, his eyes fixed on the dark water below, where the marlin pulled steadily, unseen but unyielding. The skiff smelled of fish blood (from the small tuna he’d caught the day before) and pine resin (from the plug he used to seal the hull), and his old canvas jacket—frayed at the cuffs, the one he’d worn through two hurricanes—lay draped over the stern, a quiet reminder of the storms he’d survived. He thought of the day he’d taught Manolin to cast a line—of the way the boy had stumbled, his small hands fumbling with the reel, saying “Santiago, I’ll never get it right,” of the way he’d laughed and showed him again, slow and patient, of the way the boy’s eyes had lit up when he finally hooked a sardine, his face bright with pride. He’d been alone since Manolin’s parents had made him fish with another boat, he thought—not just alone in the skiff, but alone in the way only old men are when the sea is their only companion—but lately, the line in his hand felt like a lifeline: not just to the marlin, but to the part of him that refused to give up, the part that still believed in “salao” being just bad luck, not a sentence. A seagull cried overhead, and he blinked, returning to the present. He shifted his grip on the line, wincing as the rough cord rubbed against a raw spot on his palm, and reached down to sip from the coffee can. He thought of the stories the other fishermen told—of big marlins that got away, of men who lost their nerve, of boats that sank in sudden gales—and he smiled. He wasn’t like them, he thought. He didn’t care about the money or the praise; he cared about the fight, about proving to himself that he still had it in him to be a good fisherman, to be a man. He tightened his hold on the line again, feeling the marlin’s pull grow stronger, more determined. It was tired, he could tell—tired the way he was tired—but it wasn’t giving up. Neither was he, he decided. He’d stay with it as long as it took, even if his hands bled, even if his back ached, even if the sun burned his skin raw. It was a small thing, this fight, but it was his, a way to bridge the gap between the young man he’d been and the old man he was now. He thought of Manolin’s smile, of the taste of fresh fish cooked over a fire, of the way the sea looked at dawn when the light turned the water pink, and for a second, he didn’t feel lonely anymore—he felt alive, not just a fisherman or an old man, but Santiago, the boy who’d once dreamed of catching the biggest marlin in the Gulf, finally seeing that the dream wasn’t about the fish, but about the fight itself.

text: Now the sun was hotter as it rose and the old man felt it on his back and he knew he was rowing well but he had not yet seen the bird again. He did not remember when he had first started to talk aloud when he was by himself. He had sung at nights sometimes when he was alone steering on his watch in the smacks or in the turtle boats. He had probably started to talk aloud when alone when the boy had left. But he did not remember. He and the boy had talked little and only when it was necessary. They talked at night or when they were storm - bound by bad weather. It was considered a virtue not to talk unnecessarily at sea and the old man had always considered it so and respected it. But now he said his thoughts aloud many times since there was no one that they could annoy. "If the others heard me talking out loud they would think that I am crazy," he said aloud. "But since I am not crazy, I do not care." The radio announced the baseball games of the American League and the National League. He could not follow them now but he knew that the great players were in the game and he knew that the Yankees would win against all the others. But he did not know whether the Mets had won today. "There is always something to think about," he said. "But I have no thoughts for them now." The old man could see the white, wide - open tail of the male and the quick darting of the female as she swam. text: He had, besides the things before mentioned, twelve marbles, part of a jew’s-harp, a piece of blue bottle-glass to look through, a spool cannon, a key that wouldn’t unlock anything, a fragment of chalk, a glass stopper of a decanter, a tin soldier, a couple of tadpoles, six fire-crackers, a kitten with only one eye, a brass doorknob, and a dog-collar—but no dog—the latter having been traded away for a fraction of a kite. He had had a nice, good, idle time all the while—plenty of company—and the fence had three coats of whitewash on it! If he hadn’t run out of whitewash he would have bankrupted every boy in the village. Tom said to himself that it was not such a hollow world, after all. He had discovered a great law of human action, without knowing it—namely, that in order to make a man or a boy covet a thing, it is only necessary to make the thing difficult to attain. If he had been a great and wise philosopher, like the writer of this book, he would now have comprehended that Work consists of whatever a body is obliged to do, and that Play consists of whatever a body is not obliged to do. And this would help him to understand why constructing artificial flowers or performing on a treadmill is work, while rolling ten-pins or climbing Mont Blanc is only amusement. There are wealthy gentlemen in England who drive four-horse passenger-coaches twenty or thirty miles on a daily line, in the summer, because the privilege costs them considerable money; but if they were offered wages for the service, that would turn it into work and then they would resign. Tom’s mind was made up now. He was content. He having faithfully fulfilled his contract with Aunt Polly, he reaped the reward of his virtue. She inspected the fence with great satisfaction, and said: “Tom, I didn’t think you’d have the job done so well and so quick. It looks splendid, Tom. You might have a rest tomorrow.” Tom’s heart leaped for joy—he had got out of the whole thing.

text:
AN AVENGER
SHORTLY after finding his wife in flagrante delicto Fyodor Fyodorovitch Sigaev was standing in Schmuck and Co.‘s, the gunsmiths, selecting a suitable revolver. His countenance expressed wrath, grief, and unalterable determination.

“I know what I must do,” he was thinking. “The sanctities of the home are outraged, honour is trampled in the mud, vice is triumphant, and therefore as a citizen and a man of honour I must be their avenger. First, I will kill her and her lover and then myself.”

He had not yet chosen a revolver or killed anyone, but already in imagination he saw three bloodstained corpses, broken skulls, brains oozing from them, the commotion, the crowd of gaping spectators, the post-mortem. . . . With the malignant joy of an insulted man he pictured the horror of the relations and the public, the agony of the traitress, and was mentally reading leading articles on the destruction of the traditions of the home.

The shopman, a sprightly little Frenchified figure with rounded belly and white waistcoat, displayed the revolvers, and smiling respectfully and scraping with his little feet observed:

“. . . I would advise you, M’sieur, to take this superb revolver, the Smith and Wesson pattern, the last word in the science of firearms: triple-action, with ejector, kills at six hundred paces, central sight. Let me draw your attention, M’sieu, to the beauty of the finish. The most fashionable system, M’sieu. We sell a dozen every day for burglars, wolves, and lovers. Very correct and powerful action, hits at a great distance, and kills wife and lover with one bullet. As for suicide, M’sieu, I don’t know a better pattern.”

The shopman pulled and cocked the trigger, breathed on the barrel, took aim, and affected to be breathless with delight. Looking at his ecstatic countenance, one might have supposed that he would readily have put a bullet through his brains if he had only possessed a revolver of such a superb pattern as a Smith-Wesson.

“And what price?” asked Sigaev.

“Forty-five roubles, M’sieu.”

“Mm! . . . that’s too dear for me.”

text: The carriage rolled along the smooth gravel drive, and Elizabeth's eyes widened as Pemberley House came into view—its white stone facade gleaming in the morning sun, its columns standing tall and graceful, its windows reflecting the soft blue of the sky. Mr. Gardiner, her uncle, leaned forward with a smile. "Well, Lizzy, what do you think? Worth the journey, is it not?" Elizabeth nodded, unable to find words. She had expected grandeur—had heard tales of Darcy's wealth—but nothing had prepared her for the quiet elegance of the place, the way the house blended seamlessly with the rolling hills and the tranquil lake beyond. They stepped down from the carriage, and the gardener, an elderly man with a weathered face, greeted them warmly. "Mr. Darcy is not at home, sir," he said to Mr. Gardiner, "but he bade me show you the grounds and the house—any part you wish to see. He said visitors from Meryton are always welcome." Elizabeth's heart skipped a beat. Darcy had remembered her connection to Meryton, had gone out of his way to be kind—despite the harsh words they had exchanged at the ball, despite her refusal of his proposal. They wandered through the gardens first: beds of vibrant roses in full bloom, paths lined with lavender that filled the air with its sweet scent, a small waterfall trickling into a pond where ducks floated lazily. The gardener pointed out trees that had been planted by Darcy's father, flower beds tended to by Darcy himself every morning when he was at home. "He's a good master, miss," the old man said, noticing Elizabeth's interest. "Kind to the servants, generous to the village. Never turns away anyone in need." Elizabeth listened, a strange feeling settling in her chest—regret, perhaps, or something softer. She thought of Wickham's tales of Darcy's cruelty, of her own willingness to believe the worst of him, of how she had judged him without knowing the truth. The house, when they entered, was no less impressive: high ceilings, tasteful furnishings, walls adorned with paintings that felt like old friends rather than ostentatious displays. In the library, shelves stretched from floor to ceiling, filled with books that showed a mind curious and well-read. "He spends many hours here, sir," the gardener said. "Especially in the evenings, when the house is quiet." As they climbed the stairs to the bedrooms, Elizabeth caught sight of a portrait hanging in the hallway—a painting of Darcy, done when he was a young man. His features were the same—sharp, proud, handsome—but there was a softness in his eyes that she had never noticed before. She stared at it, her thoughts racing. This was not the arrogant, unfeeling man she had thought she knew. This was a man who loved his home, who cared for his servants, who had a heart that, despite his reserve, was capable of kindness.

It would have been easy to lengthen the list of Arab authors here made use of; but little would have been gained for Geography by reference to works equally deficient in judgment and originality. The authors chiefly relied on are, El Bekrí, Ibn Khaldún, and Ibn Baṭúṭah. El Idrísí is analysed in some passages, chiefly for the sake of explaining certain discrepancies between him and the first-named writer, and to estimate the weight due to his authority. The conjectures scattered through the following pages are much fewer than the nature of the subject and the course of investigation would have permitted; but it was thought advisable to keep conjectures within bounds, even where they could not have interfered with the reasoning. Reserve and circumspection are especially necessary for an author whose conclusions differ widely from those of his precursors in the same field of inquiry, and who aims at deciding definitively questions which have long divided the judgments of the learned. Reference to the systems of recent authors has been, in general, avoided, lest the frequent recurrence of the language of refutation might give the whole an air of controversy. Pains have been also taken to abridge whatever was not strictly geographical, the object here aimed at being properly the consideration of geographical questions, the careful and satisfactory discussion of which demands a special treatise.

The mode here adopted of writing the Arabic names, is fully explained in the Journal of the Royal Geographical Society, vol. VII. p. 245; but in its application will probably be found much unsteadiness and imperfection, arising partly from the want of familiarity with it, and partly from the difficulty of setting exact bounds to the employment of a foreign orthography, which jars disagreeably with the necessary reference to the orthography of our modern travellers.

text: The warm summer sun shone down on Piccadilly, gilding the tops of the buses and turning the shop windows into pools of light. Clarissa Dalloway walked slowly, her gloved hand loosely holding the string of pearls around her neck, her mind wandering like the pigeons that fluttered across the pavement. The air smelled of fresh bread from the bakery, of petrol from the passing cars, of the faint, sweet perfume of lilacs someone carried in a bouquet. For a moment, she felt young again—younger than the middle-aged woman she was, the wife of Richard Dalloway, the hostess planning a dinner party that evening. She passed a park bench where she and Peter Walsh had sat as teenagers, laughing and arguing, dreaming of the lives they would lead. 'We thought we'd change the world,' she whispered to herself, a faint smile playing on her lips. But the world had changed them instead—Peter had gone to India, married a woman Clarissa had never met, and she had settled into the quiet routine of a politician's wife, her days filled with teas and committee meetings, her nights with dinners and small talk. She thought of Sally Seton, the wild, passionate girl who had once kissed her in the garden at Bourton, who had promised they would live 'free as birds.' Now Sally was married too, a mother of five, her fire dimmed by domesticity. A breeze picked up, lifting the hem of her dress, and Clarissa closed her eyes, breathing in the scent of the city. She thought of Septimus Warren Smith, the young veteran she had heard about—shell-shocked, haunted by the war, a man who had lost his grip on life. 'We all live lives of quiet desperation,' she thought, a shiver running down her spine. Not that her life was desperate—not really. She had a loving husband, a comfortable home, friends who admired her. But there was something missing, something she had felt as a girl, something that had faded like the memory of Bourton's garden. She opened her eyes, watching a group of children chase each other down the street, their voices loud and carefree. For a moment, she envied them—their lack of self-consciousness, their ability to live in the moment. She had spent so much of her life performing, of being 'Mrs. Dalloway,' that she sometimes forgot who Clarissa was beneath the pearls and the polite smiles. 'I am more than a hostess,' she said silently. 'I am more than a wife.'

text: A ceramic vase is a delicate, decorative, and practical artwork made by shaping clay, glazing, and firing it at high temperatures to create a hard, smooth, and durable container widely used in homes, exhibitions, and cultural ceremonies. Its appearance varies greatly in shape, including tall cylindrical forms, curved bottle shapes, wide-mouthed bowls, and slender elegant designs, often decorated with painted patterns, carved textures, colored glazes, or traditional motifs that reflect artistic styles of different regions and eras. Ceramic vases originated in ancient civilizations and have evolved into important art pieces representing craftsmanship, aesthetics, and cultural identity. Fine porcelain vases feature translucent surfaces, delicate colors, and smooth textures, while pottery vases show rougher, more natural textures with earthy tones. Many vases display hand-painted scenes of flowers, landscapes, birds, or traditional patterns, turning simple containers into beautiful decorative artworks. Functionally, ceramic vases hold fresh or dried flowers, decorate living rooms, studies, and halls, and preserve cultural traditions as collectible items. In traditional ceremonies, vases symbolize prosperity, beauty, and harmony, often used as gifts for festivals, weddings, and important celebrations. Collectors value ancient ceramic vases for their historical significance, craftsmanship rarity, and artistic charm. Modern artists continue to innovate vase designs, combining traditional techniques with contemporary aesthetics to create unique and fashionable pieces. Ceramic vases are durable, easy to clean, and resistant to corrosion, maintaining their appearance for many years. Museums display valuable antique vases to show the development of ceramic art and cultural heritage. Creating a fine ceramic vase requires skillful shaping, precise glazing, and controlled firing, with every step influencing the final quality. As both practical utensils and artistic treasures, ceramic vases bridge daily life and art, bringing beauty and culture into ordinary spaces. Their elegant shapes, rich decorations, and long history make them beloved artworks worldwide.

text:
Gross anatomy of a monocotyl stem.—Obtain a fresh cornstalk,—preferably one that has begun to tassel,—and observe its external characters. How are the internodes divided from one another? What is the use of the very firm, smooth epidermis? Notice a hollow, grooved channel running down one side between the joints, or nodes; does it occur in all of them? Is it on the same side or on the opposite sides of alternate internodes? Follow one of these grooves to the node from which it originates; what do you find there? After studying the internal structure of the stalk, you will understand why this groove should occur on the side of an internode bearing a bud or fruit.

Cut a cross section midway between two nodes, and observe the composition of the interior; of what does the bulk of it appear to consist? Notice the arrangement of the little dots, like the ends of cut-off threads, that are scattered through the pith; where are they most abundant, toward the center or the circumference? Make a vertical section through one of the nodes. Cut a thin slice of the pith, hold it up to the light, and examine with a hand lens. Observe that it is composed of a number of oblong cells packed together like bricks in a wall. These are filled with protoplasm and cell sap, and constitute what is known to botanists as the parenchyma or fundamental tissue from which all the other tissues are derived. Apply the iodine test; in what parts does starch occur most abundantly?

Draw out one of the woody threads running through the pith. Break away a bit of the epidermis, and see how very closely they are packed on its inner surface. Trace the course of the veins in the bases of the leaves; find their point of union with the stem; with what part of it do they appear to be continuous? Has this anything to do with the greater abundance of fibers near the epidermis? Can you follow the fibers through the nodes, or do they become confused and intermixed with other threads there? (If a stalk of sugar cane can be obtained, the ring of scars left by the vascular bundles as they pass from the leaves into the stem will be seen beautifully marked just above the nodes.)

If there is an eye or bud at the node, see if any of the threads go into it. Can you account now for the depression that occurs in the internode above the eye?

Make drawings of both cross and vertical sections, showing the points brought out in your examination of the cornstalk.

text:
George walked on for some way, pondering over what he had heard, and then all of a sudden broke out into a loud whistle. It was a clear, triumphant sound, telling of a victory gained over self. George was merrier than ever that evening, and amused his mother and Janet with an account of all that had gone on at the night school. He said not a word about Larkins, however, and went to bed with the determination of rising with the lark the following morning.


He woke long before daybreak, so anxious was he to begin painting, and by the time he had dressed himself, and got a pair of steps from a neighbour's yard (he had asked for the loan of them the night before), it was light enough for him to begin work. It was only in one part that the wall required painting. And George found that he should have enough paint and to spare, even after he had given the wall a second coat.

His face beamed with pleasure as he made this discovery. What was he going to do with the paint he should have left? No doubt he would be glad to paint a certain chest which his father had once given him. A coat of paint would make it as good as new, and it looked very shabby at present. George had often longed to be able to paint it. He had finished giving the first coat to the cottage wall long before it was time for him to go to work. Upon entering the cottage, he found Janet busy at work lighting the fire.

"Have you got all that paint to spare, George?" she cried, as she looked into the paint-pot.

"I must paint the wall over again to-night, Janet; but even then I shall have a good bit of paint to spare."

"Then you can do your chest, George, and my stool, and Edwin's little cart, and—"

"Nay, nay, Janet, I have something else to do with my paint," cried George, as he put about half of that which remained into an old paint-pot belonging to his father, and left the cottage, carrying the rest with him.

Larkins lived in the same street as George Horbrook. He was standing moodily at the door of his father-in-law's cottage, thinking over the events of the last night, when he saw George Horbrook approaching, paint-pot in hand.

He put on a sort of defiant look, for he thought George was come to make game of him.

text: It was not a great while after the affair of the pipe, that one morning shortly after breakfast, Ahab, as was his wont, ascended the cabin-gangway to the deck. There most sea-captains usually walk at that hour, as country gentlemen, after the same meal, take a few turns in the garden. Soon his steady, ivory stride was heard, as to and fro he paced his old rounds, upon planks so familiar to his tread, that they were all over dented, like geological stones, with the peculiar mark of his walk. Did you fixedly gaze, too, upon that ribbed and dented brow; there also, you would see still stranger foot-prints—the foot-prints of his one unsleeping, ever-pacing thought. But on the occasion in question, those dents looked deeper, even as his nervous step that morning left a deeper mark. And, so full of his thought was Ahab, that at every uniform turn that he made, now at the main-mast and now at the binnacle, you could almost see that thought turn in him as he turned, and pace in him as he paced; so completely possessing him, indeed, that it all but seemed the inward mould of every outer movement. “D’ye mark him, Flask?” whispered Stubb; “the chick that’s in him pecks the shell. ’Twill soon be out.” The hours wore on;—Ahab now shut up within his cabin; anon, pacing the deck, with the same intense bigotry of purpose in his aspect. It drew near the close of day. Suddenly he came to a halt by the bulwarks, and inserting his bone leg into the auger-hole there, and with one hand grasping a shroud, he ordered Starbuck to send everybody aft. “Sir!” said the mate, astonished at an order seldom or never given on ship-board except in some extraordinary case. “Send everybody aft,” repeated Ahab. “Mast-heads, there! come down!”

text: Oil painting is a classic, expressive, and internationally influential art form that uses pigments mixed with drying oil on canvas, wood panels, or cardboard, characterized by rich colors, strong texture, layered coverage, and long-lasting preservation. It features vivid color expression, smooth or textured brushstrokes, strong light and shadow contrast, and realistic or abstract visual effects that meet diverse aesthetic needs. Oil paints allow artists to create layered, blended colors, thick impasto textures, and delicate details, enabling the performance of portraits, landscapes, still life, history paintings, and abstract compositions. Unlike other painting media, oil paints dry slowly, allowing artists to modify, blend, and adjust over an extended period, achieving precise and rich artistic effects. Traditional oil painting emphasizes realistic representation, perspective, light source, and spatial structure, while modern styles include impressionism, expressionism, cubism, and surrealism, expanding creative boundaries. The canvas surface is usually treated with gesso to provide a stable, absorbent foundation that protects the paint layer. Artists use brushes of various sizes, palette knives, rags, and even fingers to create different textures and strokes. Oil paintings have strong durability, resisting fading and deterioration for hundreds of years when properly preserved, making them highly collectible. Many classic oil paintings are preserved in major museums worldwide as treasures of human art. Oil painting training emphasizes color theory, sketching foundation, modeling ability, and creative thinking. As a major art form in Western art history, oil painting has profoundly influenced global artistic development and has been widely integrated and innovated in Eastern art contexts. Modern oil painting combines traditional techniques with contemporary concepts, expressing social phenomena, emotional experiences, and philosophical thoughts. Its rich color, flexible expression, and long-lasting quality make oil painting one of the most respected and valuable art forms. It carries human emotion, aesthetic pursuit, and cultural memory through visual language.

text: The midnight in Tomas’s solitude in his Prague apartment was quiet—quiet enough that the tick of the antique clock on the mantel blended with the faint hum of the refrigerator and the sound of distant streetcars (their bells echoing through empty streets) , mixing with the cool, paper-scented air of the books piled on the coffee table. He sat on the wooden chair (its legs uneven, propped up with a folded napkin) , a beat-up Leica camera in his right hand (Teresa’s, she’d left it when she’d gone back to the country, said it “carried too many memories”) and a crumpled letter from Sabina in his left (her handwriting elegant, words laced with that familiar irony: “Freedom’s just another kind of cage, Tomas—don’t you see?”) , his eyes fixed on the window, where the lights of Prague Castle glowed faintly through the mist—each flicker a reminder of the choices he’d made: leaving Geneva for her, trading casual lovers for quiet nights, swapping the lightness of detachment for the weight of commitment. The air smelled of coffee (from the half-empty mug on the side table) and ink (from the pen he’d been using to write medical notes) , and his white coat—still stained with antiseptic from the hospital—hung over the back of the chair, a quiet reminder of the life he’d once lived: the operating room’s precision, the fleeting intimacy of one-night stands, the belief that “lightness” was the only way to avoid being crushed by life’s weight. He thought of the day Teresa had first arrived at his apartment—of the way she’d stood in the doorway, rain-soaked and nervous, holding a suitcase and that same camera, of the way he’d hesitated before letting her in, of the way she’d taken a photo of him sleeping that night, a photo he’d found later tucked in his medical textbook. He’d thought love was a choice then, he realized—not just a feeling, but a decision to keep choosing someone, even when the lightness of freedom called louder. But now, the camera in his hand felt like a paradox: not just a tool to capture moments, but a symbol of the contradiction in his chest—the way he craved the quiet weight of Teresa’s presence, yet still missed the lightness of walking away, the way he’d chosen commitment but still wondered what it would be like to be unshackled again. A gust of wind rattled the window, and he flinched, tucking the camera into his lap as if protecting it from the night. He could hear a neighbor’s radio playing a folk song, soft and mournful, and for a second, he wanted to turn it off—to silence the reminder of the country Teresa loved, the country he’d never fully embraced. He thought of what Kundera had said to him once (or was it something he’d read? The line between memory and philosophy blurred) : “The heaviest of burdens crushes us, we sink beneath it, it pins us to the ground. But in love, the heaviness becomes lightness.” He’d scoffed then, thinking it was just romantic nonsense, just another way people lied to themselves about the weight of love. But now, as he sat there, listening to the clock tick and the streetcar bells fade, he wondered if it was true. Maybe weight wasn’t a cage, he thought—maybe it was a anchor, maybe the “lightness” he’d chased for so long was just emptiness, maybe loving Teresa wasn’t a burden but the only thing that made him feel real, feel like he wasn’t just floating through life.

text: In a quiet suburban backyard, the firefly observer spread a checkered blanket on the grass and sat cross-legged, her eyes fixed on the growing twilight. As the sun dipped below the roofline, tiny fireflies began to emerge—each a small, glowing speck with soft, amber light flickering from their abdomens. They flitted in erratic, bouncy paths, their light winking on and off like scattered stars fallen to earth, while the surrounding oak trees stood as tall, shadowy silhouettes against the indigo sky.The air felt warm, carrying the sweet, heady scent of jasmine from a nearby bush, and the grass beneath the blanket was still soft from the afternoon’s light rain, leaving a cool, damp tingle on her bare ankles. She held her breath, watching a cluster of fireflies hover above a patch of daisies; their glowing lights synchronized for a moment, creating a gentle, pulsing glow before they scattered again. A faint, rustling breeze passed through, carrying the distant chirp of crickets and making the fireflies’ light sway slightly as they flew.As darkness deepened, more fireflies appeared, their glowing bodies turning the backyard into a magical, twinkling landscape. The observer smiled, leaning back to stare up at the way their light cut through the dim air—soft, warm, and fleeting. The sweet jasmine scent lingered, mixing with the earthy smell of damp soil, and the warm air wrapped around her like a soft shawl. For a while, she just sat there, letting the quiet magic of the glowing fireflies and the gentle summer night wash over her, a small, perfect moment of connection with nature’s quiet wonders.

text: "I see none. A promise is a promise,—certainly not 'less' when spoken to God than when spoken to man." "Well, I am tired of the subject," said Diana pettishly. "The upshot of it all is that you encourage Beryl to set up herself against me." "You mistake me," said Millicent quietly. "I should be very sorry to see Beryl opposing you for the sake of opposition. She owes you far too much. But I think you will agree with me here, when you have considered the matter. Children, is it not a pity you should waste your morning indoors this fine day?" She often call them "children" thus, in her motherly tender way, and the boys liked the word from her lips, though a good many young fellows of their age would not have liked it. "Why not take a walk—Beryl and Pearl and Ivor?" "And Escott," her other son said. "Are you up to it this morning?" Escott said, "Quite," and a general stir followed. Millicent went out of the room with them, and when the quartette had disappeared, she came back, to find Diana shedding angry tears. "As if I had not worry enough already," she said. "It really is too bad. The girl will be perfectly unbearable." "But, Di, it is evidently a question of conscience." "Oh, nonsense! I don't believe it. She likes oppose me, and to make a fuss. Conscience is the excuse for everything in these days. But I intend to have my own way in the matter. I will not be baulked by a girl's whims." "I hardly see how you can obtain your way. It would be better to yield gracefully in the beginning than to be defeated in the end, putting aside more serious considerations. Beryl has simply to tell Mr. Bishop that she has no wish for Confirmation, or even to do no more than decline to answer any questions, and she will not be admitted." "Beryl will do what I choose, or she will be sorry for it. Why, I had no such fuss with Pearl. She said 'Yes' at once, and went through the classes, and I am sure she looked a perfect picture in her white veil. Everybody was noticing her. She was like a little bride." Millicent felt that the discussion was hopeless. "As for making such a fuss about feelings, the less people say the more they feel, as a rule. I don't believe in all that talk about religion. It is a pure case of conceit and obstinacy. Beryl likes to go against me on all occasions, and always did. But she shall learn to submit, or I will have no more to do with her. Not wish for Confirmation, indeed! Your boys were not so absurd, say what you like in defence of Beryl." "They did wish for it, Di. That made all the difference." "Of course they did, and so would any person with proper feelings. 'I' wished it when I was a girl. I never thought of putting it off. And it is not that your boys are so tremendously religious either. Escott may be inclined that way—sickly people often are,—but Ivor is just like any other young man."

text:
“Hey, take his little coat!” Deniska shouted from somewhere far below.
His coat and bundle flung up from far below fell close to Yegorushka. Anxious not to think of anything, he quickly put his bundle under his head and covered himself with his coat, and stretching his legs out and shrinking a little from the dew, he laughed with content.
“Sleep, sleep, sleep, . . .” he thought.
“Don’t be unkind to him, you devils!” he heard Deniska’s voice below.
“Good-bye, lads; good luck to you,” shouted Kuzmitchov. “I rely upon you!”
“Don’t you be uneasy, Ivan Ivanitch!”
Deniska shouted to the horses, the chaise creaked and started, not along the road, but somewhere off to the side. For two minutes there was silence, as though the waggons were asleep and there was no sound except the clanking of the pails tied on at the back of the chaise as it slowly died away in the distance. Then someone at the head of the waggons shouted:
“Kiruha! Sta-art!”
The foremost of the waggons creaked, then the second, then the third. . . . Yegorushka felt the waggon he was on sway and creak also. The waggons were moving. Yegorushka took a tighter hold of the cord with which the bales were tied on, laughed again with content, shifted the cake in his pocket, and fell asleep just as he did in his bed at home. . . .
When he woke up the sun had risen, it was screened by an ancient barrow, and, trying to shed its light upon the earth, it scattered its beams in all directions and flooded the horizon with gold. It seemed to Yegorushka that it was not in its proper place, as the day before it had risen behind his back, and now it was much more to his left. . . . And the whole landscape was different. There were no hills now, but on all sides, wherever one looked, there stretched the brown cheerless plain; here and there upon it small barrows rose up and rooks flew as they had done the day before. The belfries and huts of some village showed white in the distance ahead; as it was Sunday the Little Russians were at home baking and cooking—that could be seen by the smoke which rose from every chimney and hung, a dark blue transparent veil, over the village. In between the huts and beyond the church there were blue glimpses of a river, and beyond the river a misty distance. But nothing was so different from yesterday as the road. Something extraordinarily broad, spread out and titanic, stretched over the steppe by way of a road.

text: We resumed business; and while plying our spoons in the bowl, thinks I to myself, I wonder now if this here has any effect on the head? What’s that stultifying saying about chowder-headed people? “But look, Queequeg, ain’t that a live eel in your bowl? Where’s your harpoon?” Fishiest of all fishy places was the Try Pots, which well deserved its name; for the pots there were always boiling chowders. Chowder for breakfast, and chowder for dinner, and chowder for supper, till you began to look for fish-bones coming through your clothes. The area before the house was paved with clam-shells. Mrs. Hussey wore a polished necklace of codfish vertebra; and Hosea Hussey had his account books bound in superior old shark-skin. There was a fishy flavor to the milk, too, which I could not at all account for, till one morning happening to take a stroll along the beach among some fishermen’s boats, I saw Hosea’s brindled cow feeding on fish remnants, and marching along the sand with each foot in a cod’s decapitated head, looking very slip-shod, I assure ye. Supper concluded, we received a lamp, and directions from Mrs. Hussey concerning the nearest way to bed; but, as Queequeg was about to precede me up the stairs, the lady reached forth her arm, and demanded his harpoon; she allowed no harpoon in her chambers. “Why not?” said I; “every true whaleman sleeps with his harpoon—but why not?” “Because it’s dangerous,” says she. “Ever since young Stiggs coming from that unfort’nt v’y’ge of his, when he was gone four years and a half, with only three barrels of ile, was found dead in my first floor back, with his harpoon in his side; ever since then I allow no boarders to take sich dangerous weepons in their rooms at night. So, Mr. Queequeg” (for she had learned his name), “I will just take this here iron, and keep it for you till morning. But the chowder; clam or cod to-morrow for breakfast, men?” “Both,” says I; “and let’s have a couple of smoked herring by way of variety.”

text: Millicent's hand came on Pearl's. "Was he insensible?" she asked. "No," sobbed Pearl. "He couldn't—couldn't move." Then Escott came back, having happily found at home the first doctor at whose house he had called; and immediately afterwards Beryl drove to the door in a fly. "Mother, I am coming too," Escott said decidedly. "I told the doctor we would call for him in ten minutes, or less." Then the two were gone, and the stir was over. "Well,—I shall decide to get home as soon as possible," Diana said, in rather an injured tone. "This sort of thing really is too much for one's nerves. I declare—nobody has thought of Uncle Josiah all this time. Just like Millie! He will be dreadfully angry not to have been told. Well, it cannot be helped now. Do stop crying, Pearl." The tone was not exactly unkind, but certainly it was not sympathising. Pearl crouched down in a corner of the sofa, burying her face in the cushions, and sobbing still in a kind of exhausted way, as if she had no strength to leave off. Beryl longed to go to her, but dared not. "Come,—the best place for you is bed," said Diana. Pearl silently declined to move, and Diana made no attempt to enforce her own mandate. Mr. Crosbie presently came in, and heard the whole story from Diana's lips, gaps in knowledge being lavishly filled up with suppositions. The old gentleman waxed impatient, and questioned Pearl, but she only crouched lower in her corner, and would not speak. When further pressed, she started up and ran away. "The best thing you can do is to go and put her to bed," Diana observed carelessly to Beryl,—"if you wish to make yourself useful." Beryl's heart bounded at the suggestion, though her manner showed no particular pleasure. She obeyed immediately, only to find Pearl's door locked. Pearl turned for some time a deaf ear to raps, but it was at length opened. "May I come in?" asked Beryl. "No, I don't want anybody," Pearl said, holding the door against her. "Please let me be alone." "But you will make yourself ill, if you cry so. Aunt Di told me to come." "I don't care. If you would only leave me alone—" "I need not stay long. Just let me help you to undress." "I don't want help. I'm—I'm not going to bed—till—till I know how Ivor is." She ceased resistance suddenly, and threw herself on the couch, sobbing as much as ever. Beryl entered and stood over her, a good deal at a loss how to act. "Pearl, is Ivor very much hurt indeed?" she asked at length. "Don't you think you would feel better if you could speak about it?" Pearl shook her head and moaned. Beryl suddenly bethought herself of a certain mode of school-treatment for a certain hysterical child. She brought a basin of water to a chair near, and began bathing Pearl's flushed face and disordered hair with a wet sponge. Pearl did not resist, but seemed rather to like it, and the violent crying lessened.

text: Westbrook High’s annual “Global Connections Week” brought together students from 12 countries, including exchange students from Japan, Brazil, India, and Kenya. The theme was “Share Your Story, Build a Bridge”— a chance for everyone to showcase their culture and learn from one another. “Cultures are like books— you can’t judge them by their cover,” said Ms. Patel, the event organizer, hanging colorful flags from different nations in the auditorium. “This week, we’ll cook together, dance together, and create art that blends our traditions.” One of the most popular activities was the “International Food Fair.” Mia, a Brazilian exchange student, made feijoada (a black bean stew) with her teammate Leo. “My mom taught me this— it’s served at family gatherings in Brazil,” she explained, stirring the pot. Across the table, Akira from Japan demonstrated making sushi rolls, while Priya from India passed out samosas (spiced potato pastries). “Try combining the samosa with a little chili sauce— that’s how we eat it at home!” Priya laughed as students lined up to taste. Another highlight was the “Cultural Fusion Art Project.” Teams of mixed international and local students were tasked with creating a mural that merged two or more cultures. The team with Amara (Kenya), Jake (USA), and Lila (Mexico) decided to blend Maasai beadwork patterns, American street art, and Mexican papel picado (cut-paper banners). “Maasai beads represent community,” Amara said, gluing colorful beads onto the canvas. Jake added spray-paint details of a city skyline, and Lila cut paper banners with traditional Mexican motifs. “It looks like a party of cultures!” their teacher commented when they finished. On the final day, students performed traditional dances. The Brazilian group danced the samba to lively drums, while the Indian students performed a bhangra routine. Then, everyone joined in a global dance circle, mixing steps from different countries. “I never thought I’d be dancing samba with someone who knows how to do the Kenyan ngoma!” said Tom, a local student, laughing as he followed Amara’s movements. As the week ended, students exchanged small gifts— Akira gave origami cranes, Mia handed out Brazilian coffee beans, and Amara shared beaded bracelets. “I came here worried no one would understand my culture,” Amara said. “But now I feel like we’re all part of one big family.” Jake nodded: “Learning that our ‘differences’ are just things we haven’t tried yet was the best part.” For Westbrook High’s students, Global Connections Week wasn’t just a school event. It was a lesson that culture is a gift to share, not a barrier to overcome— that listening, laughing, and creating together turns strangers into friends, and the world into a place where everyone’s story matters.

text: The evening sun dipped low over the Salinas River, turning the water a pale gold that shimmered where the current rippled. Lennie sat cross-legged in the tall grass, his big hands cupped around a dead mouse—its small body stiff, its fur matted with dirt, the same one he'd accidentally crushed that morning when he'd squeezed it too hard. The air smelled of damp earth and the faint, sweet scent of yellow wildflowers that grew along the bank, mixing with the warm air that carried the distant sound of the ranch hands' laughter. He paused, lifting the mouse to his face, and whispered, 'George ain't gonna like this.' He'd promised George he wouldn't pick up no more mice, wouldn't get them killed with his 'dumb strength.' But he couldn't help it—they were soft, so soft, and he just wanted to hold something that didn't yell at him, didn't hit him, didn't call him a fool. He thought of the farm they talked about, the one with alfalfa for the rabbits, with a white picket fence around the house, with a kitchen where they'd make beans every night. 'An' we'll live off the fatta the lan',' George would say, and Lennie would smile, because he knew George wouldn't lie. Not about the rabbits. A leaf fell from a willow tree above him, landing on his shoulder. He brushed it off, his eyes still on the mouse. He thought of Curley's wife, her red dress bright against the hay in the barn, her voice soft when she'd asked him to feel her hair. 'It's real soft, ain't it?' she'd said. And he'd said yes, and he'd held it, and then she'd yelled, and he'd grabbed harder, and then—he couldn't think about the rest. It was like when he'd killed the puppy, like when he'd broken Curley's hand. His strength was a monster, hiding inside him, waiting to get out. He set the mouse down gently, as if it might wake up, and stood up. The river gurgled past, quiet now, like it was keeping his secret. He walked to the bank, staring at his reflection—his big shoulders, his thick arms, his eyes wide and scared. George had told him, if anything bad happened, to come here, to wait by the river. 'I'll find ya,' George had said. 'Don't you move.' So he'd waited, sitting in the grass, holding the mouse, thinking about the rabbits. The wind picked up, carrying the smell of supper from the ranch—steak and potatoes, George's favorite. Lennie's stomach growled, but he didn't move. He just sat there, watching the sun sink lower, turning the sky pink and orange. He thought of the farm again, of the rabbits in their cages, of George sitting on the porch smoking a cigarette. 'Soon,' he whispered to himself. 'Soon we'll get the farm. Soon we won't have to move no more.' He picked up the mouse again, tucking it into his pocket, and waited. He didn't know what he'd done was so bad. He just knew he wanted George to come, to tell him it was okay, to talk about the rabbits. That's all he ever wanted.

The conversation went on for about an hour longer, and apparently made a deep impression on Andrey Yefimitch. He began going to the ward every day. He went there in the mornings and after dinner, and often the dusk of evening found him in conversation with Ivan Dmitritch. At first Ivan Dmitritch held aloof from him, suspected him of evil designs, and openly expressed his hostility. But afterwards he got used to him, and his abrupt manner changed to one of condescending irony.
Soon it was all over the hospital that the doctor, Andrey Yefimitch, had taken to visiting Ward No. 6. No one—neither Sergey Sergevitch, nor Nikita, nor the nurses—could conceive why he went there, why he stayed there for hours together, what he was talking about, and why he did not write prescriptions. His actions seemed strange. Often Mihail Averyanitch did not find him at home, which had never happened in the past, and Daryushka was greatly perturbed, for the doctor drank his beer now at no definite time, and sometimes was even late for dinner.
One day—it was at the end of June—Dr. Hobotov went to see Andrey Yefimitch about something. Not finding him at home, he proceeded to look for him in the yard; there he was told that the old doctor had gone to see the mental patients. Going into the lodge and stopping in the entry, Hobotov heard the following conversation:
“We shall never agree, and you will not succeed in converting me to your faith,” Ivan Dmitritch was saying irritably; “you are utterly ignorant of reality, and you have never known suffering, but have only like a leech fed beside the sufferings of others, while I have been in continual suffering from the day of my birth till to-day. For that reason, I tell you frankly, I consider myself superior to you and more competent in every respect. It’s not for you to teach me.”
“I have absolutely no ambition to convert you to my faith,” said Andrey Yefimitch gently, and with regret that the other refused to understand him. “And that is not what matters, my friend; what matters is not that you have suffered and I have not. Joy and suffering are passing; let us leave them, never mind them. What matters is that you and I think; we see in each other people who are capable of thinking and reasoning, and that is a common bond between us however different our views. If you knew, my friend, how sick I am of the universal senselessness, ineptitude, stupidity, and with what delight I always talk with you! You are an intelligent man, and I enjoyed your company.”

text: The afternoon sun filtered through the dusty windows of Aureliano Buendía’s workshop, casting long, slanted shadows over the workbench cluttered with metal shavings and half-finished goldfish. He sat on a wooden stool, his gnarled hands gripping a pair of tongs, as he dipped a piece of molten gold into a bucket of cold water—sizzle—the steam curling up to fog his spectacles. For years, he’d done this: melt gold, cast it into tiny fish, melt the fish again when he’d made twenty, a endless cycle that kept his hands busy and his mind from wandering too far into the past. But today, the past wouldn’t stay away. He thought of his father, José Arcadio Buendía, staring at the sky through a telescope, muttering about celestial maps that no one else could see. He thought of his sister Úrsula, bent over her loom, weaving cloth that held the patterns of their family’s joys and sorrows. He thought of the children who’d grown up and left, of the wars he’d fought and forgotten, of the love he’d lost and buried like a secret. “All of us,” he said aloud, his voice dry as the dust on the windowsill, “we’re just spinning in circles. The same loneliness, the same mistakes, the same end.” The tongs slipped in his hand, and the half-cast goldfish clattered onto the workbench. He stared at it—its scales incomplete, its eyes nothing but empty indentations—and suddenly, he saw it: the whole family, in that fish. His father’s obsession, his mother’s stubbornness, his own endless casting and melting—all of it, a loop that never broke. He reached for the crucible of molten gold, ready to pour another fish, but when he tilted it, nothing came out. Then the butterfly flew away, and the child ran after it, disappearing around the corner. The street was empty again. Aureliano went back to his workbench. He picked up the broken crucible pieces, swept the metal shavings into a pile, and sat down. He didn’t have any more gold to melt, but he picked up the tongs anyway, clamping them around an imaginary piece of metal. “One more,” he said. “Just one more.” Even if the cycle didn’t break, even if the loneliness came back, he would keep going. That’s what the Buendías did. They kept going—through wars, through rains, through the quiet, endless years—because that’s all they knew how to do.

text: The autumn sun hung low over Tara's cotton fields, turning the dry brown stalks to gold as a faint wind carried the distant rumble of cannons—soft at first, then louder, a constant throb that made Scarlett O'Hara's hands shake as she folded her mother's silk handkerchiefs into a wooden trunk. She'd been at it for an hour, packing the few valuables they could take: her mother's pearl necklace, her father's silver watch, the china teacups that had belonged to her grandmother. The rest— the tapestries on the walls, the velvet sofas in the parlor, the paintings of her ancestors—would have to stay, left to the mercy of the approaching Yankees. Mammy stood in the doorway, her black face set in a frown, her hands clasped tight around her apron strings. 'Miss Scarlett, you ain't packin' right,' she said, her voice sharp but worried. 'You gotta take more dresses—them fine silk ones ain't gonna keep you warm if we gotta run. And you forgot Miss Suellen's doll—she'll squall fit to bust when she sees it's left.' Scarlett bit her lip, folding a crisp white blouse more roughly than she meant to. 'Mammy, we don't have time for dolls,' she said, trying to keep her voice steady. 'The Yankees could be here by sundown. Pa's out back with the horses, and Suellen's cryin' in her room, and someone's gotta—' She stopped, swallowing hard. The cannons rumbled again, closer now, and she thought of Ashley, off fighting with the Confederates, and Melanie, weak from childbirth, waiting in the bedroom upstairs. 'I know, Miss Scarlett,' Mammy said, her tone softening. She crossed the room, taking the blouse from Scarlett's hands and folding it neatly. 'But you can't go carryin' all this worry by yourself. Miss Ellen'd want you to be strong—for the family.' Scarlett nodded, staring at the trunk. It was half-full, but it felt like a mountain. She thought of the Tara she'd known as a child— the laughter on the porch, the smell of jasmine in the garden, the sound of her mother's piano. Now it all felt fragile, like a dream that might shatter any second. She walked to the window, pulling back the heavy velvet curtain to look out at the fields. A few slaves hurried past, carrying sacks of corn, their heads down, and in the distance, she saw the outline of the smoke—thin, gray, and growing closer. 'I won't let them take Tara,' she said, more to herself than to Mammy. Her jaw tightened, and she wiped a stray tear from her cheek—angry at herself for crying. 'I'll never let them take it. No matter what.' Mammy smiled, a small, proud smile. 'That's my Miss Scarlett,' she said. 'Now come on—let's get that trunk packed. We got a long road ahead.' Scarlett picked up another dress, her hands steadier now. The cannons still rumbled, but somewhere deep inside her, a fire had lit—a stubborn, fierce thing that wouldn't be put out. For Tara, for her family, she'd fight. She'd do anything.

text:
The Flaubert school or group lasted sufficiently long in France, though, after the late War, its influence was completely washed out by a sort of eclecticism whose main features it is very difficult to trace and into whose ramifications I do not intend to enter, for it has had practically no time to influence the work of Anglo-Saxon novel writers. Flaubert, Maupassant, Turgenev, the Gourmonts, Daudet, and the rest of those who had their places at Brébant’s died in their allotted years, the last survivor of any prominence being Anatole France, whose death was greeted by an outburst of furious hatred in France such as can seldom have greeted the passing of a distinguished figure. That was because the French young, saddened and rendered starving by the War which just preceded France’s death, turned with loathing from the rather débonnaire aloofness of the author of Histoire Comique. And indeed if we Anglo-Saxons had suffered in the least as much as those Latins I might well expect to find myself lynched for writing what I have done above. I have seldom witnessed anything to equal the dismay of a great French gathering of littérateurs when their honoured guest, an English novelist of distinction and indeed of internationally public literary functions, told them in quite immaculate French that all he knew of writing he had from France, and that all that he had from France he had learned from the works of Guy de Maupassant! If he had gone round that great assembly and had, with his glove, flicked each one of the guests in the face, he could not have caused greater consternation. Nevertheless it is true that Maupassant must have had more influence on the Anglo-Saxon writer of to-day than any other writer of fiction, Henry James possibly excepted.

In England, meantime, slightly before the 1890’s, the solid vogue of—or the somnolent rumination over—the three-volumed nuvvle of commerce had been seriously threatened by the slow spread of the idea that writing might be an art, by a tremendous drop in the prices at which books might be sold and by revolutionary attacks on Victorian conventional morality.

text: At the close of the afternoon service we returned by an exposed and hilly road, where the bitter winter wind, blowing over a range of snowy summits to the north, almost flayed the skin from our faces. I can remember Miss Temple walking lightly and rapidly along our drooping line, her plaid cloak, which the frosty wind fluttered, gathered close about her, and encouraging us, by precept and example, to keep up our spirits, and march forward, as she said, "like stalwart soldiers." The other teachers, poor things, were generally themselves too much dejected to attempt the task of cheering others. How we longed for the light and heat of a blazing fire when we got back! But, to the little ones at least, this was denied: each hearth in the schoolroom was immediately surrounded by two rows of great girls, and the little ones had to crouch behind them, with their thin mantles to cover them. We had a little consolation in the shape of a double ration of bread - a whole, instead of a half, slice - with the delicious addition of a thin scrape of butter: it was the hebdomadal treat to which we all looked forward from Sabbath to Sabbath. I generally contrived to reserve a moiety of this bounteous repast for myself; but the remainder I was invariably obliged to part with. The Sunday evening was spent in repeating, by heart, the Church Catechism, and the fifth, sixth, and seventh chapters of St. Matthew; and in listening to a long sermon, read by Miss Miller, whose irrepressible yawns attested her weariness. A frequent interlude in these performances was the enactment of the part of Eutychus by some half - dozen of the little girls, who, overpowered with sleep, would fall down, if not out of the third loft, yet off the fourth form, and be taken up half - dead. The remedy was, to thrust them forward into the centre of the schoolroom, and oblige them to stand there till the sermon was finished; and if some of them, by chance, fell again, the rest kept them up by supporting them on the arms and shoulders.

text: The autumn night in Carla’s farmhouse kitchen was damp—damp enough that the windows fogged at the edges, and the only warmth came from the embers in the woodstove, casting a dim orange glow over the chipped enamel table. Carla sat on a wooden chair, her hands twisting the frayed hem of her apron, her eyes fixed on the rain tapping against the windowpane, each drop leaving a dark streak that blurred the view of the muddy lane leading to the highway. The sink was piled with unwashed dishes, a half-empty jar of jam sat open on the counter, and the radio in the corner played a country song so quiet she could barely hear the words—just a slow, sad melody that matched the tightness in her chest. She thought of Clark—of the way he’d yelled at her that afternoon, his face red with anger, because she’d forgotten to mend the fence around the chicken coop, because the eggs had gotten cold, because “nothing she did was ever right.” She’d stood there, nodding, saying “sorry,” the way she always did, even though she’d been up since dawn, feeding the horses, hauling water, cleaning the barn—all the things he never bothered with. Later, he’d brought her a cup of coffee, his voice softening, saying “I didn’t mean it,” and she’d smiled, saying “I know,” even though she didn’t. She never knew, not really—never knew when the anger would come, when the kindness would fade, when she’d wake up and realize she was just going through the motions, day after day, year after year. The rain picked up, and Carla stood up, walking to the window. She wiped a spot clear with her sleeve, looking out at the lane—dark, empty, leading to a world she barely remembered. She thought of the day she’d run away with Clark, at 18, leaving her parents’ house in the city, leaving her part-time job at the bookstore, leaving the friends who’d told her “he’s not good for you.” She’d thought they were wrong, thought love was enough—thought the farm, the animals, the quiet would make her happy. Now, she wondered if they’d been right. Wondered if she’d traded one cage for another, if the “freedom” she’d wanted had just been an illusion. She picked up the jar of jam, twisting the lid shut. The radio song ended, and a news report came on—something about a woman who’d left her husband, moved to the coast, started a new life. Carla listened, her breath catching.

text:
"I don't know." Beryl hesitated, but her reserve was not proof against Miss Carmichael's thawing influence. "I thought it was 'that,'" she said. "I thought that if I were like Pearl, people would take to me, of course."

"If you were like Pearl, people in general might run after you more. But being run after for a pretty face does not mean being loved."

"But people do love Pearl, and they don't care for me," said Beryl, finding it a relief to unburden her mind to one who could, at least in some measure, feel with her. "I heard an old servant say of me once, when I was a child, that nobody ever could care for me, because I was so ugly and disagreeable. And I suppose it is true. I never expect anything else now."

Miss Carmichael sat looking at her.

"You may have been disagreeable as a child," she said. "I do not find you so now,—only I should like to unbend you a little. It was a wrong thing for a child ever to hear said. Has your life since been embittered by those words?"

"I don't know. I couldn't forget them, of course," said Beryl slowly.

"Have you kept them in mind, and allowed them to sour your intercourse with others?"

"I don't know," she repeated, and then she suddenly found herself in danger of following Hester's example. "I couldn't help it. I used to be very miserable, for a long long while. And then I thought it was no good to mind, and I settled that I would just keep to myself, and let other people alone, and be brave and not care."

"And shut up your heart against the many who would willingly enter it. Poor child!"

"There hasn't been—anybody," said Beryl.

"No one who ever could have loved you? How can you tell?"

"Except Mademoiselle at school. She said she would be my friend, and she gave me a ring, and I wrote to her and she never answered me. People are all alike."

"I would trust Mademoiselle a little longer. There may be unknown causes for the delay. People all alike! Nay, my dear, you don't know much yet about human nature."

"They are all alike to me," said Beryl. "And I don't care to have friends who only just become friends because they are sorry for me. If people don't really like me for myself, I would much rather be left alone."

"You are not like me there. If people are kind and loving, I don't pretend to get to the bottom of their motives. It is a hopeless task. I never yet succeeded in getting to the bottom of my own."

Then she rose, crossed over, and placed a hand on each of Beryl's shoulders.

"Hester and I will try not to be sorry for you," she said. "Look up at me, Beryl. We should be sorry for most people who feel as you feel, but you are of too independent a spirit to want pity, so we will offer none. Still, do you not think you would like to have a little love from us?"

Beryl looked up, as directed,—composedly at first, but a changed expression came soon. Her mood melted, and her eyes filled.

Miss Carmichael bent down and kissed her forehead.

"It is no such hard task," she said. "There is plenty of lovable stuff below, my dear, if you don't smother it up. Now mind, there is to be no steeling of your little heart against us. You are to be at home here, and to run in whenever you feel lonely. You understand? I hear Hettie coming, and you may go into the conservatory and gather some cherry-pie for yourself. People who don't like to be pitied, don't like to be caught crying, I know. Run, my dear, and you will come back all right."

Mishenka could not picture his future spouse in his imagination except as a tall, plump, substantial, pious woman, stepping like a peacock, and, for some reason, with a long shawl over her shoulders; while Masha was thin, slender, tightly laced, and walked with little steps, and, worst of all, she was too fascinating and at times extremely attractive to Mishenka, and that, in his opinion, was incongruous with matrimony and only in keeping with loose behaviour. When Anna Akimovna had promised to give Masha a dowry, he had hesitated for a time; but once a poor student in a brown overcoat over his uniform, coming with a letter for Anna Akimovna, was fascinated by Masha, and could not resist embracing her near the hat-stand, and she had uttered a faint shriek; Mishenka, standing on the stairs above, had seen this, and from that time had begun to cherish a feeling of disgust for Masha. A poor student! Who knows, if she had been embraced by a rich student or an officer the consequences might have been different.
"Why don't you wish it?" Anna Akimovna asked. "What more do you want?"
Mishenka was silent and looked at the arm-chair fixedly, and raised his eyebrows.
"Do you love some one else?"
Silence. The red-haired Masha came in with letters and visiting cards on a tray. Guessing that they were talking about her, she blushed to tears.
"The postmen have come," she muttered. "And there is a clerk called Tchalikov waiting below. He says you told him to come to-day for something."
"What insolence!" said Anna Akimovna, moved to anger. "I gave him no orders. Tell him to take himself off; say I am not at home!"
A ring was heard. It was the priests from her parish. They were always shown into the aristocratic part of the house—that is, upstairs. After the priests, Nazaritch, the manager of the factory, came to pay his visit, and then the factory doctor; then Mishenka announced the inspector of the elementary schools. Visitors kept arriving.

text: Lola and her little brother Milo loved exploring the backyard after school. One day, Milo pointed to a spot under the oak tree: 'Look, Lola! There's a big buzz over there!' They crept closer and saw a group of bees flying in and out of a small hole in the tree. 'Whoa—they're building something!' Milo whispered. Lola pulled out her science notebook—she'd learned about bees in class. 'They're making a beehive,' she said. 'Bees work together to make honey for their family.' Milo's eyes widened. 'Can we watch them? Please?' Lola nodded, but she remembered their teacher's rule: 'Never disturb bees—they're busy and need space.' They sat on the grass a few feet away, watching quietly. The bees zoomed from flower to flower, their legs covered in yellow pollen. 'They look like tiny delivery trucks!' Milo laughed. Every day, they visited the beehive. Lola drew pictures of the bees in her notebook, labeling their wings and antennae. Milo counted how many bees flew in each minute. One afternoon, a rainstorm hit. 'Will the bees be okay?' Milo asked, clutching Lola's hand. Lola bit her lip. 'I think so—beehives are warm and dry inside.' When the rain stopped, they ran to check. The bees were flying again, as if nothing had happened. 'See? They're tough,' Lola said. A week later, Lola noticed something sticky on the tree near the hive. 'It's honey!' she exclaimed. A worker bee landed on a nearby flower, and Lola smiled. 'They did it—they made honey for their queen.' That weekend, they told their mom about the beehive. 'Bees are very important,' Mom said, handing them a jar of honey. 'They help flowers grow by carrying pollen. Without bees, we wouldn't have many fruits and vegetables.' Lola and Milo looked at each other—they felt proud to have watched the bees' hard work. The next day, they hung a sign on the oak tree: 'Bee Friends—Please Keep Your Distance.' They brought a shallow dish of water to the backyard, just like their teacher had suggested, so the bees could drink. As they sat on the grass, watching the bees buzz happily, Milo said, 'I love our bee family.' Lola nodded. 'Me too. They taught us that working together makes big things happen.'

text: The village of Holcomb stands on the high wheat plains of western Kansas, a lonesome area that other Kansans call 'out there.' Some seventy miles east of the Colorado border, the countryside, with its hard blue skies and desert-clear air, has an atmosphere that is rather more Far Western than Middle West. The local accent is barbed with a prairie twang, a ranch-hand nasalness, and the men, many of them, wear narrow frontier trousers, Stetsons, and high-heeled boots with pointed toes. The land is flat, and the views are awesomely extensive; horses, herds of cattle, a white cluster of grain elevators rising as gracefully as Greek temples are visible long before a traveler reaches them. Holcomb, too, can be seen from great distances. Not that there's much to see—simply an aimless congregation of buildings divided in the center by the main-line tracks of the Santa Fe Railroad, a haphazard hamlet bounded on the south by a brown stretch of the Arkansas (pronounced 'Ar-kan-sas') River, on the north by a highway, Route 50, and on the east and west by prairie lands and wheat fields. After rain, or when snowfalls thaw, the streets, unnamed, unshaded, unpaved, turn from the thickest dust into the direst mud. At one end of the town stands a stark old stucco structure, the roof of which supports an electric sign—DANCE—but the dancing has ceased and the advertisement has been dark for several years. Nearby is another building with an irrelevant sign, this one in flaking gold on a dirty window—HOLCOMB BANK. The bank closed in 1933, and its former counting rooms have been converted into apartments. It is one of the town's two 'apartment houses,' the second being a ramshackle mansion known, because a good part of the local school's faculty lives there, as the Teacherage. But the majority of Holcomb's homes are one-story frame affairs, with front porches.

text: The rainy night in Comala’s ruins smelled of wet earth and rot—rot from the fallen adobe walls, from the overgrown weeds that pushed through the cracks in the floor, from the memories that lingered like ghosts. Juan Preciado sat on a splintered wooden chair, his mother’s letter crumpled in his hand, the ink smudged by the rain that seeped through the broken roof. A single tallow candle burned on the rickety table beside him, its flame flickering so wildly it cast distorted shadows on the walls, shadows that looked like people moving. He thought of his mother—of her weak voice in her last days, of the way she’d held his hand and said, “Go to Comala, Juan. Find your father. Tell him I forgave him.” She’d spoken of Pedro Páramo like he was a god, like he was the answer to every question Juan had ever had. But here, in this empty village, with the rain pouring and the wind howling through the windows, Pedro Páramo felt like a ghost. A ghost, or a lie. The candle sputtered, and for a second, the shadow on the wall looked like a woman—tall, with long dark hair, her dress blowing like a sheet. Juan jumped, gripping the letter tighter. He thought of Doña Eduviges, the old woman who’d talked to him at the village entrance, her eyes milky with blindness. “This village is full of dead people, boy,” she’d said. “They talk. They walk. They wait.” He’d laughed then, thought she was crazy. But now, he wasn’t so sure. He unfolded the letter, reading the words again, even though he knew them by heart: “He was a proud man, Juan. But he loved me. I think he loved me.” Love. The word tasted bitter in his mouth. If Pedro Páramo had loved her, why had he left? Why had he let her die alone, in a tiny room in a town far from Comala? Why had he never even sent a letter, never even asked about his son? The rain beat harder against the roof, and a board creaked somewhere in the house. Juan stood up, walking to the window, and pressed his face against the cold glass. Outside, the street was empty, just mud and stones and the dark shapes of collapsed houses. He thought of the stories the villagers had told—stories of Pedro Páramo stealing land, of him killing men who stood in his way, of him leaving a trail of broken hearts and empty graves. Was this the man his mother had loved? Was this his father? He walked back to the table, blowing out the candle. The room went dark, except for the faint light of the moon peeking through the clouds. He thought of his mother again, of her face when she’d talked about Comala—how her eyes had lit up, how she’d smiled like she was remembering a dream. “It was a beautiful village once,” she’d said. “Full of flowers. Full of music.” Now, it was just dust. Just bones. Just ghosts.

text: That was my first conversation with him. But I was to have many others, for although he avoided society as much as possible, we could not help meeting now and then on the stairs or in the passage, and in the evenings, when he was sitting in his room smoking his pipe and I was sitting in mine reading, we often heard each other moving about. I remember one evening in particular. My aunt was out and I was alone in the house when the door - bell rang. I opened the door and saw a very pretty young woman standing there. When she asked for Mr. Haller, I recognized her as the person in the photograph which hung in his room. I showed her the way to his room and then went back to my own. She stayed upstairs for a while, and then I heard them coming downstairs together, laughing and talking. I was very surprised that this recluse should have a sweetheart, and such a young and pretty one too. I began to wonder all over again about him and his life. But within an hour he was back again alone, and I heard him dragging himself wearily up the stairs and then pacing up and down his room like a caged wolf for hours. The light in his room was on all night and did not go out until nearly morning. I knew nothing of their relationship, but I would like to add that I saw him with the woman once again. They were walking arm - in - arm in one of the streets of the town and he looked very happy. I was again struck by the fact that his usually sad and lonely face could look so young and charming. Then I understood the young woman and also my aunt’s partiality for him. But that evening when he came home he was as sad and wretched as ever.
