text:
Next morning the minister was sitting in the rocking chair on the verandah of the grazier’s house. He had a prayer book in one hand and a handkerchief in the other, with which he lazily disputed the right of the flies to roost on his veil. This gave an undulating motion to the chair which was very soothing after old Rosey’s bumping. He saw a pair of brown hands part the awning enclosing the verandah. Then a black head, held in the position of a butting animal, came in view. Free of the screen, the head craned upwards. He saw a flat, shrewd face, with black beady eyes set either side of a bridgeless nose. A wisp of dried grass hung from the wide mouth.

“Sis wants er ride in thet ther cock ’orse yer in,” said the mouth, ejecting the grass with considerable force in his direction.

Sis’ had worked her head in by this. She was fair, with nondescript hair and eyes, and she was “chawrin’”.

“Wer’s ther cock ’orse, Jinny?” she asked, for the chair was not rocking.

“Ridey it an’ let ’er see it; an’ undo this,” commanded Jinny.

“Come round to the front,” said the minister mildly, and pointing to the opening opposite the door.

They came in and walked up to him, with hoods hanging by the strings down their backs.

“Have you come alone?”

“The ether uns er comin’. Me an’ Sis giv’ ’em ther slip; we didn’ wanter ’ump ther dash kid.”

“How far have you walked?”

“Yer parst our place yesserday mornin’. Didn’ yer see me an’ ther billy? Gosh, we nigh bust oursels at ther way yer legs stuck out. Fust I thort yer wus ole Keogh. Yer rides jes’ like er Chinymun.” The dark one did all the talking.

“Our Sis wants er ride in this,” she continued. She gave the chair a lurch that sent the parson’s feet in the air. To avoid the threatened repetition he gripped both sides and planted his feet firmly on the boards.

The younger one poked a stem of dried grass from her mouth through the mesh of the veil in a line with his left ear. Thoroughly routed, he sprang up, and the elder child leapt in.

“’Ere they cum, Jinny,” warned Sis.

Jinny peeped through the awning. “So they is. You gammon ter them we aint cum, w’en they arsts yer,” she said to the parson, “an’ we’ll sneak roun’ ther back. Eh, Sis?”

text: The winter night pressed against the windows of Holly's Manhattan apartment, turning the streetlights outside to fuzzy gold that spilled over the cluttered coffee table—half-empty martini glasses, a crumpled silk scarf, a pack of cigarettes with one left. Holly sat on the windowsill, her bare feet dangling above the floor, and held Cat close to her chest—his fur still matted from hiding under the couch during the party, his purr a faint vibration against her ribs. The air smelled of leftover champagne and the strong, sweet scent of gardenias from the wilted bouquet on the mantel, mixing with the cold draft that seeped through the cracked window frame. She stared at the cars passing below, their headlights streaking like silver lines across the wet pavement, and thought of Fred—her brother, the one she sent money to every month, the only person who'd ever made her feel like she belonged somewhere. He was in the army now, stationed in Texas, and his letters were short, full of talk about cows and dust storms, like he didn't know how to say what he really felt. Just like her, she thought. Just like everyone in this city—running so fast to get away from something, they forget to stop and see what they're running toward. A taxi honked loudly outside, and Cat twitched his ears, pressing closer to her. She stroked his head, her fingers brushing the scab on his ear (from a fight with a stray down the street), and smiled—a small, sad smile that didn't reach her eyes. 'You're the only one who doesn't want something from me, huh?' she whispered, her voice hoarse from singing too much at the party. 'No one asks you to be someone you're not. No one tells you where to stay, or when to go.' She looked around the apartment—the peeling wallpaper, the record player with a broken needle, the suitcase in the corner that was always packed, just in case. This wasn't a home, not really. It was a place to sleep, a place to throw parties, a place to hide from the people who wanted to 'tame' her—like Doc Golightly, who'd married her when she was just fourteen, or the men who bought her drinks and thought that meant she owed them something. The clock on the mantel struck midnight, its chime loud and sharp in the quiet. Cat jumped off her lap, curling up on the couch, and Holly stood up slowly, her legs stiff from sitting so long. She walked to the window, pressing her palm against the cold glass, and stared at the Tiffany's sign in the distance—its blue light soft and steady, like a promise. She'd always said that's where she felt safest, where nothing bad could happen to her. But tonight, even that thought didn't make her feel better.

text: "Arthur Radley just stays in the house, that's all," said Miss Maudie. "Wouldn't you stay in the house if you didn't want to come out?" "Yessum, but I'd wanta come out. Why doesn't he?" Miss Maudie's eyes narrowed. "You know that story as well as I do." "I never heard why, though. Nobody ever told me why." Miss Maudie settled her bridgework. "You know old Mr. Radley was a foot-washing Baptist…" "Are you one, too?" "I'm not so sure of that. I'm just a Baptist." "Don't you all believe in foot-washing?" "We do. At home in the bathtub." "But we can't take communion with you all—" Evidently deciding that defining primitive Baptisteries was easier than defining the primal source of her particular communion, Miss Maudie said, "Foot-washers believe any pleasure is a sin. Did you know some of 'em came out of the woods one Saturday and passed by here and told me me and my flowers were going to hell?" "Your flowers, too?" "Yes ma'am. That was part of it, along with everything but readin' the Bible and prayin'." With that picture of Miss Maudie being seared in various Protestant hells, we decided we didn't believe in that stuff any more, particularly as the gospel of the Primitive Baptists would not save one human being we knew. Miss Maudie on a Sunday was a different person from Miss Maudie on a weekday. She was not at all like the other ladies in town, most of whom spent their time doing things for the sick. Mrs. Grace Merriweather had been doing that for years, but she was the only one who did, as far as I could tell. Miss Maudie was our friend. She had never told on us, had never played cat-and-mouse with us, she was not at all interested in our private lives. She was our age for all intents and purposes.

text: Now these three mates—Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask, were momentous men. They it was who by universal prescription commanded three of the Pequod’s boats as headsmen. In that grand order of battle in which Captain Ahab would probably marshal his forces to descend on the whales, these three headsmen were as captains of companies. Or, being armed with their long keen whaling spears, they were as a picked trio of lancers; even as the harpooneers were flingers of javelins. And since in this famous fishery, each mate or headsman, like a Gothic Knight of old, is always accompanied by his boat-steerer or harpooneer, who in certain conjunctures provides him with a fresh lance, when the former one has been badly twisted, or elbowed in the assault; and moreover, as there generally subsists between the two, a close intimacy and friendliness; it is therefore but meet, that in this place we set down who the Pequod’s harpooneers were, and to what headsman each of them belonged. First of all was Queequeg, whom Starbuck, the chief mate, had selected for his squire. But Queequeg is already known. Next was Tashtego, an unmixed Indian from Gay Head, the most westerly promontory of Martha’s Vineyard, where there still exists the last remnant of a village of red men, which has long supplied the neighboring island of Nantucket with many of her most daring harpooneers. In the fishery, they usually go by the generic name of Gay-Headers. Tashtego’s long, lean, sable hair, his high cheek bones, and black rounding eyes—for an Indian, Oriental in their largeness, but Antarctic in their glittering expression—all this sufficiently proclaimed him an inheritor of the unvitiated blood of those proud warrior hunters, who, in quest of the great New England moose, had scoured, bow in hand, the aboriginal forests of the main. But no longer snuffing in the trail of the wild beasts of the woodland, Tashtego now hunted in the wake of the great whales of the sea; the unerring harpoon of the son fitly replacing the infallible arrow of the sires. To look at the tawny brawn of his lithe snaky limbs, you would almost have credited the superstitions of some of the earlier Puritans, and half-believed this wild Indian to be a son of the Prince of the Powers of the Air. Tashtego was Stubb the second mate’s squire.

text: “From up there, from Nijni,” she answered; “but I did not walk here, I came by boat. One does not walk on water, you little imp.” This was ludicrous, incomprehensible, and untrue; upstairs there lived a bearded, gaudy Persian, and in the cellar an old, yellow Kalmuck who sold sheepskins. One could get upstairs by riding on the banisters, and if one fell, one simply rolled downstairs—so how could one come by boat? I did not believe my grandmother. “Then why is mamma crying?” “Because your father is dead,” she said, “and she is crying for him.” “Why did he die?” “He was stricken down by God,” she replied evasively; but I knew very well that God punished my father because he had often boxed my ears, and I thought that perhaps God had killed him because he had done the same to mamma. I decided to question my grandmother about this. “Did God kill papa because he hit mamma?” My grandmother did not answer, but bent down to the trunk and began rummaging among my clothes. For a long time she was silent; then, when she had found what she wanted, she straightened herself up, wiped the sweat from her face with her sleeve, and said: “Your father was a dear man, a good man; and now he is with God. God will take care of him better than we can.” I was not at all satisfied with this reply. It seemed to me that God was not at all kind, and that he was to be feared; I had no confidence in him whatever, for I had often been punished by him myself. He never came to see me, but I knew that he was always there, watching me through the window-panes. When I thought of God, I pictured to myself a large, heavy, dark blue cloud, which moved slowly across the sky, and when it came near the house, I hid myself under the bedclothes. I was more afraid of God than of my grandfather, and I felt sure that he would never forgive my father for hitting mamma.

text: Dill stretched, yawned, and said altogether too casually. "I know what, let's go for a walk." He sounded fishy to me. Nobody in Maycomb just went for a walk. "Where to, Dill?" Dill jerked his head in a southerly direction. Jem said, "Okay." When I protested, he said sweetly, "You don't have to come, little lady." "You don't have to go, remember—" Jem didn't like to be reminded of his failures. It seemed that the only thing he had learned from Atticus was the art of cross - examination. "Scout, we ain't gonna do anything, just go around the block and back." We walked in silence along the sidewalk, listening to the pops and squeaks of the porch swings and the soft night talk of people on front porches as we passed. Every now and then we heard Miss Stephanie Crawford's shrill laugh. "Well?" said Dill. "Okay," said Jem. "Scout, why don't you go on home?" "What are you gonna do?" It seemed that Dill and Jem were going to peep in at one of the side windows, the one with the loose shutter, and try to get a look at Boo Radley. I could go home if I wanted, but I would have to keep my mouth shut. That was all. "But why tonight?" I asked. "Because it's easier to see in the dark, because Atticus is so deep in a book he won't hear us, and because if Boo Radley kills us we'll miss school instead of vacation. Besides, it's more fun at night anyway." Jem said did I understand. “There are Varlamov’s men!” someone shouted in the street.

After having his cry out, Yegorushka went out of the shed and, walking round a big puddle, made his way towards the street. The waggons were standing exactly opposite the gateway. The drenched waggoners, with their muddy feet, were sauntering beside them or sitting on the shafts, as listless and drowsy as flies in autumn. Yegorushka looked at them and thought: “How dreary and comfortless to be a peasant!” He went up to Panteley and sat down beside him on the shaft.

“Grandfather, I’m cold,” he said, shivering and thrusting his hands up his sleeves.

“Never mind, we shall soon be there,” yawned Panteley. “Never mind, you will get warm.”

It must have been early when the waggons set off, for it was not hot. Yegorushka lay on the bales of wool and shivered with cold, though the sun soon came out and dried his clothes, the bales, and the earth. As soon as he closed his eyes he saw Tit and the windmill again. Feeling a sickness and heaviness all over, he did his utmost to drive away these images, but as soon as they vanished the dare-devil Dymov, with red eyes and lifted fists, rushed at Yegorushka with a roar, or there was the sound of his complaint: “I am so dreary!” Varlamov rode by on his little Cossack stallion; happy Konstantin passed, with a smile and the bustard in his arms. And how tedious these people were, how sickening and unbearable!

Once—it was towards evening—he raised his head to ask for water. The waggons were standing on a big bridge across a broad river. There was black smoke below over the river, and through it could be seen a steamer with a barge in tow. Ahead of them, beyond the river, was a huge mountain dotted with houses and churches; at the foot of the mountain an engine was being shunted along beside some goods trucks.

text: He clenched his teeth as he said this, and a cruel smile came on his lips. He was glad that he was "not afraid to say" what he thought, and that he had decided so firmly. "I'll have to see them, though," he went on thinking, "and tell them all, and let them see... But what about Dounia? She, too, is expecting something from me. And what about mother? Of course, they're all looking to me. 'You are our one comfort, you are everything to us,' mother says. Oh, mother!" He felt that if he could only break off this marriage, he would set his mother and sister free at once, and they would all be happy together again as they used to be. At least, they would be happy in the future. But he had to take steps, and take them quickly. And yet he could not bring himself to begin those steps. He paced up and down his little room for a long time; every minute he went to the door, listened, but... he was not ready yet. At last, when he had convinced himself that everything was quiet downstairs, he suddenly put on his hat and slipped out of the room. He had not thought at all about where he was going. All he knew was that he must make an end of it all that day, once for all, or he would not go on living. He went straight to the house on the canal bank where Sonia lived. It was an old green house of three storeys. He found the porter and obtained from him vague directions as to the whereabouts of Kapernaumov, the tailor. Having found in the corner of the courtyard the entrance to the dark and narrow staircase, he mounted to the second floor and came out into a gallery that ran round the whole second storey over the yard. While he was wandering in the darkness, uncertain where to turn for Kapernaumov's door, a door opened three paces from him; he mechanically took hold of it.

text: A few words from Isaac Ware's admirable chapter on "The Origin of Proportions in the Orders" may serve to show the importance of proportion in all schemes of decoration, and the necessity of conforming to certain rules that may at first appear both arbitrary and incomprehensible. "An architect of genius," Ware writes (alluding to the latitude which the ancients allowed themselves in using the orders), "will think himself happy, in designing a building that is to be enriched with the Doric order, that he has all the latitude between two and a half and seventeen for the projecture of its capital; that he can proportion this projecture to the general idea of his building anywhere between these extremes and show his authority. This is an happiness to the person of real genius;... but as all architects are not, nor can be expected to be, of this stamp, it is needful some standard should be established, founded upon what a good taste shall most admire in the antique, and fixed as a model from which to work, or as a test to which we may have recourse in disputes and controversies." If to these words be added his happy definition of the sense of proportion as "fancy under the restraint and conduct of judgment," and his closing caution that "it is mean in the undertaker of a great work to copy strictly, and it is dangerous to give a loose to fancy without a perfect knowledge how far a variation may be justified," the unprofessional reader may form some idea of the importance of proportion and of the necessity for observing its rules. If proportion is the good breeding of architecture, symmetry, or the answering of one part to another, may be defined as the sanity of decoration. The desire for symmetry, for balance, for rhythm in form as well as in sound, is one of the most inveterate of human instincts. Yet for years Anglo-Saxons have been taught that to pay any regard to symmetry in architecture or decoration is to truckle to one of the meanest forms of artistic hypocrisy. The master who has taught this strange creed, in words magical enough to win acceptance for any doctrine, has also revealed to his generation so many of the forgotten beauties of early art that it is hard to dispute his principles of æsthetics. As a guide through the byways of art, Mr. Ruskin is entitled to the reverence and gratitude of all; but as a logical exponent of the causes and effects of the beauty he discovers, his authority is certainly open to question. For years he has spent the full force of his unmatched prose in denouncing the enormity of putting a door or a window in a certain place in order that it may correspond to another; nor has he scrupled to declare to the victims of this practice that it leads to abysses of moral as well as of artistic degradation.

text: In decorating the walls of a room, the first point to be considered is whether they are to form a background for its contents, or to be in themselves its chief decoration. In many cases the disappointing effects of wall-decoration are due to the fact that this important distinction has been overlooked. In rooms that are to be hung with prints or pictures, the panelling or other treatment of the walls should be carefully designed with a view to the size and number of the pictures. Pictures should never be hung against a background of pattern. Nothing is more distressing than the sight of a large oil-painting in a ponderous frame seemingly suspended from a spray of wild roses or any of the other naturalistic vegetation of the modern wall-paper. The overlaying of pattern is always a mistake. It produces a confusion of line in which the finest forms lose their individuality and significance. It is also important to avoid hanging pictures or prints too close to each other. Not only do the colors clash, but the different designs of the frames, some of which may be heavy, with deeply recessed mouldings, while others are flat and carved in low relief, produce an equally discordant impression. Every one recognizes the necessity of selecting the mouldings and other ornamental details of a room with a view to their position in the scheme of decoration; but few stop to consider that in a room hung with 46 pictures, the frames take the place of wall-mouldings, and consequently must be chosen and placed as though they were part of a definite decorative composition. Pictures and prints should be fastened to the wall, not hung by a cord or wire, nor allowed to tilt forward at an angle. The latter arrangement is specially disturbing since it throws the picture-frames out of the line of the wall. It must never be forgotten that pictures on a wall, whether set in panels or merely framed and hung, inevitably become a part of the wall-decoration. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, in rooms of any importance, pictures were always treated as a part of the decoration, and frequently as panels sunk in the wall in a setting of carved wood or stucco mouldings. Even when not set in panels, they were always fixed to the wall, and their frames, whether of wood or stucco, were made to correspond with the ornamental detail of the rest of the room. Beautiful examples of this mode of treatment are seen in many English interiors of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and some of the finest carvings of Grinling Gibbons were designed for this purpose.

"Why were you not up at the station to see father off Janet?" asked George when he came home from work.

"There would have been no one to see to baby, George, and Edwin seemed to want to go so much."

"You are a good little thing, Janet."

"I am sure I didn't think Janet cared a bit about going," said Edwin, whose conscience was whispering to him that he had not acted quite unselfishly, "or I would have stayed with baby."

"And how did you get on at work to-day, George?" asked his mother.

"Very well," he replied; "my shoulder pained me far less than yesterday. Matthew Hale says I have got over the worst of it, and that I shall soon feel no pain at all."

George spoke very cheerfully, and his mother little thought that he had something to trouble him, for all he seemed so gay.

Larkins was jealous of him already. He had soon found out that George meant to work, and that he was not going to be "one of them," as Ned expressed it. By "them" he meant the set of idle boys in Northcliffe.

Larkins himself was obliged to work, or he would have starved, for he had a step-father who would never support him in idleness; but every spare minute he could find, he made one of the gang of idlers.

George still went to the Sunday school, and this was one great cause of the unkindness of Larkins, who never let pass an opportunity of doing him an unkind action. One day, George asked his teacher what he ought to do, for at times such unkindness was very hard to bear.

"Your course is very plain, George," she said. "We must bear anything rather than do what we know would be displeasing to God. It is He alone whom you need fear. There was once a very good man who used to say those very words: 'I fear God, and therefore there is none other that I need fear.'"

Nearly a week had elapsed since John Horbrook had left home, when one evening, as George entered the cottage after leaving work, he found his mother sitting by the fire, her face radiant with happiness, and an open letter lying upon her lap.

text: The men gave a shout of triumph. They saw, as they had expected, that the animals were in flight. And now, without waiting for orders, they broke into a run and charged after them. This was just what Snowball had intended. As soon as they were well inside the yard, the three horses, the three cows, and the rest of the pigs, who had been lying in ambush in the cowshed, suddenly emerged in their rear, cutting them off. Snowball now gave the signal for attack. He himself dashed straight for Jones. Jones saw him coming, raised his gun and fired. The pellets scored bloody streaks along Snowball's back, and a sheep dropped dead. Without hesitation, Snowball flung his fifteen stone against Jones's legs. Jones was hurled into a pile of dung, and his gun flew out of his hands. But the most terrifying spectacle of all was Boxer, rearing up on his hind legs and striking out with his great iron-shod hoofs like a stallion. His very first blow took a stable-lad from Foxwood on the skull and stretched him lifeless in the mud. At the sight, several men dropped their sticks and tried to run. Panic overtook them, and the next moment all the animals together were chasing them round and round the yard. They were gored, kicked, bitten, trampled on. There was not an animal on the farm that did not take vengeance on them after his own fashion. Even the cat suddenly leaped off a roof onto a cowman's shoulders and sank her claws in his neck, at which he yelled horribly. At a moment when the opening was clear, the men were glad enough to rush out of the yard and make a bolt for the main road. And so, within five minutes of their invasion, they were in ignominious retreat, with the geese hissing after them and pecking at their calves all the way.

text:
“His Excellency?” I queried.

“Oh dear, Lionel! How dense you are!” she said, throwing her bag upon the table, and sinking into a chair beside the fireplace. “You remember Felix Zuroff, the little black-haired Russian, who presided at the meeting into which you so unfortunately tumbled. We call him His Excellency, as he is the representative of others.”

I remembered distinctly the beetle-browed foreigner, apparently head of that criminal gang, who at the moment of my innocent intrusion were dividing their spoils.

“Yes, I know,” I ejaculated. “But is His Excellency still in power?”

“Most certainly. And his right hand is Lisely Hatten—or the Contessina, as she is just now known. It is almost time the great coup was brought off. Everything is arranged for it.”

“The woman who prevented our meeting in Kensington Gardens.”

“Ah! I suspected as much,” said my undersized visitor—the woman who called me husband.

According to her story, I had married her at the Kensington Registry Office. I intended to confirm that, for it would not be in the least difficult.

“Tuggy Wilson, who was recently shot, was one of us—was he not?” I asked her.

“Of course. Dufour killed him, we know. There was, however, a good reason. It’s most fortunate that he has got clear.”

“What was the reason?” I inquired eagerly.

“Oh, a quarrel over a woman, I hear.”

“A woman? Who?” I asked.

“I don’t know. You see, I’ve been out of England for months—ever since I came to you after the Avignon affair and we made our compact. The police have searched Europe for the packet, but they’ve never found it. And they are not likely to, eh?” she asked, with a knowing look.

“It’s not my affair,” I declared.

“Well, who knows where it is if you don’t?” laughed the mysterious Illona.

“I really don’t follow you,” I answered her.

She rose, and, standing determinedly before me, said:

“Now look here, Lionel. I’ll be really angry with you in a minute, if you pretend all this silly ignorance.”

“It’s not pretence. I don’t know,” I protested.

“What?” she cried angrily. “When I risk everything to come here to see and talk to you, you mean to stand there and tell me you are in ignorance of the great coup we effected on the road outside Avignon just after midnight? We had two cars traveling towards Aix-en-Provence. The first, in which you were, overtook the car with two men, and deliberately ran into it, completely wrecking it. His Excellency, Owen, Lisely, and myself were in the second car, and, on coming up, offered assistance.”

text: I could, to some one who’d get what was left in him out of him in a year and let him starve after that,” said Mr. Babcock, in a fury at his own imagining. “I won’t sell him. He’s twenty-two years old, but he’s good for a long time, decently treated; sound and can trot right along, not a bad looking fellow, chestnut, came of good stock. Think your folks’d let Poppy have him, Mark?” “I think so, I’m sure so,” said Mark, as surprised as Poppy, but rising to the occasion as she was too overcome to do. “My father said he’d like to have a horse on the place. I think he’d keep yours for Poppy, if she’d let dad use him sometimes.” “I won’t sell him,” said Mr. Babcock again, shaking his head hard. “I’d just’s lieves as not Gilbert Hawthorne’d use him. When he was a littler boy’n you are now he was as kind to animals as a lamb! But he’s to be Poppy’s horse, mind that! And her buckboard! Want to see him? Will you have him, Poppy?” “Oh, my days, my days!” cried Poppy, bursting into excited tears. “I don’t want to see him! He’s a horse, he’s alive, he goes, don’t he? Oh my, a horse! Say, I’ll die! He’ll haul me to the cemetery first thing! Oh, Mr. Babcock, you ain’t postmaster, you’re an angel, just an angel! Le’me hug you! Oh my land of lollypops, I’ll bust!” “Well, come along to the stable; it’s better for busting than the street, and you can see the horse,” said Mr. Babcock, laughing. “Here, get up off the walk! I’ll hitch him up, or do you want to ask your father first, Mark?” “No. Dad’ll say yes, but if he doesn’t I’ll bring the horse back. I’d better take a bag of oats home on the buckboard,” said Mark. Isabel and Prue had not spoken. This was too amazing to allow of speech. They silently followed to the stable, and were introduced to the horse, whose long brown nose thrust itself forward over the stall door as they entered, showing that it was used to sugar in the pockets of visitors. “I’ve done my best for you, old man; I’d keep you if I could, but you’ll be all right where you’re going. I wouldn’t sell you,” Mr. Babcock said with a quaver in his voice. Poppy solemnly took the brown face between her palms and kissed the middle of the boney nose. “My little darling, you are to be my child,” she said with rapturous tears running down her own short, freckled nose.

text: I have watched the Sacred Beetle at work in her den, so I know how she makes her pear-shaped nest. With the building-materials she has collected she shuts herself up underground so as to give her whole attention to the business in hand. The materials may be obtained in two ways. As a rule, under natural conditions, she kneads a ball in the usual way and rolls it to a favourable spot. As it rolls along it hardens a little on the surface and gathers a slight crust of earth and tiny grains of sand, which is useful later on. Now and then, however, the Beetle finds a suitable place for her burrow quite close to the spot where she collects her building-materials, and in that case she simply bundles armfuls of stuff into the hole. The result is most striking. One day I see a shapeless lump disappear into the burrow. Next day, or the day after, I visit the Beetle’s workshop and find the artist in front of her work. The formless mass of scrapings has become a pear, perfect in outline and exquisitely finished. The part that rests on the floor of the burrow is crusted over with particles of sand, while the rest is polished like glass. This shows that the Beetle has not rolled the pear round and round, but has shaped it where it lies. She has modelled it with little taps of her broad feet, just as she models her ball in the daylight. By making an artificial burrow for the mother Beetle in my own workshop, with the help of a glass jar full of earth, and a peep-hole through which I can observe operations, I have been able to see the work in its various stages. The Beetle first makes a complete ball. Then she starts the neck of the pear by making a ring round the ball and applying pressure, till the ring becomes a groove. In this way a blunt projection is pushed out at one side of the ball. In the centre of this projection she employs further pressure to form a sort of crater or hollow, with a swollen rim; and gradually the hollow is made deeper and the swollen rim thinner and thinner, till a sack is formed. In this sack, which is polished and glazed inside, the egg is laid. The opening of the sack, or extreme end of the pear, is then closed with a plug of stringy fibres. There is a reason for this rough plug—a most curious exception, when nothing else has escaped the heavy blows of the insect’s leg. The end of the egg rests against it, and, if the stopper were pressed down and driven in, the infant grub might suffer. So the Beetle stops the hole without ramming down the stopper.

text: Call me Ishmael. Some years ago—never mind how long precisely—having little or no money in my purse, and nothing particular to interest me on shore, I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part of the world. It is a way I have of driving off the spleen and regulating the circulation. Whenever I find myself growing grim about the mouth; whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever I find myself involuntarily pausing before coffin warehouses, and bringing up the rear of every funeral I meet; and especially whenever my hypos get such an upper hand of me, that it requires a strong moral principle to prevent me from deliberately stepping into the street, and methodically knocking people’s hats off—then, I account it high time to get to sea as soon as I can. This is my substitute for pistol and ball. With a philosophical flourish Cato throws himself upon his sword; I quietly take to the ship. There is nothing surprising in this. If they but knew it, almost all men in their degree, some time or other, cherish very nearly the same feelings towards the ocean with me. There now is your insular city of the Manhattoes, belted round by wharves as Indian isles by coral reefs—commerce surrounds it with her surf. Right and left, the streets take you waterward. Its extreme downtown is the battery, where that noble mole is washed by waves, and cooled by breezes, which a few hours previous were out of sight of land. Look at the crowds of water-gazers there. Circumambulate the city of a dreamy Sabbath afternoon. Go from Corlears Hook to Coenties Slip, and from thence, by Whitehall, northward. What do you see?—Posted like silent sentinels all around the town, stand thousands upon thousands of mortal men fixed in ocean reveries. Some leaning against the spiles; some seated upon the pier-heads; some looking over the bulwarks of ships from China; some high aloft in the rigging, as if striving to get a still better seaward peep. But these are all landsmen; of week days pent up in lath and plaster—tied to counters, nailed to benches, clinched to desks. How then is this? Are the green fields gone? What do they here ?

text:
Against hope he turned and looked along the road; felt every pocket, lifted his feet, and looked under the mat. His companion, in reply, said she had not seen it since his visit to the shanty.

“My Gord!” he said, “Mag’s a fair terror!” He was greatly troubled till the braggart in him gave an assertive flicker. “Know wot I’ll do ter Lizer soon’s she begins ter start naggin’ at me?” He intended this question as an insoluble conundrum, and waited for no surmises. “Fill ’er mug with this!” The shut fist he shook was more than a mugfull. “’Twouldn’ be ther first time I done it, not ther lars’.” But the anticipation seemed little comfort to him.

The rest of the journey was done in silence, and without even a peep at the sky. When they came to the homestead gate he said his throat felt as though a “goanner” had crawled into it and died. He asked her for a pin and clumsily dropped it in his efforts to draw the collar up to his ears, but had better luck with a hair-pin.

He appeared suddenly subdued and sober, and as he took his seat after closing the gate, he offered her his hand, and said, hurriedly, “No ’arm done, an’ no ’arm meant; an’ don’t let on ter my missus—thet’s ’er on the verander—thet we come be ther shanty.”

It was dusk, but through it she saw that the woman was dusky too.

“Boss in, Lizer?” There was contrition and propitiation in his voice.

“You’ve bin a nice blanky time,” said his missus, “an’ lucky fer you: Billy Skywonkie ’e ain’t.”

With bowed head, his shoulders making kindly efforts to hide his ears, he sat silent and listening respectfully. The woman in the buggy thought that the volubility of the angry half-caste’s tongue was the nearest thing to perpetual motion. Under her orders both got down, and from a seat under the open window in the little room to which Lizer had motioned, she gave respectful attention to the still rapidly flowing tirade. The offence had been some terrible injustice to a respectable married woman, “slavin’ an’ graftin’ an’ sweatin’ from mornin’ ter night, for a slungin’ idlin’ lazy blaggard.” In an indefinable way the woman felt that both of them were guilty, and to hide from her part of the reproof was mean and cowardly. The half-caste from time to time included her, and by degrees she understood that the wasted time of which Lizer complained was supposed to have been dissipated in flirtation. Neither the shanty nor Mag had mention.

text: The Old Bailey was a criminal court, and the prisoner at the bar was a young man of about five-and-twenty, well-grown and well-looking, with a sunburnt cheek and a dark eye. His hair was dark, and his beard, which he wore in the fashion of the time, was dark, and neatly trimmed. He stood quietly, with his hands resting on the rail before him, and his eyes fixed on the judge. The trial was for treason. The prisoner was accused of having, on various occasions, carried letters between France and England, for the purpose of aiding the enemy. The witnesses were two men and a woman. The first witness, a tall, thin man with a sallow face, swore that he had seen the prisoner in France, talking with known rebels. The second witness, a short, fat man with a red nose, swore that he had received a letter from the prisoner, containing information about the English army. The woman, who was pale and trembling, swore that she had seen the prisoner hiding letters in his coat. The prisoner listened to all this with a calm expression. When his turn came to speak, he denied all the charges. He said that he had never been in France, except on one occasion, when he had gone there to visit a sick friend. He said that he had never written any letters to the enemy, and that the witnesses were lying. He spoke clearly and firmly, and there was something in his manner that made the jury look at him with interest. Mr. Stryver, the prisoner's lawyer, was a loud, energetic man. He cross-examined the witnesses sharply, and succeeded in making several contradictions in their stories. The tall, thin man could not remember the exact date when he had seen the prisoner in France. The short, fat man could not produce the letter he claimed to have received. The woman admitted that she had been paid to give evidence against the prisoner. As the trial went on, the crowd in the court became more and more interested. Some people whispered that the prisoner was innocent, while others said that he was guilty. The judge, a stern-looking man with a grey wig, listened carefully to all the evidence. When Mr. Stryver had finished his cross-examination, the judge summed up the case to the jury. He told them that it was their duty to decide whether the prisoner was guilty or not, based on the evidence before them.

text: “Ship, ahoy! Hast seen the White Whale?” So cried Ahab, once more hailing a ship showing English colours, bearing down under the stern. Trumpet to mouth, the old man was standing in his hoisted quarter-boat, his ivory leg plainly revealed to the stranger captain, who was carelessly reclining in his own boat’s bow. He was a darkly-tanned, burly, good-natured, fine-looking man, of sixty or thereabouts, dressed in a spacious roundabout, that hung round him in festoons of blue pilot-cloth; and one empty arm of this jacket streamed behind him like the broidered arm of a hussar’s surcoat. “Hast seen the White Whale?” “See you this?” and withdrawing it from the folds that had hidden it, he held up a white arm of sperm whale bone, terminating in a wooden head like a mallet. “Man my boat!” cried Ahab, impetuously, and tossing about the oars near him—“Stand by to lower!” In less than a minute, without quitting his little craft, he and his crew were dropped to the water, and were soon alongside of the stranger. But here a curious difficulty presented itself. In the excitement of the moment, Ahab had forgotten that since the loss of his leg he had never once stepped on board of any vessel at sea but his own, and then it was always by an ingenious and very handy mechanical contrivance peculiar to the Pequod, and a thing not to be rigged and shipped in any other vessel at a moment’s warning. Now, it is no very easy matter for anybody—except those who are almost hourly used to it, like whalemen—to clamber up a ship’s side from a boat on the open sea; for the great swells now lift the boat high up towards the bulwarks, and then instantaneously drop it half way down to the kelson. text: I first heard of Ántonia on what seemed to me an interminable journey across the great midland plain of North America. I was ten years old then; I had lost both my father and mother within a year, and my Virginia relatives were sending me out to my grandparents, who lived in Nebraska. I travelled in the care of a mountain boy, Jake Marpole, one of the 'hands' on my father's old farm under the Blue Ridge. He was now going West to work for my grandfather. Jake's experience of the world was not much wider than mine. He had never been in a railway train until the morning when we set out together to try our fortunes in a new world. We went all the way in day-coaches, becoming more sticky and grimy with each stage of the journey. Jake bought everything the newsboys offered him: candy, oranges, brass collar buttons, a watch-charm, and for me he bought a copy of "Life of Jesse James," which I remember as one of the most satisfactory books I have ever read. Beyond Chicago we were under the protection of a friendly passenger conductor, who knew all about the country to which we were going and who gave us a great deal of advice in exchange for our confidence. He seemed to us an experienced and worldly man who had been almost everywhere; in his conversation he threw out lightly the names of distant states and cities. He wore the rings and pins and badges of different fraternal orders to which he belonged. Even his cuff-buttons were engraved with hieroglyphics, and he was more inscribed than an Egyptian obelisk. When he smoked, he smoked with theatrical effect and gesture, blowing smoke-rings and carrying his cigarette in the long amber holder which was then in vogue. I recognized him as one of the important people of the world, truly sophisticated. The conductor told us we were in Nebraska now, and that was the first word which made us feel that we had really left home. He said we were to look out the window, and we should see that the land was different. And so it was. The earth was much paler than in Virginia, the sky was a more intense blue, and the wind never stopped blowing. There was nothing but land: not a country at all, but the material out of which countries are made. The wagon-ruts were deep, as if this land had been travelled over many times before we came, though in truth it was still very new.

text: The apartment balcony's railing was cold with morning dew, and when Tereza touched the wet shirt hanging on the line, she felt the fabric cling to her fingertips—soft cotton, still smelling of the lavender detergent she loved. Below, the street was waking up: a man jogged past, headphones on, his breath fogging in the cool air; a baker unlocked his shop door, flipping the 'Open' sign with a clink. The smell of fresh croissants drifted up, sweet and buttery, mixing with the faint scent of rain from last night's shower. She thought of Tomas, her husband, who'd left early for work—his kiss quick, his smile distracted, the way he'd hesitated before saying, 'I'll be home for dinner.' She'd watched him walk down the stairs, her chest tight with that familiar anxiety: Was he hiding something? Would he come back different? For weeks, she'd checked his phone, asked too many questions, clung to him like he might disappear if she let go. A sparrow landed on the railing, tilting its head at her. Tereza held out her hand, and it hopped closer, then flew off with a chirp. She laughed, a small, surprised sound. She thought of the first time they'd met—she'd been a waitress, spilling coffee on his suit, and he'd smiled instead of getting angry. Back then, she'd felt light, not heavy; hopeful, not scared. When had love turned into a cage? She picked up the shirt, shaking out the wrinkles. The sun climbed higher, warming the balcony, drying the dew on the railing. For a second, she saw it clearly: the checking, the clinging, the anxiety—they were all her way of trying to 'fix' love, to make it predictable. But love wasn't meant to be fixed. It was meant to be felt, even the messy parts—the hesitation, the doubt, the moments of distance. The baker set a tray of croissants on the windowsill, and a child ran up, pointing and laughing. Tereza leaned against the railing, watching them. She didn't need to control Tomas, or their love. She just needed to trust that they were both there, choosing each other, even when it was hard. She folded the dry shirt and carried it inside, placing it on Tomas's chair. The coffee pot gurgled in the kitchen, filling the apartment with warmth. For the first time in months, she didn't feel anxious. She felt light, like the air after rain—fresh, open, full of possibility. When the door opened later, Tomas walked in, holding a bunch of daisies. Tereza smiled, walking to him. She didn't ask where he'd been. She just hugged him, feeling his arms around her, and knew that this—this quiet, unforced moment—was the love she'd been searching for all along.

text: The October sun hung low over the Nebraska prairie, turning the endless fields of wheat into a sea of gold that rippled in the wind. Ántonia Shimerda walked beside the horse-drawn reaper, her sleeves rolled up to her elbows, her hands calloused from tying wheat sheaves into neat bundles. Her skirt, a faded blue, was tucked into her boots to keep it from dragging in the straw, and a red handkerchief was tied around her head to hold back her dark hair. Jim Burden, who'd come to help the Shimerda family harvest, drove the reaper, his eyes fixed on the row ahead—cutting a straight line through the wheat, the machine's blades singing as they sliced through the stalks. The air smelled of ripe wheat and dry grass, and the only sounds were the wind whistling across the prairie, the creak of the reaper's wheels, and Ántonia's soft laughter when the horse stopped to nibble at a clump of clover. By midday, the sun grew warmer, and they stopped to rest under a lone cottonwood tree—its leaves turning yellow, fluttering down like confetti. Ántonia pulled a canvas bag from her pocket, handing Jim a crust of black bread and a piece of dried sausage. 'Eat,' she said, smiling. 'We have many bundles left before sunset.' Jim took the food, watching her as she ate—her face flushed from the work, her eyes bright as she talked about the winter ahead, about storing hay for the horses and making preserves from the last of the garden's tomatoes. After resting, they went back to work, the reaper moving faster now as the wind picked up. Ántonia's little brother, Yulka, ran out from the family's sod house, carrying a bucket of water, his bare feet kicking up dust. 'Sister! Papa says to drink!' he called, waving. Ántonia wiped her hands on her skirt and walked over, kneeling to give Yulka a hug before taking a long drink from the bucket. As the sun began to set, painting the sky in shades of pink and orange, they finished the last row of wheat. Jim stopped the reaper, and Ántonia stood up, stretching her back—her shoulders sore, but her smile wide. The field was dotted with wheat bundles, like little brown houses, and the air felt cooler now, carrying the smell of wood smoke from the sod house's chimney. 'We did good,' Ántonia said, looking out at the field. Jim nodded, feeling proud—proud of the work they'd done, proud to be part of this vast, quiet prairie. Yulka ran back, jumping up and down, asking if they could ride the reaper home. Ántonia laughed, lifting him onto the seat beside Jim, and they started toward the sod house—slowly, so Yulka could wave at the wheat bundles as they passed, the last light of the sun gilding the prairie around them.

text: Chinese dumplings jiaozi are beloved savory treats, instantly recognizable by their iconic halfmoon shaped folds—each one a little work of art, often pinched along the edges to seal in flavor. Their wrappers are thin yet surprisingly elastic, made from a simple mix of flour and water that turns gently translucent when cooked, allowing glimpses of the colorful filling inside: a vibrant mix of ground pork or chicken for a lighter option, finely chopped cabbage bright green when raw, softening as it cooks, and plump shrimp pink and briny, adding sweetness—all tossed with minced scallions for extra freshness. How you cook them transforms their texture entirely:  When boiled or steamed, dumplings plump up slightly, their surfaces becoming smooth and shiny from absorbing steam, with a tender, delicate bite.  Panfried dumplings known as guotie or “potstickers” are a textural delight: the top stays soft, while the bottom crisps up into a crispy, golden crust that crackles when you bite into it—perfect for dipping. Tastewise, every dumpling is a burst of savory goodness. The filling is deeply seasoned with grated ginger for warmth, minced garlic for aroma, a splash of soy sauce for umami, and sometimes a drizzle of sesame oil for richness—all coming together to create a juicy center that oozes slightly when you break the wrapper. The dough itself balances the filling: soft and pillowy in boiled or steamed versions, or offering a satisfying crunchy contrast in panfried ones. A dip in black vinegar with a dash of chili oil, if you like elevates the flavor further, cutting through richness with a tangy kick. Culturally, dumplings are far more than food—they’re a symbol of celebration and connection. During Chinese New Year, families gather to make and eat jiaozi: their halfmoon shape resembles ancient Chinese gold or silver ingots, symbolizing wealth and prosperity for the new year. Wrapping dumplings together is also a cherished family activity, with generations sharing tips on folding techniques from simple pleats to intricate designs and chatting as they work—making the process as meaningful as the meal itself. They’re also served at family reunions or festivals, embodying togetherness. Their preparation is simple but joyful, relying on four key steps that turn basic ingredients into comfort food: 1. Wrapping: A small spoonful of filling is placed in the center of a wrapper. The edges are folded over to form a halfmoon shape, then pinched or pleated tightly to seal—this prevents filling from leaking out during cooking. It’s a step often done in groups, with everyone adding their own touch to the folds. 2. Boiling: Dumplings are dropped into boiling water sometimes with a pinch of salt to keep wrappers from sticking. They float to the surface when done, ready to be scooped out and served hot—ideal for a quick, comforting meal. 3. Steaming: Steaming in a bamboo steamer lined with cabbage leaves or parchment to prevent sticking retains the filling’s juiciness and keeps the wrapper tender. The gentle heat ensures the filling cooks through without drying out, making this the healthiest option. 4. Panfrying: Dumplings are first seared in oil until the bottom turns golden and crispy, then a splash of water is added to the pan, and it’s covered to steam the tops. Once the water evaporates, the crust crisps up again—resulting in the classic potsticker texture. Whether boiled, steamed, or panfried, Chinese dumplings are a testament to how simple ingredients, prepared with care, can become a cultural staple—one that brings people together, one juicy bite at a time.

text: With the worthless parasitical human beings gone, there was more for everyone to eat. There was more leisure too, inexperienced though the animals were. They met with many difficulties - for instance, later in the year, when they harvested the corn, they had to tread it out in the ancient style and blow away the chaff with their breath, since the farm possessed no threshing machine - but the pigs with their cleverness and Boxer with his tremendous muscles always pulled them through. Boxer was the admiration of everybody. He had been a hard worker even in Jones's time, but now he seemed more like three horses than one; there were days when the entire work of the farm seemed to rest on his mighty shoulders. From morning to night he was pushing and pulling, always at the spot where the work was hardest. He had made an arrangement with one of the cockerels to call him in the mornings half an hour earlier than anyone else, and would put in some volunteer labour before the regular day's work began, which was always the most needed. His answer to every problem, every setback, was "I will work harder!" - which he had adopted as his personal motto. But everyone worked according to his capacity. The hens and ducks, for instance, saved five bushels of corn at the harvest by gathering up the stray grains. No one stole, no one grumbled over his rations, the quarrels and bite - fights of former days had almost disappeared. There was no shirking, or almost no shirking. Mollie, it was true, was not good at getting up in the mornings, and had a way of leaving work early on the ground that there was a stone in her hoof. And the cat was somewhat peculiar. She was never seen when there was work to be done, but appeared promptly at meal - times and then purred loudly, as if nothing whatever were the matter. But she always had an excellent excuse, and was indeed most affectionate to everyone. Old Benjamin, the donkey, seemed quite unchanged since the Rebellion. He worked just as hard as he had done in Jones's time, never shirked, and never volunteered for extra work either. About the Rebellion and its results he would express no opinion. When asked whether he was not happier now that Jones was gone, he would say only "Donkeys live a long time. None of you has ever seen a dead donkey." And the others had to be content with this cryptic answer.

As they walked through the forest of pillars, the intricate carvings of gods and hieroglyphs told silent stories of a civilization long vanished. The silence itself was profound, broken only by the distant cry of a bird and the soft scuff of their own shoes on the ancient stone. It was a place of overwhelming grandeur and a haunting sense of the past, a past that was violent, magnificent, and utterly remote from the present day. They emerged presently from the gloom of the hypostyle hall into the open space before the sacred lake. Here the light was clearer, the sky a pale, washed-out blue. A few tourists stood about, their voices hushed as if by common consent. A guide was droning on in French about the priests who had once performed their ablutions in the now stagnant water. Linnet, slipping her hand through Simon's arm, said, 'It's rather frightening, isn't it? So much effort… for nothing.' Simon pressed her arm. 'Oh, I don't know. It's lasted a pretty long time.' text: The mist hung heavy over the cobblestone streets of Paris, cold and damp, as Sydney Carton walked slowly toward the grim prison where Charles Darnay lay condemned to death. His coat was pulled tight against the night chill, his hands stuffed in his pockets, his face hidden in the shadow of his hat—an outward sign of the emptiness he had carried for years. The air smelled of gunpowder and smoke, of the distant shouts of revolutionaries, of the faint scent of candle wax from the windows of nearby houses where families huddled in fear. Every step felt like a weight, not just of the stone beneath his boots, but of the wasted life he had lived—of the talent unused, the love unspoken, the potential squandered. He had always been a man of contradictions: brilliant yet lazy, witty yet melancholy, capable of great kindness yet trapped in self-loathing. He had loved Lucie Manette from afar, watching her marry Darnay with a broken heart but a silent blessing. He had seen in Darnay the goodness he himself could never seem to grasp—the stability, the honor, the joy in living that had eluded him. For years, he had wandered through life like a ghost, drinking to numb the pain of his own inadequacy, convinced he was nothing but a disappointment to everyone, including himself. But now, as he neared the prison, a quiet resolve settled over him. He thought of Lucie's smile, of the way her eyes lit up when she looked at Darnay, of the children they had together—a family built on love and hope. He thought of the promise he had made to her long ago: 'I would give my life to keep you and yours from harm.' At the time, he had thought it a hollow words, a fleeting moment of sentimentality. But now, it felt like a purpose—a reason to finally do something worth remembering, something that would make his life mean something. The prison loomed ahead, its stone walls towering against the dark sky, guards pacing at the gates with muskets in hand. Carton's heart raced, not with fear, but with a strange sense of peace. He had planned everything carefully, swapping places with Darnay in the dead of night, using his uncanny resemblance to the prisoner to slip into the cell undetected. He knew he would not survive the morning—would not live to see the guillotine's blade fall—but he did not care. For the first time in his life, he felt alive, truly alive, in the knowledge that he was giving someone else the chance to live. He thought of his own childhood, of the loneliness and neglect that had shaped him, of the man he might have been if he had chosen a different path. Regret gnawed at him, but it was not the paralyzing regret of years past.

And, from there to seeing that it is not individuals but enterprises or groups that succeed or fail is a very small step to take. And then immediately there suggests itself the other fact that it is not the mere death and still less the mere marriage of an individual that brings to an end either a group or an enterprise. It is perhaps going too far to say that no man is indispensable, but it is far more usual to find that, when a seemingly indispensable individual disappears for one reason or another from an enterprise, that adventure proceeds with equanimity and very little shock. I suppose the most co-operative and at the same time the most one-man concern of to-day is the newspaper or the periodical publication, and I suppose that in my time I must have been acquainted with something at least of the affairs of at least a hundred journals or periodicals each of them of necessity more or less autocratically conducted, simply because a journal running along and having to appear on a stated day, it is hardly ever practicable to get together an editorial committee soon enough to make momentous decisions that may have to be arrived at in a minute or two. Yet almost the first discovery that the most strong-minded of editors makes after he has got the periodical of his founding running for a month or two is that it is the periodical that has taken charge—and the most notable fact of journalism is that even when the most noted of editors suddenly dies his paper in the immense majority of cases goes on running in perfect tranquillity and with no apparent change for a period sufficiently long to make it perfectly manifest that the great man was not in the least indispensable.

And, as with newspapers, so with nearly all the other enterprises of life. I am not of course saying that no great man exists or no founder of great enterprises, though I should imagine that there must be even more mute inglorious Miltons than ever got a chance of putting their epics before the public.

text: The autumn night in Yu Zhan'ao’s spot beside the sorghum field in Gaomi, Shandong was fiery—fiery enough that the smell of ripe sorghum filled the air and the distant rumble of Japanese artillery shook the ground, mixing with the pungent scent of kaoliang liquor from his gourd. He sat on a pile of dry sorghum stalks (golden from the autumn sun, brittle under his weight), a dented copper liquor gourd in his hands (filled with home-brewed kaoliang, its surface polished smooth by years of use) and a tattered cotton jacket beside him, his eyes fixed on the flickering torches in the distance, their light cutting through the mist like blades of fire. The air smelled of gunpowder (from the skirmish earlier that day) and earth (turned over by the hooves of horses), and a blood-stained knife—his father’s old weapon, its blade still sharp—lay stuck in the ground beside him, a silent witness to the battles he’d fought. He thought of the day he’d met Jiu’er—of the way she’d stood in the sorghum field, her red dress bright against the green stalks, of the way she’d laughed when he offered her a sip of liquor, of the way she’d said “A man who fights for his land is worth loving,” her voice clear as a bell. He’d fought for her, he thought—fought the Japanese who burned their villages, fought the landlords who stole their grain, fought the ghosts of his past that tried to drag him down—but lately, the liquor tasted bitter: the bloodshed felt endless, the loss too heavy, the line between “hero” and “butcher” growing thin with each life he took. A gust of wind swept through the sorghum field, sending stalks rustling like whispers. He lifted the gourd to his lips, taking a long drink—its liquor burning his throat, a reminder that he was still alive. He thought of his father, who’d died with the knife in his hand, saying “Protect the land, protect the people,” and of Jiu’er, who’d poured liquor on the sorghum to set fire to the Japanese tanks, her laugh echoing even as the flames swallowed her. Those memories were hot, like the liquor in his gourd—painful, but keeping him from freezing into stone.

text: The first ray of spring sun slanted over the gabled roofs of Middlemarch's market square, touching the weathered stone cross at its center—its carvings softened by years of rain and frost, yet still holding the faint outline of a shepherd and his flock. The square, usually quiet at this hour, hummed with a gentle bustle: farmers in rough tweed coats unloaded crates of turnips and carrots from their carts, their boots crunching on the last of the night's frost; a baker's cart, stacked with loaves of crusty brown bread and sweet currant buns, rumbled over the cobblestones, its wheels singing a low, rhythmic tune. Mrs. Garth, her bonnet tied neatly under her chin, walked along the row of stalls, a wicker basket on her arm. She paused at a vendor's cart heaped with daffodils—their golden petals glowing like small suns, their green stems still damp with dew—and exchanged a few words with the old woman tending them, who smiled and tucked an extra bloom into Mrs. Garth's basket. Nearby, a blacksmith's apprentice polished a horseshoe, its metal glinting in the sun, while a group of children chased a stray dog that had stolen a crust of bread, their laughter echoing off the whitewashed walls of the inn. A market woman spread a cloth over her stall, arranging jars of honey—their amber contents thick and glossy—and bunches of herbs: thyme, rosemary, and sage, their scents mixing with the smell of fresh bread and damp earth. The town crier, his red coat bright against the muted tones of the square, stood on the steps of the town hall, clearing his throat before announcing the day's notices, his voice carrying over the chatter of the crowd. As the sun climbed higher, the frost melted away, leaving the cobblestones damp and glistening. Mrs. Garth, her basket now full, stopped to watch a group of women weaving daffodils into a garland for the church door, their fingers nimble as they twisted the stems together. A young farmer offered her a handful of wild primroses, their pale yellow petals peeking out from his palm, and she thanked him, tucking them beside the daffodils. The square was a tapestry of small, vital moments: the clink of a pitcher as a vendor poured cider, the soft rustle of cloth as a seamstress displayed her wares, the warm smile between strangers exchanging news. It was a place where the rhythms of the earth and the lives of its people wove together—where spring's first blooms met the steady work of the land, and where every face held a thread in the quiet, unbroken story of the town. A place that felt not just like a square of stone, but like the very heart of Middlemarch itself.

text: I quickly followed suit, and descending into the bar-room accosted the grinning landlord very pleasantly. text: 124 was spiteful. Full of a baby's venom. The women in the house knew it and so did the children. For years each put up with the spite in his own way, but by 1873 Sethe and her daughter Denver were its only victims. The grandmother, Baby Suggs, was dead, and the sons, Howard and Buglar, had run away by the time they were thirteen years old—as soon as merely looking in a mirror shattered it (that was the signal for Buglar); as soon as two tiny hand prints appeared in the cake (that was it for Howard). Neither boy waited to see more; another kettleful of chickpeas smoking in a heap on the floor; soda crackers crumbled and strewn in a line next to the doorsill. Nor did they wait for one of the relief periods: the weeks, months even, when nothing was disturbed. No. Each one fled at once—the moment the house committed what was for him the one insult not to be borne or witnessed a second time. Within two months, in the dead of winter, their leaving was followed by the arrival of a baby ghost. A plate of food would be left on the table and later found with a tiny fistful scooped out. A lamp would topple for no reason. A pile of laundry, neatly folded, would be found thrown about the room. All this the women accepted as part of life's package. Baby Suggs, who had been a source of uncomplicated pride and joy for eight children (each one of whom she delivered herself), had no time for the antics of the unhappy dead. She had what she believed were reasons for not wanting to step foot in 124 again. Sethe, her daughter-in-law, who had not known the glory days of the plantation, who had arrived with her children after the war, accepted the haunting as part of the furniture. Denver, however, who had been born on the water and whose earliest memories were of crouching in a woodshed with her mother and a ghost, loved the ghost. It was the only other person in the house, and the two of them played together. Denver would sit on the stairs and watch the baby ghost crawl up the steps, its tiny hands leaving wet prints on the wood. She would follow the prints with her finger, tracing the path of the ghostly visitor.

But that gold watch he sought was the innermost life of the fish. And now it is struck; for, starting from his trance into that unspeakable thing called his “flurry,” the monster horribly wallowed in his blood, overwrapped himself in impenetrable, mad, boiling spray, so that the imperilled craft, instantly dropping astern, had much ado blindly to struggle out from that phrensied twilight into the clear air of the day. At last, gush after gush of clotted red gore, as if it had been the purple lees of red wine, shot into the frighted air; and falling back again, ran dripping down his motionless flanks into the sea. His heart had burst!

text:
"I am come to offer you one of my new cottages, Horbrook," said Mrs. Clay, as John came forward with a bow. "You bear an excellent character in Northcliffe, and so does your son George; and I shall have much pleasure in taking you for a tenant."

John Horbrook made a still lower bow, to give him time to think what he should say. It so took him by surprise, it seemed all too good to be true, there must be some mistake, and he must tell the lady the whole truth.

"I cannot thank you enough for your kind offer, ma'am," he said at last; "but I've heard say you object to large families, and there are ten of us, ma'am. And we are not very well-to-do in the world, although if God gives me health and strength, I hope to better myself before long."

"I know all, Horbrook," said Mrs. Clay, "and I know also that you are a thoroughly honest man, and merit all that your neighbours say of you. I repeat the offer I just made to you of one of the new cottages, and I hope God may grant many years of happiness in it. You have brought up your son George in the right way too; his master speaks most highly of him."

John Horbrook's face beamed with honest pride. "He has always been a good lad, and he was his mother's principal comfort whilst I was away. It has always been his wish that we should have one of your new cottages, ma'am."

"It was he who first spoke to me about it," said Mrs. Clay. "And now you may look upon the matter as settled, and you can take your wife and choose which cottage you would prefer. You shall have the first choice," saying which Mrs. Clay drove away, leaving John and his son in a state of the most perfect happiness.


In less than a fortnight, the Horbrooks were comfortably settled in their new home, where there was ample room for John to carry on his trade of shoemaker, and he soon had as much work as he could do.

He was never once behindhand with his rent. And the rent-book, regularly paid up, was one of the ornaments of the little round table in the window of their sitting-room. Both he and his wife lived to see George grow up and become a master mason.

He thought of the wars—of the smoke that had blackened the skies over Macondo, of the blood that had soaked the earth, of the men he’d killed with his own hands. He’d fought for freedom, for justice, for a world without tyranny, but in the end, he’d become just another tyrant, signing death warrants with the same indifference as the men he’d overthrown. He thought of the letter he’d written to his wife, Úrsula, years ago, telling her he’d “found his purpose,” but now he knew the truth—purpose was just a lie people told themselves to avoid the loneliness that lurked in every heart. The oil lamp flickered, casting long shadows over the walls. Aureliano set the goldfish down, running his fingers over the rough wood of the workbench. All of them, trapped in the same cycle of loneliness and death, just like every Buendía before them. A breeze blew through the open window, carrying the distant sound of a woman singing a folk song—soft, sad, a reminder of the world outside the old house. Aureliano stood up, walking to the window, and looked out at the empty street. Macondo was quiet now, the chaos of the wars long gone, but the loneliness remained, thick as the dust in his workshop. He thought of the gypsies who’d come to town when he was a boy, bringing strange inventions and stories of far-off lands, and how he’d dreamed of leaving Macondo, of escaping the fate of his family. text: Father Laurence, the parish priest of Middleton, was returning home from Holwick on a dark night in the late spring. He had come from the bedside of a dying woman and the scene was unpleasantly impressed on his mind. Sarah Moulton had certainly not been a blessing to her neighbours, but, in spite of that, he felt sorry for the delicate child left behind, as he did not see what was to become of it. He felt very troubled, too, about the poor creature, herself, for was not his task the cure of souls? Not that Sarah Moulton was much of a mother; but perhaps any kind of a mother was better than nothing, and the poor child had loved her; yet now she was gone, and the little one was alone in the world. The road wound through a thick wood, and the trees creaked and moaned in the light wind that had sprung up. The moon was hidden by clouds, and the only light came from the faint glow of his lantern, which flickered and threatened to go out at every gust. Father Laurence pulled his cloak closer about him; it was not only the cold that made him shiver, but a strange sense of unease that had come over him since he left Holwick. As he rounded a bend in the path, he heard a soft whimpering sound. At first he thought it might be some small animal, but as he drew nearer, he realized it was a child. He held up his lantern, and the light fell on a little girl huddled beneath an oak tree. She could not have been more than six years old, with matted fair hair and a thin, ragged dress that offered no protection against the chill night air. Her face was streaked with tears, and her small body shook with cold and fear. “Who are you, my child?” Father Laurence asked gently, kneeling down beside her. The girl looked up at him with wide, dark eyes. She did not answer, but shrank back as if afraid. “Do not be frightened,” he said, his voice softening. “I am Father Laurence, the priest from Middleton. I will not hurt you.”

text: The spring sun filtered through the oak leaves, dappling the floor of the wood with patches of golden light that shifted as the wind stirred the branches. Connie Chatterley sat on a rough wooden bench outside the small cottage, her back against the weathered stone wall, a handful of pale pink wild cherry blossoms in her hand. The petals were soft against her fingers, one by one drifting to the ground as she brushed her thumb over them—slow, absent movements, like her mind was somewhere far from the quiet of the woods. She'd left the big house an hour ago, slipping past the servants, past the empty drawing room where her husband Clifford spent his days typing endless manuscripts about coal mines and industrial progress. "Connie, we must think of the future," he'd said that morning, his voice flat, his eyes never leaving the page. But the future felt like a gray fog to her—no color, no warmth, no touch that wasn't polite, distant, safe. A bird chirped nearby, a clear, bright sound that made her look up. She watched it flit from branch to branch, its wings a flash of brown against the green, and for a second she felt a tightness in her chest—sharp, sudden, like a memory she couldn't quite grasp. It was the feeling of being alive, not just existing: the feel of rain on her face, the sound of a laugh that wasn't forced, the weight of someone's hand in hers that didn't let go. She stood up, brushing the grass from the hem of her silk robe—soft, cream-colored, the kind of thing Clifford liked her to wear, "fit for a lady of the manor." But today it felt like a cage, scratchy against her skin, too tight around her shoulders. She walked a few steps into the woods, the moss soft under her bare feet, and stopped at a small stream. The water gurgled over smooth stones, clear and cold, and she knelt down to dip her fingers in it. The chill made her gasp, and for a second the fog in her head lifted. She looked at her reflection in the water—her hair messy, her cheeks flushed, her eyes bright with something she hadn't seen there in years. Not sadness, not resignation. Longing. For something real. For someone who saw her, not just "Lady Chatterley," not just Clifford's wife.

text: The rain beat against the windows of Netherfield Park’s drawing room, a steady, soft patter that mixed with the crackle of the fire in the hearth. Elizabeth Bennet sat alone on a high-backed armchair, a letter clutched in her hands—Mr. Darcy’s letter, the one he’d handed her that afternoon, his face pale, his voice tight, before he’d turned and walked away into the rain. She’d barely glanced at it then, too angry at his proposal, too hurt by his admission that he’d stood in the way of Jane and Bingley, too repulsed by the idea that he could ever think she might accept him. She’d stuffed it into her pocket, determined to forget it, to hate him more for his arrogance. But now, alone with the fire and the rain, curiosity had gotten the better of her. She unfolded the letter slowly, her fingers brushing the crisp paper. The firelight gilded the edges, turning his neat, firm handwriting into something almost warm—something that didn’t match the cold, proud man she thought she knew. “Dear Miss Bennet,” it began. She read on, her breath catching as he wrote of Wickham—of Wickham’s lies about his past, of his attempt to elope with Darcy’s young sister, Georgiana, for her fortune. Her heart sank. She’d believed Wickham, his charm, his tales of injustice—how could she have been so blind? Then came the part about Jane. Darcy’s voice, on the page, sounded almost regretful: he’d thought Jane didn’t return Bingley’s affection, that her calm demeanor was indifference. He’d acted out of what he thought was kindness, he wrote, not malice. Elizabeth’s throat tightened. She thought of Jane’s quiet sadness, of how she’d tried to hide her broken heart—and how she, Elizabeth, had dismissed Darcy’s role in it without a second thought. She set the letter down for a moment, staring into the fire. The flames danced, casting shadows on the walls, and she thought of all the times she’d judged Darcy too quickly—his silence at the ball, his reserve with her family, his refusal to explain himself. She’d called him proud, but wasn’t she just as guilty? Proud of her own judgment, too quick to believe the worst, too slow to see the truth. “I have been blind, prejudiced, absurd,” she whispered, the words hanging in the air. The rain outside grew louder, as if echoing her thoughts. She picked up the letter again, reading the final lines—his hope that she might reconsider him, his willingness to answer any questions—and felt something she hadn’t felt before: not anger, not hatred, but a strange, uneasy sort of respect. The fire popped, sending a shower of sparks up the chimney. Elizabeth folded the letter carefully, tucking it back into her pocket.
