text: The high-speed train stands as the ultimate pinnacle of contemporary rail transportation, seamlessly integrating cutting-edge engineering, advanced materials science, and revolutionary control systems into a single cohesive marvel that reshapes the very fabric of modern travel and connects cities and regions like never before. Unlike slower, conventional trains, which rely on outdated mechanical structures, inefficient energy conversion, and limited speed capabilities, high-speed trains boast exceptional speed, unparalleled stability, and remarkably minimized energy consumption, perfectly coupling aerodynamic design with superior traction technology to achieve smooth, efficient, and eco-friendly operation that redefines the standards of public transportation. During peak travel hours, when millions of commuters and travelers depend on reliable, fast, and comfortable transportation to reach their destinations, high-speed trains operate with unmatched precision, adhering to strict schedules and ensuring passengers arrive on time while avoiding the congestion, delays, and uncertainties that plague other forms of transit such as cars, buses, or even airplanes. Compared to air travel, which demands lengthy security checks, crowded terminals, expensive tickets, and frequent cancellations due to weather conditions or technical issues, high-speed trains offer a more relaxed, stress-free journey, allowing travelers to work, relax, read, or enjoy the scenery without the restrictions of airport regulations, the anxiety of flight delays, or the discomfort of cramped airplane seats. Even in regions with complex terrains, such as mountainous areas, coastal lines, high-altitude plateaus, and dense urban centers, high-speed trains demonstrate remarkable adaptability, employing advanced signal systems, precision braking technology, intelligent climate control, and reinforced tracks to navigate challenging environments and maintain consistent performance, safety, and comfort. Without advanced communication technologies, such as 5G-enabled control centers, real-time monitoring systems, and satellite navigation, the safe and efficient operation of high-speed trains would be impossible, as they rely on continuous data exchange between the train, the control center, and nearby stations to prevent collisions, adjust speed, and ensure the well-being of every passenger and crew member on board. That unwavering reliability has made high-speed trains a symbol of national pride in many countries, representing technological progress, economic growth, and improved quality of life for citizens across urban and rural areas alike. Its sleek, aerodynamic body, composed of high-strength aluminum alloys and lightweight composite materials, is specifically designed to reduce air resistance to a minimum, allowing the train to reach incredible speeds while maintaining stability and fuel efficiency. The train’s interior is designed with meticulous attention to detail, featuring spacious, ergonomic seats with adjustable headrests and legroom, large panoramic windows that offer stunning views of the passing landscape, silent air conditioning systems that maintain a comfortable temperature, high-speed Wi-Fi for connectivity, and comprehensive entertainment systems (including screens and charging ports) that turn travel into a delightful experience rather than a tedious chore. This focus on user comfort and convenience has revolutionized public perception of rail travel, making high-speed trains a preferred choice for business travelers, families, tourists, and daily commuters alike. Moreover, high-speed trains have reshaped regional economies by connecting major cities within hours, creating new business hubs, boosting tourism, and improving accessibility to remote areas, thereby fostering social integration, cultural exchange, and economic development across entire regions. They operate on dedicated tracks that eliminate conflicts with freight trains, ensuring optimal safety and efficiency, while their intelligent power management systems minimize carbon emissions and environmental impact, making them a sustainable alternative to air and road transportation. Achieving speeds exceeding 350 kilometers per hour (and in some cases, up to 400 kilometers per hour for experimental models), high-speed trains maintain exceptional stability through advanced active suspension systems, precision wheel-rail technology, and real-time vibration damping, ensuring a smooth ride even at maximum speed. They achieve this level of performance through rigorous testing, continuous innovation, and strict maintenance protocols, with teams of engineers and technicians working around the clock to inspect, repair, and upgrade the trains and tracks to guarantee safety and reliability. In recent decades, high-speed rail has expanded rapidly across the globe, with countries like China, Japan, France, Germany, and Spain investing billions of dollars in infrastructure development, train manufacturing, and technological upgrades, solidifying its position as one of the most important transportation innovations of the 21st century. Whether for daily commuting between cities, long-distance travel for business or leisure, or regional tourism to explore new places, high-speed trains continue to play a vital role in shaping the future of mobility, offering a sustainable, efficient, and convenient alternative that addresses the growing demands of modern society and connects people in ways that were once unimaginable.

text:
“Well, and to what do I owe the honor of this visit, Monsieur Hipwell?” he asked coldly, speaking with a strong foreign accent. His appearance might have been that of an under-servant at an hotel. He was uncouth and unwashed. His finger-nails were uncared for and dirty, and his black beard ragged and untrimmed. And yet, this man, with his active and ingenious brain, controlled one of the most daring and successful gangs of motor-bandits in Europe.

And I was one of the few who knew his true identity, a secret that the police of Europe would give much to learn. I recollect that the drama of the situation caused me to hesitate.

“I have called to see you on several urgent matters,” I said. “I wish to be quite frank and open with you, without any unfriendliness, but rather as one of your friends and assistants.”

“Bien! That is well,” he grunted approvingly, stirring quickly in his great crimson chair, in which he sat as though he were a judge. “We are friends—bien! trés bien! And now further. Continue.”

“First, I wish to hand you these,” I said bluntly, drawing out the string of fine pearls.

He took them in his hands, ran them slowly through his fingers, and again grunted approbation.

“Afraid to keep them any longer, eh?” he laughed, with a sarcastic curl of his lips. “Well, I’m really not surprised. In your position it would be a bit awkward for your family, and for your Foreign Office at Downing Street, wouldn’t it—hein?”

“That is just my point, monsieur,” I said quickly. “As you well know, I quite inadvertently stumbled into your private affairs on that foggy night, and you very naturally believed that girl Hatten’s allegation that I was a police-spy. By now, however, you surely have established my innocence—that just by a freak of circumstance I blundered in on you. Have you yet forgiven me?” I asked very seriously.

“Most certainly I have. I am always just, Monsieur Hipwell. None of those who were under me have ever accused me of either parsimony or injustice.”

text: One of the most striking phosphorescent fishes is a small shark, Squalus fulgens, also described and figured by Kner as Leius ferox, which, in general appearance, somewhat resembles the black or brown nurse (or Scymnus) of our Southern coast. This interesting light-giver was discovered by Dr. Bennett, and the following is his version of the find: "Being[100] dark when I first saw it shining in the net, it resembled a Pyrosoma, emitting, as it did, a bright phosphorescent light. This was in latitude 2° 15′ south, longitude 163° west. The length of my specimen was five inches and a half. It is not a little singular that my brother, the late D. F. Bennett, obtained a specimen of this fish in the same latitude, and another in latitude 55° north, longitude 110° west. The first was taken in the daytime, and was ten inches in length,—much larger in size than my specimen. The second was taken at night, and its entire length was a foot and a half: both were alive when captured, and fought fiercely with their jaws, tearing the net in several places. On placing my fish in sea-water, and observing it in the dark cabin, it swam about for some time, emitting a bright phosphoric light; and when this had become so faint as to be almost imperceptible, it was readily rekindled on the animal being disturbed or excited. My specimen was of a perfectly black color, and died about four hours after it had been taken. The luminosity was retained for some hours after life was extinct. "The form of the shark, as indeed its whole structure, is peculiar. It no doubt belongs to the subgenus Scymnus. My specimen having been accidentally lost, I am unable to give a minute description of it. My brother was more fortunate. I will, therefore, give his account of so novel and interesting a fish. The body is cylindrical, rather slender, and tapers finely towards the tail. Its prevailing color is dusky brown; a broad black band, or collar, passes around the throat; and the fins are partially margined with white (my specimen, being small and young, varied in this respect, being black, with the fins of a less intensity of color); the skin rough,[101] as is usual in the shark tribe. The number of gill-apertures is five on each side. The fins are short, and for the most part disposed in a round form; the dorsals are two in number, small, and placed far back; the tail-fin is unequally divided, the upper being the longest and largest lobe.

text: They are never tired of talking about the beauty of their country, and one cannot deny that they make a great deal of it, for the beauty of the place attracts strangers, and the money spent by the strangers enriches the inn - keepers, and so brings in money to the town by means of the taxes.One fine autumn day, M. de Rênal was walking with his wife on the Cours de la Fidélité, he was speaking with a very serious air, and Mme. de Rênal was listening, while her eyes were uneasily following the movements of her three children. The eldest, who was about eleven years old, kept coming near the parapet, and seemed inclined to climb over it. Then a gentle voice called out the name of Adolphe, and the child gave up his project. Mme. de Rênal seemed to be about thirty years old, and was still quite good - looking."He will be sorry for it, that fine gentleman from Paris," said M. de Rênal in an angry tone, his face paler than usual. "I have friends at court too...."Although I should very much like to devote two hundred pages to the description of provincial life, I do not feel myself at liberty to subject the reader to the long - windedness and the subtle twists and turns of provincial conversation.The fine gentleman from Paris, who was so odious in the eyes of the mayor of Verrières, was no other than M. Appel. Two days previously, he had contrived to gain admission, not only to the prison and the workhouse of Verrières, but also to the hospital, which was managed by the mayor and the principal inhabitants of the town in their capacity as trustees."But," said Mme. de Rênal timidly, "since you manage the poor people's welfare so honestly, what can this gentleman from Paris do to you?""They come to find fault, and then they write articles in the Liberal newspapers."

text: Before she could answer, the screen door slammed. Coral appeared in the doorway, a thin girl of thirteen with her father’s fair hair and her mother’s nervous eyes. Behind her stood a man in a police uniform, his jacket unbuttoned, a revolver hanging at his hip. It was the lieutenant from the provincial town, his face marked with a thin scar that ran from his eyebrow to his jawline. Fellows recognized him from the few times he had been called to the police station to sign papers. The lieutenant nodded, his gaze sweeping coldly around the room. “Captain Fellows,” he said. His voice was flat, with none of the deference Fellows sometimes got from local officials. “I’m looking for a man. A priest. He’s been seen in this district.” Fellows felt a chill run down his spine. Everyone knew the government’s orders—priests were to be arrested, their churches closed. He had heard rumors of a fugitive priest hiding in the hills, but he had tried not to listen. “A priest?” he said, forcing a laugh. “I haven’t seen any priests around here. We’re Protestants, you know.” “The child said the same,” the lieutenant replied, his eyes fixing on Coral. “But I thought I’d check the premises anyway. Just to be sure.” Coral stepped forward before Fellows could speak. “You can’t search our house,” she said firmly. Her voice trembled a little, but her chin was raised. “We haven’t done anything wrong.” The lieutenant’s scarred face tightened. He took a step closer to the girl, and Fellows put a hand on her shoulder, pulling her back. “There’s no need for that,” he said quickly. “We have nothing to hide, but—” “It’s against the law to refuse a search,” the lieutenant interrupted. But there was no real threat in his tone. He seemed tired, as if he had already searched a dozen houses that day and expected nothing. After a long, tense pause, he shrugged. “Very well. But if you see him—any man acting suspiciously, asking for food, keeping to himself—you’ll report it. Remember, you’re a foreigner here. We’ve been kind enough to let you stay.”

text: The winter sun streamed through the tall windows of the hospital ward, casting pale golden rectangles on the white sheets of the beds. Frederick Henry lay propped up on pillows, his injured leg in a plaster cast, his eyes fixed on the snow-covered roof-tops of Milan beyond the glass. The air smelled of antiseptic and fresh linen, of the faint smoke from the heater in the corner, a stark contrast to the gunpowder and mud he'd grown used to at the front. For weeks, he'd drifted between sleep and wakefulness, the pain in his knee a constant reminder of the war he'd left behind—the trenches, the artillery fire, the friends who'd fallen beside him. A soft knock at the door pulled him from his thoughts. Catherine Barkley stood in the doorway, her nurse's uniform crisp and neat, her hair tied back in a simple bun, a smile playing on her lips. 'Hello, Frederick,' she said, her voice quiet but warm. He felt a surge of something he hadn't felt in months—hope, or maybe just the relief of seeing a familiar face in a world turned upside down. She'd been a nurse at the field hospital where he'd first been treated, and in the chaos of war, they'd found a kind of solace in each other's company. She crossed the room, pulling a chair beside his bed, and took his hand in hers—her fingers cool and gentle against his calloused palm. 'How's the leg?' she asked, her thumb brushing lightly over his knuckles. He shrugged, wincing slightly as he shifted position. 'Better than it was. Not better than it will be when this war is over.' Catherine nodded, her smile fading. They both knew the war wouldn't end soon, that the fighting would go on, that more men would die, more lives would be broken. But for now, in this quiet room, they could pretend—pretend that the war didn't exist, that they were just two people, not a soldier and a nurse, not victims of a conflict bigger than themselves. He thought of the nights he'd spent in the trenches, huddled in the cold, listening to the shells explode in the distance, wondering if he'd live to see morning. He thought of the way the war had changed him—hardened him, made him cynical, made him doubt everything he'd once believed in. But Catherine was different. With her, he felt soft again, felt human. She didn't talk about heroism or duty or patriotism. She talked about the weather, about the books she'd read, about the little café in Milan where they could get good coffee and pastries.

text:
I soon learned to know this flower better. On the little prince's planet the flowers had always been very simple. They had only one ring of petals; they took up no room at all; they were a trouble to nobody. One morning they would appear in the grass, and by night they would have faded peacefully away. But one day, from a seed blown from no one knew where, a new flower had come up; and the little prince had watched very closely over this small sprout which was not like any other small sprouts on his planet. It might, you see, have been a new kind of baobab.
The shrub soon stopped growing, and began to get ready to produce a flower. The little prince, who was present at the first appearance of a huge bud, felt at once that some sort of miraculous apparition must emerge from it. But the flower was not satisfied to complete the preparations for her beauty in the shelter of her green chamber. She chose her colours with the greatest care. She adjusted her petals one by one. She did not wish to go out into the world all rumpled, like the field poppies. It was only in the full radiance of her beauty that she wished to appear. Oh, yes! She was a coquettish creature! And her mysterious adornment lasted for days and days.
Then one morning, exactly at sunrise, she suddenly showed herself.
And, after working with all this painstaking precision, she yawned and said:
"Ah! I am scarcely awake. I beg that you will excuse me. My petals are still all disarranged…"
But the little prince could not restrain his admiration:
"Oh! How beautiful you are!"
"Am I not?" the flower responded, sweetly. "And I was born at the same moment as the sun…"
The little prince could guess easily enough that she was not any too modest-- but how moving-- and exciting-- she was!
"I think it is time for breakfast," she added an instant later. "If you would have the kindness to think of my needs--"
And the little prince, completely abashed, went to look for a sprinkling - can of fresh water. So, he tended the flower.

text: Mr. Joseph Giebenrath was in no way remarkable or different from his fellow - citizens. He had a sturdy, healthy body like most of them, a mediocre talent for business, and an undisguised, heartfelt worship of money. In addition, he had a small house with a garden, a family grave in the cemetery, a somewhat liberalized and empty religious belief, a proper respect for God and the authorities, and a blind obedience to the iron - clad rules of bourgeois etiquette. He drank a fair amount of wine, but never got drunk. He engaged in some not - entirely - above - board transactions on the side, but never exceeded the limits permitted by the law. He called the poor paupers and the rich show - offs. He was a member of the Chamber of Commerce and went to the "Eagle" Club every Friday to play nine - pin bowling. He also never missed a bread - baking day, a tasting - dinner, or a sausage - soup party. He smoked cheap cigars at work and better ones after dinner and on Sundays. In every respect, his inner life was philistine. If he had any feelings, they had long since been covered with dust; they consisted only of traditional, vulgar family ideas, pride in his only son, and the occasional impulse to be charitable to the poor. His intelligence did not extend beyond a natural, sharply defined cunning and skill in dealing with numbers. His reading was confined to the newspaper, and for his artistic enjoyment, the annual amateur theatrical performance of the Chamber of Commerce and an occasional visit to the circus were sufficient. He could have exchanged names and houses with any of his neighbors without causing any change. Deep in his heart, he had the same eternal suspicion of any  extraordinary power or person as all the other fathers in the town, and the same instinctive hostility, out of jealousy, towards everything unusual, more free, more refined, and thoughtful. That is enough to say about him. Only a profound satirist would have been able to depict the mediocrity of his life and its unconscious tragedy. But he had a son, and about his son, there is much more to be said.

text: It is not the least among the strange things bred by the intense artificialness of sea-usages, that while in the open air of the deck some officers will, upon provocation, bear themselves boldly and defyingly enough towards their commander; yet, ten to one, let those very officers the next moment go down to their customary dinner in that same commander’s cabin, and straightway their inoffensive, not to say deprecatory and humble air towards him, as he sits at the head of the table; this is marvellous, sometimes most comical. Wherefore this difference? A problem? Perhaps not. To have been Belshazzar, King of Babylon; and to have been Belshazzar, not haughtily but courteously, therein certainly must have been some touch of mundane grandeur. But he who in the rightly regal and intelligent spirit presides over his own private dinner-table of invited guests, that man’s unchallenged power and dominion of individual influence for the time; that man’s royalty of state transcends Belshazzar’s, for Belshazzar was not the greatest. Who has but once dined his friends, has tasted what it is to be Cæsar. It is a witchery of social czarship which there is no withstanding. Now, if to this consideration you superadd the official supremacy of a ship-master, then, by inference, you will derive the cause of that peculiarity of sea-life just mentioned. Over his ivory-inlaid table, Ahab presided like a mute, maned sea-lion on the white coral beach, surrounded by his warlike but still deferential cubs. In his own proper turn, each officer waited to be served. They were as little children before Ahab; and yet, in Ahab, there seemed not to lurk the smallest social arrogance. With one mind, their intent eyes all fastened upon the old man’s knife, as he carved the chief dish before him. I do not suppose that for the world they would have profaned that moment with the slightest observation, even upon so neutral a topic as the weather. No! And when reaching out his knife and fork, between which the slice of beef was locked, Ahab thereby motioned Starbuck’s plate towards him, the mate received his meat as though receiving alms; and cut it tenderly; and a little started if, perchance, the knife grazed against the plate; and chewed it noiselessly; and swallowed it, not without circumspection. For, like the Coronation banquet at Frankfort, where the German Emperor profoundly dines with the seven Imperial Electors, so these cabin meals were somehow solemn meals, eaten in awful silence; and yet at table old Ahab forbade not conversation; only he himself was dumb.

text:
“Selling isn’t one bit like begging, you know, it’s going into business, Isa. But don’t, if you don’t want to! Let Poppy have all we raise and sell it, and keep the money,” suggested Mark.

“Oh, she never would,” declared Isabel. “Besides, it’s rather backing out. I’ll go, but I do feel rather queer about it.”

At the last minute, as it happened, Isabel did not go. Her mother telephoned for her to come home because a friend of her mother’s, who had not seen Isa since she was a baby, had unexpectedly arrived on a tour which she was making in her car, and Isabel had to be summoned home to see her for the brief hour which was all that she could spare to visit Mrs. Lindsay.

So all that Isabel shared of this expedition to market with Prue’s lettuce and Poppy’s radishes was storing the baskets, two of them, under the seat of the buckboard and seeing her friends start. After this she ran home.

Hurrah was in no mood for hurrying; the day was growing warm, the air heavy, showers threatened to come up at night. Poppy sat straight and stiff, driving, with Prue beside her. Mark sat on the end of the buckboard, dangling his long legs, amusing himself by turning the toes of his shoes toward each other, and admiring his ribbed brown stockings, or else experimenting in keeping his legs out stiff and straight while he raised himself on his hands and tried to hold himself thus as long as he could while they jolted along.

They had decided to go first of all to Mrs. Wilkins’. She was a merry, kindly old lady, nearing seventy, so friendly to children that half of the youngsters in Greenacres called her “Grandma Wilkins,” though she had no grandchild to give her the title.

“Whoa!” shouted Poppy, louder than was necessary, since Hurrah was not in the least deaf. She hoped that Mrs. Wilkins would hear and come out.

This happened, and when she appeared on her piazza Poppy called:

“Radishes! Round, red radishes! Raised by a Red-head! Round red radishes!” in a voice worthy of her new occupation.

“For goodness’ sake, Poppy! And you, Prudence Wayne! And Mark Hawthorne! Are you turning into hucksters? Well, I want to know!” cried Mrs. Wilkins.

text:
Kashtanka ran up and down and did not find her master, and meanwhile it had got dark. The street lamps were lighted on both sides of the road, and lights appeared in the windows. Big, fluffy snowflakes were falling and painting white the pavement, the horses’ backs and the cabmen’s caps, and the darker the evening grew the whiter were all these objects. Unknown customers kept walking incessantly to and fro, obstructing her field of vision and shoving against her with their feet. (All mankind Kashtanka divided into two uneven parts: masters and customers; between them there was an essential difference: the first had the right to beat her, and the second she had the right to nip by the calves of their legs.) These customers were hurrying off somewhere and paid no attention to her.
When it got quite dark, Kashtanka was overcome by despair and horror. She huddled up in an entrance and began whining piteously. The long day’s journeying with Luka Alexandritch had exhausted her, her ears and her paws were freezing, and, what was more, she was terribly hungry. Only twice in the whole day had she tasted a morsel: she had eaten a little paste at the bookbinder’s, and in one of the taverns she had found a sausage skin on the floor, near the counter —that was all. If she had been a human being she would have certainly thought: “No, it is impossible to live like this! I must shoot myself!”But she thought of nothing, she simply whined. When her head and back were entirely plastered over with the soft feathery snow, and she had sunk into a painful doze of exhaustion, all at once the door of the entrance clicked, creaked, and struck her on the side. She jumped up. A man belonging to the class of customers came out. As Kashtanka whined and got under his feet, he could not help noticing her. He bent down to her and asked:
“Doggy, where do you come from? Have I hurt you? O, poor thing, poor thing. . . . Come, don’t be cross, don’t be cross. . . . I am sorry.”
Kashtanka looked at the stranger through the snow-flakes that hung on her eyelashes, and saw before her a short, fat little man, with a plump, shaven face wearing a top hat and a fur coat that swung open.

text:
To give a new value to such confused materials, we must have recourse to a new and improved method of treating them.

The course here followed is, to examine the Arab authors of greatest value, and to develope, as completely as possible, the information found in them, their meaning being collected altogether from internal evidence, and without any regard to extrinsic systems. Where their statements are clear, natural, and consistent, no attempt has been made to interfere with or strain them by arbitrary conjectures. Where, on the other hand, they are obscure, absurd, or contradictory, care has been taken to inquire,—1st, What were the sources or channels of the author’s information? 2ndly, How far it must be taken in strictness, or may claim the latitude allowed to the language of ordinary discourse? 3rdly, The state of knowledge, and prevalent geographical systems in the writer’s time? 4thly, What portions may be looked upon as original or authentic, and what as founded on inference or surmise?—The point of greatest difficulty, and which demands the utmost care and perspicacity, is to distinguish between the language of experience and that of system; to separate the original information from the supplementary additions made to it, for the purpose of filling up or rounding the description, or of reconciling it with theoretical conceptions.

In all parts of the world, and in every age, the human mind moves in a constant cycle. In like stages of its progress it occupies similar positions, and goes through the same round of error. This truth is exemplified in the history of Geography, as well as in that of every other branch of human knowledge. The corrections made in our maps of Africa during the last three centuries; those made by Ptolemy in the geography of the same quarter of the globe, written by Marinus Tyrius; and those of which the great Alexandrian himself stands in need, are nearly all reducible to one common rule. The errors to which systematical geography tends, while it is not as yet founded on science, are so fully shown by experience, that we can safely derive from our knowledge of them a principle of rectification, applicable to all the materials of unscientific geography, presented to our notice, and obviously needing correction. The endeavour to trace errors according to fixed analogies, will at least lead us from mere conjecture towards a rule of reason.

text: These interesting light-givers are perhaps more common than we are aware of, from the fact that nocturnal investigations in the woods are not frequent, nearly all the discoveries being the result of accident. A small, luminous fungus has been observed in the Andaman Islands. Gandichand found one in Manilla, while Dr. Hooker, as we have seen, refers to the presence of one in the Sikkim Himalayas. These curious families of fungi are not only ornamental, but useful. In European countries the common mushroom enjoys the widest popularity as an esculent, especially the cultivated varieties. The meadow mushroom is scarcely inferior, though stronger in flavor, and is preferred by many to the cultivated species. In France the champignon is largely eaten; and in Austria a kind which has no admirers in England finds a constant place in the markets during the summer. Truffles and morels are favorites not only in Europe, but also in the vales of Cashmere, where two or three species of morels are dried for consumption throughout the year. The great puff-ball is increasing in reputation as a breakfast delicacy in Great Britain, while the chantarelle and the hedgehog fungus are esteemed by many. Numerous other species are more or less eaten by mycophagists, although they are never found in the public markets. A species of Boletus, cut in slices and dried, may be purchased throughout the year in most of the Continental cities. In Tahiti the Jew's ear is dried in large quantities and exported to China; while a species of agaric comes into the markets of Singapore, and another dried agaric is sent from the Cabul hills and the plains of north-western India. Several species of Cyttaria are eaten in the southern parts of South America, and in Australia a native kind is a favorite article of food. Indeed, a very long catalogue might be made of the species which are more or less consumed in different parts of the world. The cultivation of fungi for esculent purposes has not hitherto been successful with any other species than the ordinary mushroom. Attempts were made in France to cultivate truffles, at first apparently with considerable promise, but ultimately without much satisfaction. There is no good reason to suppose it impossible or improbable that many species might be devoted to experiments in that direction. Some species of Polyporus have been employed as styptics, or beaten till soft and used as amadon. One species in Burmah has a good reputation as an anthelmintic. Some species of Polysaccum and Geaster are employed medicinally in China. Species of Elaphomyces were at one time supposed to possess great virtues now deemed apocryphal. Ergot, developed on rye, wheat, and the germen of various grasses, still maintains its position in the pharmacopœia; but is almost the only fungus now employed, and that sparingly, by the legitimate medical practitioner.

text: “Clear away the boats! Luff!” cried Ahab. And obeying his own order, he dashed the helm down before the helmsman could handle the spokes. The sudden exclamations of the crew must have alarmed the whale; and ere the boats were down, majestically turning, he swam away to the leeward, but with such a steady tranquillity, and making so few ripples as he swam, that thinking after all he might not as yet be alarmed, Ahab gave orders that not an oar should be used, and no man must speak but in whispers. So seated like Ontario Indians on the gunwales of the boats, we swiftly but silently paddled along; the calm not admitting of the noiseless sails being set. Presently, as we thus glided in chase, the monster perpendicularly flitted his tail forty feet into the air, and then sank out of sight like a tower swallowed up. “There go flukes!” was the cry, an announcement immediately followed by Stubb’s producing his match and igniting his pipe, for now a respite was granted. After the full interval of his sounding had elapsed, the whale rose again, and being now in advance of the smoker’s boat, and much nearer to it than to any of the others, Stubb counted upon the honor of the capture. It was obvious, now, that the whale had at length become aware of his pursuers. All silence of cautiousness was therefore no longer of use. Paddles were dropped, and oars came loudly into play. And still puffing at his pipe, Stubb cheered on his crew to the assault. Yes, a mighty change had come over the fish. All alive to his jeopardy, he was going “head out”; that part obliquely projecting from the mad yeast which he brewed. *It will be seen in some other place of what a very light substance the entire interior of the sperm whale’s enormous head consists. Though apparently the most massive, it is by far the most buoyant part about him. So that with ease he elevates it in the air, and invariably does so when going at his utmost speed. Besides, such is the breadth of the upper part of the front of his head, and such the tapering cut-water formation of the lower part, that by obliquely elevating his head, he thereby may be said to transform himself from a bluff-bowed sluggish galliot into a sharppointed New York pilot-boat.

But a maid-servant came and said:
"Marya Grigoryevna is going, madam."
Olga Mihalovna jumped up, tidied her hair and hurried out of the room.
"Marya Grigoryevna, what is the meaning of this?" she began in an injured voice, going to meet Marya Grigoryevna. "Why are you in such a hurry?"
"I can't help it, darling! I've stayed too long as it is; my children are expecting me home."
"It's too bad of you! Why didn't you bring your children with you?"
"If you will let me, dear, I will bring them on some ordinary day, but to-day . . ."
"Oh, please do," Olga Mihalovna interrupted; "I shall be delighted! Your children are so sweet! Kiss them all for me. . . . But, really, I am offended with you! I don't understand why you are in such a hurry!"
"I really must, I really must. . . . Good-bye, dear. Take care of yourself. In your condition, you know . . ."
And the ladies kissed each other. After seeing the departing guest to her carriage, Olga Mihalovna went in to the ladies in the drawing-room. There the lamps were already lighted and the gentlemen were sitting down to cards.
The party broke up after supper about a quarter past twelve. Seeing her visitors off, Olga Mihalovna stood at the door and said:
"You really ought to take a shawl! It's turning a little chilly. Please God, you don't catch cold!"
"Don't trouble, Olga Mihalovna," the ladies answered as they got into the carriage. "Well, good-bye. Mind now, we are expecting you; don't play us false!"
"Wo-o-o!" the coachman checked the horses.
"Ready, Denis! Good-bye, Olga Mihalovna!"
"Kiss the children for me!"
The carriage started and immediately disappeared into the darkness. In the red circle of light cast by the lamp in the road, a fresh pair or trio of impatient horses, and the silhouette of a coachman with his hands held out stiffly before him, would come into view. Again there began kisses, reproaches, and entreaties to come again or to take a shawl. Pyotr Dmitritch kept running out and helping the ladies into their carriages.

text: The common lightning-bugs of Europe are Lampyris noctiluca (Plate IX., Fig. d) and L. splendidula (Fig. a). Their life history is an interesting study, and a brief description will apply to all. In early spring we find the little yellow eggs, perhaps gleaming with the wonderful phosphorescence, and thus finding protection, attached to blades of grass or other objects just above ground. The larva (Plate IX., Fig. c), a long, narrow, flat creature, soon appears and begins a predatory life; even being provided with an apparatus for removing the mucus of its victim. About the month of April it attains its full vigor, and during the summer changes to the pupa form, or hibernates all winter, entering a deep sleep, and assuming its new shape the following spring. We see the light from the very first in the eggs of some;[57] then in the larva, there appearing like little sacs on the under surface, one on each side of the middle line, so arranged that the insect can hide them by retracting the body, and causing them to blaze out when the abdomen is extended. Nothing in all nature is more wonderful than the changes through which these and other insects pass before attaining adult growth. The larva is a busy little creature, full of life; but, when about to change, it becomes lethargic and quiet, as if impressed with the importance of the coming metamorphosis. Finally it wriggles out of its old skin, and becomes a pupa, also luminous; exceedingly lively, yet with its motions restricted. It moves its antennæ and legs, and pushes itself along by movements of the abdomen. Finally the perfect insect appears, with its wondrous array of lights, so little understood, and which, if accompanied with the ordinary amount of heat attendant upon such a display, would soon roast or fry its possessor. As to the use of the lights, we can only conjecture. It has been shown that one insect recognized the other by it, and thus it may be a sign language; while, according to others, it is a warning to birds and other enemies.

text: The sun hung low in the sky, painting the Caribbean Sea a deep orange. Santiago sat in the stern of his small skiff, his hands raw from holding the fishing line that stretched taut into the dark water below. For three days and three nights, he'd fought this fish—this thing he hadn't yet seen, but whose pull he felt in every muscle of his body. 'Come on, old boy,' he muttered, his voice hoarse from lack of water. 'Show yourself. Let me see what I'm up against.' The line trembled, then pulled harder, yanking his hands toward the gunwale. Santiago grunted, leaning back to steady himself. He was tired—so tired his bones ached—but he wouldn't let go. This fish was his last chance, not just to sell for food, but to prove he wasn't a 'salao'—the worst form of unlucky. Slowly, so slowly, the water began to bulge. First a dark shadow, then a flash of silver as the fish rolled near the surface. Santiago's breath caught. It was a marlin—longer than his skiff, its dorsal fin sharp as a knife, its eyes like black stones staring up at the sky. 'Beautiful,' he whispered. Not a word he used often, but it fit. This fish was not just a catch. It was a worthy opponent. The marlin dove again, pulling the line so hard Santiago thought his hands might split open. He wrapped the line around his back, using his body weight to hold on. 'I'll stay with you,' he said, speaking both to the fish and to himself. 'I'll stay with you until one of us gives in.' His stomach growled—he'd eaten only a few raw tuna since the fight began—but he ignored it. Hunger was a small thing compared to the pride of this battle. He thought of the boy, Manolin, who'd begged to come with him but whose parents had said Santiago was too old, too unlucky. 'You should see this, Manolin,' he said softly. 'You'd be proud.' The sun dipped lower, and the sea turned purple. The marlin slowed, its pulls growing weaker. Santiago could feel it—they were both tired, both fighting for their lives. But Santiago had something the fish didn't: a choice to keep going, a reason to refuse defeat. 'I am not a lucky man,' he said, 'but I am a strong man. Stronger than you, old fish. Stronger than the sea.' He tightened his grip, his eyes fixed on the line. Somewhere below, the marlin was turning, getting ready for one last pull. Santiago took a deep breath, feeling the salt air fill his lungs. 'Let's finish this,' he said. And as the sun touched the horizon, he prepared to meet his opponent—face to face, with nothing but his hands, his line, and the unbreakable will to keep going.

text: We had a routine, a pattern to our days, and it gave me a sense of security. I would get up early, make the bed, and then go for a walk along the beach. He would join me later, and we would walk together, hand in hand, not speaking much, but enjoying each other's company. Then we would go back to the inn for breakfast, and after that, he would sit in the lounge and read the newspaper while I did some knitting or reading of my own. In the afternoon, we might go for another walk, or we would sit on the terrace and watch the sea. And in the evening, we would have dinner, and then go to bed early, tired but content. It was a simple life, a boring life, but we were happy. We had found a kind of peace, a peace that we had never known before. But there were times when the past would come back to haunt us, when the memories would flood our minds and we would be unable to shake off the feeling of sadness and loss. And then I would look at him, and see the pain in his eyes, and I would know that he was thinking of her, of Rebecca, the woman who had come between us, who had destroyed our happiness. The moon does funny things to people, even in dreams. I stood there, holding my breath, thinking the house was not an empty shell at all, but alive and breathing as it had been in the old days. Lights showed in the windows, and the curtains blew gently in the night wind. The door of the library must be ajar still, as we had left it, and my handkerchief lay on the table beside the bowl of autumn roses. Our room would bear evidence of us still; a little pile of books waiting to be put back on the shelves, the Times newspaper tossed aside, a cigarette end in the ashtray, our pillows propped up on the chairs where we had left them, the charred embers of the fire still smouldering in the grate, ready to flare into life with the dawn. And Jasper, our dog, would be lying on the floor, his big chin on his paws, his eyes full of wisdom, thumping his tail at the sound of our steps.

text: The rainy season had settled over Macondo, turning the clay streets into rivers of mud and wrapping the town in a thick, damp fog that made the wooden houses look like ghostly shadows. Inside his small metal workshop, Aureliano Buendía sat at a workbench cluttered with copper sheets, pliers, and half-finished little goldfish—their scales glinting faintly in the dim light from a single oil lamp. The sound of rain drummed on the tin roof, a steady, monotonous rhythm that mixed with the creak of his vice and the soft scratch of his file. He paused, wiping his hands on a greasy rag, and stared at the goldfish in front of him. Its body was almost complete, just missing the eyes—those tiny black dots that would make it seem alive, as if it might swim off the workbench and into the fog outside. He thought of his father, José Arcadio Buendía, who had once filled the house with magnets, hoping to pull gold from the river, and how the magnets had only lifted rusty nails and broken horseshoes. 'Foolishness,' Úrsula had called it, but there had been a light in his father's eyes then, a curiosity that made even the failed experiments feel like magic. The fog seeped through the cracks in the workshop walls, dampening his hair and making the copper sheets feel cold under his fingers. He picked up a tiny chisel, his hands steady despite the memories that buzzed in his head—memories of the gypsies who had brought the magnet to town, of the crowd that had gathered to watch, of his younger self clinging to his father's coat, wide-eyed and eager. Those days had been loud, full of noise and wonder, nothing like the quiet of the workshop now, where the only sounds were rain and metal and his own breath. He tapped the chisel gently, carving a small indentation for the goldfish's eye. Outside, a rooster crowed, distant and muffled by the fog, and he wondered if Úrsula was making arepas in the kitchen, the smell of corn dough mixing with the damp air. But he didn't get up. The goldfish needed its eyes, and the memories needed to be put away—for now, at least. When he finished, he held the goldfish up to the lamp. The eyes glinted, black and shiny, and for a second, he swore he saw it twitch. He smiled, a small, sad smile, and set it down next to the others. There were dozens of them, lined up on a shelf, each one a little different, each one a piece of the loneliness that had settled over him like the fog over Macondo. The rain kept falling, and the fog kept thickening, and Aureliano Buendía went back to work. There would be more goldfish tomorrow, and more memories, and the same quiet that had become his only companion. But for now, he was content—content with the metal in his hands, the rhythm of the rain, and the faint, fleeting magic of a goldfish that almost seemed alive.

text: A dirtier or more wretched place he had never seen. The street was very narrow and muddy, and the air was impregnated with filthy odours. There were a good many small shops; but the only stock in trade appeared to be heaps of children, who, even at that time of night, were crawling in and out at the doors, or screaming from the inside. The sole places that seemed to prosper amid the general blight of the place were the public-houses; and in them, the lowest, the most debased, and worst of the population were collected. Covered ways and yards, which here and there diverged from the main street, disclosed little knots of houses where drunken men and women were positively wallowing in the filth; and from several of these doorways, great ill-looking fellows were cautiously emerging, bound, as it might be, on some bad purpose. The public-houses, with gas-lights flaring out from every chink and keyhole, and illuminating the damp, grimy walls, made the street appear, by contrast, darker and more gloomy. The kennel was stagnant and filthy; and the very houses, with their crumbling plaster and rotten timbers, seemed to be in a state of decay and dissolution. The men and women, with bloated faces and tattered garments, crawled in and out like vermin. The whole place was rife with misery and squalor. In this haunt of vile and wretched characters, Oliver felt a sense of dread he had never known before. The very atmosphere was heavy with vice and poverty. They crossed the street and entered a low, dark passageway that led to a small courtyard. Here the smells were even more offensive, and the sights more deplorable. In one corner, a group of ragged boys were gambling with dirty halfpence; in another, a woman was washing some miserable rags in a broken tub of water that was black with dirt. A sickly light struggled through the single dirty window of a cellar, where some kind of workshop seemed to be in operation, and the sound of a child crying weakly came from an upstairs room where the window was patched with paper and rags. Everywhere there was evidence of the most abject poverty and neglect. The Dodger, apparently quite at home in this environment, led Oliver confidently through another narrow alley, where the overhanging upper stories of the houses nearly met overhead, shutting out what little light might have penetrated from the sky. Oliver clung closer to his companion, trembling with a confusion of fear and disgust. He had never imagined that such places could exist, and the thought that anyone could live in such conditions filled him with horror. The cheerful promises of his friend seemed now like a cruel joke, and he would have given anything to be back in the clean, if sparse, surroundings of the workhouse.

text: The mud hut's walls were made of red earth, packed hard and cracked with dryness, and the thatched roof leaked when it rained—though it hadn't rained in weeks. Martha sat on the ground, her linen skirt spread out around her, staining it with dust. July was on the roof, patching holes with dried grass, his bare feet gripping the thatch like he'd been doing it all his life. Below him, his wife, Maureen, stirred a pot over the fire, the smell of boiled maize drifting through the air. Martha's husband, Bam, was inside the hut, cleaning their only remaining gun—just in case, he said. Their children, Royce and Gina, were playing with July's kids, chasing a chicken around the yard, their laughter loud and unselfconscious. It was a sound Martha hadn't heard since they left the city, since the roads were blocked with burning cars, since they'd driven for three days with no food, no water, no idea if they'd survive. She looked down at her hands—soft, uncalloused, the nails chipped from trying to dig a vegetable patch. Before, she'd had a gardener to do that. Before, she'd had a cook, a cleaner, a driver. Before, July had called her 'Madam,' had stood with his hands behind his back when he spoke to her, had never looked her in the eye. Now, he called her 'Martha,' had given them his own hut to sleep in, had shared his last sack of maize. Now, she looked to him for help, for protection, for answers. July climbed down from the roof, brushing grass from his pants. 'Roof'll hold,' he said, nodding at her. 'Until the rains come, anyway.' Martha nodded. She wanted to thank him, but the words felt stuck in her throat. Thank you for saving our lives? Thank you for letting us live in your home? Thank you for not hating us, even though we treated you like you were less than human? She couldn't say any of it. It felt too small, too late. 'You need water?' July asked, noticing her staring at the empty bucket by the door. Martha stood up, brushing dust from her skirt. 'I can get it,' she said. She'd tried once before, had walked to the river with the bucket, had stumbled over rocks, had spilled half the water before she got back. July had watched her, not saying anything, but the next day, he'd left a full bucket by the door. July shook his head. 'I'll go,' he said. 'You stay. Maureen'll give you some maize bread soon.' He picked up the bucket and walked toward the river, his steps sure, his back straight. Martha watched him go, watched the way the sun hit his skin, the way he greeted an old man passing by with a smile and a word in Zulu. A word she didn't understand. A world she didn't understand. She thought of the city, of their house with its swimming pool and rose gardens, of the parties they'd had, of the way she'd complained about July being 'slow' or 'careless.' She thought of the signs—'Whites Only' on parks, on buses, on toilets—and how she'd never questioned them. How she'd thought they were normal, natural.

text: “HIST! Did you hear that noise, Cabaco?” It was the middle-watch: a fair moonlight; the seamen were standing in a cordon, extending from one of the fresh-water butts in the waist, to the scuttle-butt near the taffrail. In this manner, they passed the buckets to fill the scuttle-butt. Standing, for the most part, on the hallowed precincts of the quarter-deck, they were careful not to speak or rustle their feet. From hand to hand, the buckets went in the deepest silence, only broken by the occasional flap of a sail, and the steady hum of the unceasingly advancing keel. It was in the midst of this repose, that Archy, one of the cordon, whose post was near the after-hatches, whispered to his neighbor, a Cholo, the words above. “Hist! did you hear that noise, Cabaco?” “Take the bucket, will ye, Archy? what noise d’ye mean?” “There it is again—under the hatches—don’t you hear it—a cough—it sounded like a cough.” “Cough be damned! Pass along that return bucket.” “There again—there it is!—it sounds like two or three sleepers turning over, now!” “Caramba! have done, shipmate, will ye? It’s the three soaked biscuits ye eat for supper turning over inside of ye—nothing else. Look to the bucket!” “Say what ye will, shipmate; I’ve sharp ears.” “Aye, you are the chap, ain’t ye, that heard the hum of the old Quakeress’s knitting-needles fifty miles at sea from Nantucket; you’re the chap.” “Grin away; we’ll see what turns up. Hark ye, Cabaco, there is somebody down in the after-hold that has not yet been seen on deck; and I suspect our old Mogul knows something of it too. I heard Stubb tell Flask, one morning watch, that there was something of that sort in the wind.” “Tish! the bucket!”

text: It is well to parenthesize here, that of the fatal accidents in the Sperm-Whale Fishery, this kind is perhaps almost as frequent as any. Sometimes, nothing is injured but the man who is thus annihilated; oftener the boat’s bow is knocked off, or the thigh-board, in which the headsman stands, is torn from its place and accompanies the body. But strangest of all is the circumstance, that in more instances than one, when the body has been recovered, not a single mark of violence is discernible; the man being stark dead. The whole calamity, with the falling form of Macey, was plainly descried from the ship. Raising a piercing shriek—“The vial! the vial!” Gabriel called off the terror-stricken crew from the further hunting of the whale. This terrible event clothed the archangel with added influence; because his credulous disciples believed that he had specifically fore-announced it, instead of only making a general prophecy, which any one might have done, and so have chanced to hit one of many marks in the wide margin allowed. He became a nameless terror to the ship. Mayhew having concluded his narration, Ahab put such questions to him, that the stranger captain could not forbear inquiring whether he intended to hunt the White Whale, if opportunity should offer. To which Ahab answered—“Aye.” Straightway, then, Gabriel once more started to his feet, glaring upon the old man, and vehemently exclaimed, with downward pointed finger—“Think, think of the blasphemer—dead, and down there!—beware of the blasphemer’s end!” Ahab stolidly turned aside; then said to Mayhew, “Captain, I have just bethought me of my letter-bag; there is a letter for one of thy officers, if I mistake not. Starbuck, look over the bag.” Every whale-ship takes out a goodly number of letters for various ships, whose delivery to the persons to whom they may be addressed, depends upon the mere chance of encountering them in the four oceans. Thus, most letters never reach their mark; and many are only received after attaining an age of two or three years or more. Soon Starbuck returned with a letter in his hand. She’d raised him on the grassland, she thought—to ride horses before he could walk, to tell apart sheep by their bleats, to know the stars as guides for the flock—but the world outside was pulling him, bright and loud, like a river carrying away a leaf. A leaf drifted from the nearby poplar tree, landing on her spindle. She set the spindle down, reaching to pick up the leaf—its edges yellowed, a sign that winter would come soon. She thought of her mother, who’d said "The grassland changes, but our roots don’t change, Aygul. The spindle in your hand is our story." But lately, she’d wondered: if the young ones leave, who will hold the spindle? Who will remember how to weave the wool blankets, how to sing the old songs about the grassland and the sky?

text: The winter dawn broke pale over London, painting the soot-stained rooftops with a thin wash of gray that did nothing to chase away the cold—its light barely reaching the narrow alley where Oliver Twist huddled against a brick wall, his small body wrapped in a tattered woolen blanket. He held a crust of stale bread in his trembling hand, the last of the food a kind baker had given him the day before, and he nibbled at it slowly, savoring every crumb, afraid it would be his last. A stray dog trotted past, its tail tucked between its legs, and Oliver watched it go, his eyes wide with a mix of fear and longing. He'd been on his own for three days now, ever since he'd run away from the workhouse—from the cold porridge, the cruel overseers, the endless days of hauling heavy loads that made his bones ache. He didn't know where to go, didn't know if anyone would help him, but he couldn't go back. Back there, he was just a number, a small body to be worked until it broke. A cart rumbled down the street at the end of the alley, loaded with firewood, and the driver yelled at a cat that darted under his wheels. Oliver flinched, pressing himself tighter against the wall. Loud noises scared him—they always had, ever since the day he'd been beaten for asking for more porridge. He closed his eyes for a second, breathing in the sharp, frosty air, and tried to remember the last time someone had been kind to him. It was his mother, he thought—though he could barely picture her face, just the feel of her hand on his forehead, warm and soft, before she'd gone away. The bread was gone now, and his stomach growled. He wrapped the blanket tighter around himself, his teeth chattering. He looked up at the sky, where a few faint stars were still visible, and whispered a quiet prayer—not for food, not for warmth, but for someone to see him. To see that he was just a boy, not a burden, not a trouble, just a boy who wanted to be safe. A door creaked open at the end of the alley, and a young girl stepped out, carrying a bucket of water. She saw Oliver and stopped, her eyes widening. For a second, he thought she'd yell, or run back inside, but instead she walked over, slow and careful, and held out her hand. In it was a small apple, shiny and red, still warm from being inside. "Here," she said, her voice soft. "You look hungry." Oliver stared at her, then at the apple, and slowly reached out to take it. His fingers brushed hers, and he flinched again—no one had touched him gently in so long. He bit into the apple, and the sweet juice filled his mouth, and for the first time in days, he didn't feel quite so cold, quite so alone.

'I'm Maya,' she said, holding out her hand. 'Want to join my friends and me? We saved you a spot!' Lila hesitated, then smiled. 'Thanks—I'd like that.' Maya led her to a table where two boys were talking about soccer. 'This is Leo and Javi,' Maya said. 'Lila's new—she's from Portland!' Leo grinned. 'Portland has amazing hiking trails, right? I've always wanted to go there.' Suddenly, Lila felt less nervous. She talked about the forests near her old home, and the boys shared stories about their weekend soccer games. Maya asked about her favorite books, and soon they were debating the best fantasy series. When the bell rang, Maya squeezed her arm. 'We're having a study group at the library after school—you should come!' That afternoon, Lila joined the study group. They helped her figure out the school's homework system, and she shared a trick for remembering math formulas. As she walked home, she realized she'd laughed more that day than she had in weeks. By the end of the week, Lila had made three good friends. She still missed her old home sometimes, but Maplewood was starting to feel like a new one. One morning, she noticed a new boy sitting alone at lunch. She walked over, just like Maya had done for her. 'Hi, I'm Lila,' she said. 'Want to sit with my friends?' She learned that being new wasn't easy, but a little kindness could go a long way. text: The winter night in Black’s workshop at the Sultan’s palace in Istanbul was cold—cold enough that the only warmth came from a small charcoal stove, its glow gilding the tubes of mineral paint lined up on the wooden table. Black sat cross-legged on a woolen rug, a camel-hair brush in his hand and an unfinished miniature manuscript spread open before him, his eyes fixed on the half-drawn tulip whose petals he’d struggled to shape all evening. The workshop smelled of pine resin and burnt charcoal, and a stack of old miniature paintings leaned against the wall—works by his friend Elegant, who’d been killed three weeks ago for questioning the Sultan’s artistic orders. He thought of Elegant—of the way he’d laughed when they’d argued about perspective, saying “The eye should see what the heart believes, not what the Franks teach,” of the way he’d mixed lapis lazuli pigment with his fingers, staining his nails blue for days, of the way he’d whispered about “truth in art” while they worked by candlelight, his voice soft as the brushstrokes they painted. Black had disagreed then, tempted by the Western artists’ way of making figures “stand out from the page,” but now he wondered if Elegant had been right—if the beauty of their art lay in its invisibility, in the way it made the viewer feel part of the story, not just an observer. The stove crackled, and Black set down his brush, reaching for a tube of crimson paint. He twisted the cap, but it stuck, and he pulled harder, spilling a drop onto the manuscript. The red spread across the tulip’s petal, bright and harsh, like a wound. He stared at it, his throat tight. It was the same color as the blood he’d seen on Elegant’s sleeve the night they’d found him, the same color as the silk scarf Shekure had worn when he’d last seen her, the same color that haunted his dreams. He wiped the paint with his sleeve, but the stain remained, faint but visible. He thought of Shekure—of the way her hair had fallen over her shoulders when she’d brought him tea last week, of the way she’d hesitated before asking if he’d finish Elegant’s last manuscript, of the way her eyes had glistened when he’d said yes. She’d been Elegant’s fiancée once, but now she was alone, like him. He wondered if she thought of Elegant as often as he did, if she ever lay awake at night wondering who’d killed him, why.

He wore his best black tailcoat, its fabric pressed so smooth it shone slightly, its cuffs unwrinkled—just as he’d worn it for decades at Darlington Hall, just as he’d worn it when serving lords and diplomats, when he’d prided himself on being “a great butler,” when he’d thought nothing mattered more than duty. A small table beside him held a half-empty cup of tea, its surface covered in a thin film of cream that had settled hours ago. He’d poured it when he first sat down, intending to savor it, but his mind had wandered—back to Darlington Hall, back to Miss Kenton, back to the day she’d told him she was leaving to marry Mr. Benn, her eyes wet, her voice unsteady. He’d nodded then, said “I wish you every happiness,” kept his tone calm, kept his face blank—just as a great butler should. But now, sitting here in the quiet, watching the sun set, he wondered if he’d been wrong. Wondered if “greatness” was just a word he’d hidden behind, a way to avoid feeling the things he’d been taught to ignore. A breeze blew across the terrace, carrying with it the smell of wood smoke from a nearby cottage and the faint chirp of crickets. He pulled his coat a little tighter around his shoulders, not because he was cold, but because it felt like something to do— a small, proper action to keep his hands from trembling, to keep his thoughts from straying too far into the past. He’d spent his life mastering control: control of his emotions, control of his actions, control of the household he’d managed so carefully. But now, control felt like a cage. A cage he’d built himself, with every “yes, sir” and every “I shall see to it,” with every chance he’d had to say something, to feel something, and chosen not to. He thought of Miss Kenton’s letter, the one he’d received last month—short, polite, telling him she’d moved to the countryside, that her husband was well, that she sometimes thought of Darlington Hall. She hadn’t mentioned the past, hadn’t mentioned the day they’d argued about her aunt’s death, hadn’t mentioned the way he’d avoided her eyes for weeks after. He’d written back, of course—short, polite, telling her he was on a trip, that the hotel was pleasant, that he sometimes thought of Darlington Hall too. He hadn’t mentioned the past either.

text: Now that the incorruption of this most fragrant ambergris should be found in the heart of such decay; is this nothing? Bethink thee of that saying of St. Paul in Corinthians, about corruption and incorruption; how that we are sown in dishonor, but raised in glory. And likewise call to mind that saying of Paracelsus about what it is that maketh the best musk. Also forget not the strange fact that of all things of ill-savor, Cologne-water, in its rudimental manufacturing stages, is the worst. I should like to conclude the chapter with the above appeal, but cannot, owing to my anxiety to repel a charge often made against whalemen, and which, in the estimation of some already biased minds, might be considered as indirectly substantiated by what has been said of the Frenchman’s two whales. Elsewhere in this volume the slanderous aspersion has been disproved, that the vocation of whaling is throughout a slatternly, untidy business. But there is another thing to rebut. They hint that all whales always smell bad. Now how did this odious stigma originate? I opine, that it is plainly traceable to the first arrival of the Greenland whaling ships in London, more than two centuries ago. Because those whalemen did not then, and do not now, try out their oil at sea as the Southern ships have always done; but cutting up the fresh blubber in small bits, thrust it through the bung holes of large casks, and carry it home in that manner; the shortness of the season in those Icy Seas, and the sudden and violent storms to which they are exposed, forbidding any other course. The consequence is, that upon breaking into the hold, and unloading one of these whale cemeteries, in the Greenland dock, a savor is given forth somewhat similar to that arising from excavating an old city grave-yard, for the foundations of a Lying-in Hospital.

As the light grew a little stronger, the details of the squalor sharpened: the peeling paint that flaked like dead skin, the holes in the roofs where rafters poked through, the lettering on a faded sign—'Shoes Mended'—now illegible beneath layers of grime. One kicked a broken pot, sending shards skittering, and they vanished into an alley, their voices fading into the murk. “Well, you do be the great one for friends, little Poppy Redtop,” said Mr. Burke admiringly. “It’s congratulations that’s due you, an’ that’s the truth. Now I’ve met you, I might tell you my errand. I was aimin’ to see your—well, I don’t know the title you give ’em, but whoever takes care of you—Mr. Gilbert Hawthorne, ’tis. I’ll not be goin’ to the house, now I can tell you what I had to say.”

“Oh, yes, Mr. Burke,” Mark cried. “Please come. Dad will be glad enough to see you. He would be annoyed with us, with me, if you didn’t come. Please come. We all know you well through Poppy. Motherkins—my grandmother, Mrs. Hawthorne—would love to thank you for taking care of Poppy last summer.”

“You’re a little gentleman!” declared Mr. Burke, regarding with frank admiration Mark’s radiant face. “It’s no thanks are due me for pickin’ up a bit of a girl, out gettin’ herself into trouble. But I’ll go along with pleasure. I’ve something to tell your father that maybe he ought to know, an’ maybe it’s no matter. Will I lead an’ will you follow, or will we turn it the other way, an’ me follow that war horse of Poppy’s? How do you name him?”

“Hurrah,” said Poppy. “He’s not a war horse; he’s peaceful and loving.”

“’Deed, then, he looks it! An’ Hurrah is a name that couldn’t be beat for belongin’ to a horse that you own, little Redtop; you’re the one to go with a hurrah, as the sayin’ is!” Mr. Thomas Burke grinned at Poppy so warmly that she could not suspect him of looking down on Hurrah, as she at first thought he might do.

Mr. Burke went back and climbed up on his wagon, with grunts that revealed the effort it cost him, and the two vehicles took their way up to the Hawthorne house, Mr. Burke in the lead, Hurrah and his friends in the rear.

At the gateway they were met by Isabel, too excited to stand still or to wonder at Mr. Burke.

“Oh, I’ve been dying! I thought you’d never come back!” she cried, jumping from one to the other foot. “Mother’s friend went and I came back here to wait for you. I went up to the Club Room, and what do you s’pose?”

Isabel barely paused at the end of her question, which she did not expect answered. The other children murmured something, but Isabel went on hurriedly.

“Some one’s been up there, in our room! They’ve been eating, and moved things around. And they took out a pillow!”

“Who?” demanded the other three together.

All at once he hears a fearful tramping. . . . A crowd of soldiers, with red faces and bath brooms under their arms, move in step along the boulevard straight upon him. Grisha turns cold all over with terror, and looks inquiringly at nurse to know whether it is dangerous. But nurse neither weeps nor runs away, so there is no danger. Grisha looks after the soldiers, and begins to move his feet in step with them himself.
Two big cats with long faces run after each other across the boulevard, with their tongues out, and their tails in the air. Grisha thinks that he must run too, and runs after the cats.
“Stop!” cries nurse, seizing him roughly by the shoulder. “Where are you off to? Haven’t you been told not to be naughty?”
Here there is a nurse sitting holding a tray of oranges. Grisha passes by her, and, without saying anything, takes an orange.
“What are you doing that for?” cries the companion of his travels, slapping his hand and snatching away the orange. “Silly!”
Now Grisha would have liked to pick up a bit of glass that was lying at his feet and gleaming like a lamp, but he is afraid that his hand will be slapped again.
“My respects to you!” Grisha hears suddenly, almost above his ear, a loud thick voice, and he sees a tall man with bright buttons.
To his great delight, this man gives nurse his hand, stops, and begins talking to her. The brightness of the sun, the noise of the carriages, the horses, the bright buttons are all so impressively new and not dreadful, that Grisha’s soul is filled with a feeling of enjoyment and he begins to laugh.
“Come along! Come along!” he cries to the man with the bright buttons, tugging at his coattails.
“Come along where?” asks the man.
“Come along!” Grisha insists.
He wants to say that it would be just as well to take with them papa, mamma, and the cat, but his tongue does not say what he wants to.

text:
Concerning the officers of the whale-craft, this seems as good a place as any to set down a little domestic peculiarity on ship-board, arising from the existence of the harpooneer class of officers, a class unknown of course in any other marine than the whale-fleet.
The large importance attached to the harpooneer’s vocation is evinced by the fact, that originally in the old Dutch Fishery, two centuries and more ago, the command of a whale ship was not wholly lodged in the person now called the captain, but was divided between him and an officer called the Specksnyder. Literally this word means Fat-Cutter; usage, however, in time made it equivalent to Chief Harpooneer. In those days, the captain’s authority was restricted to the navigation and general management of the vessel; while over the whale-hunting department and all its concerns, the Specksnyder or Chief Harpooneer reigned supreme. In the British Greenland Fishery, under the corrupted title of Specksioneer, this old Dutch official is still retained, but his former dignity is sadly abridged. At present he ranks simply as senior Harpooneer; and as such, is but one of the captain’s more inferior subalterns. Nevertheless, as upon the good conduct of the harpooneers the success of a whaling voyage largely depends, and since in the American Fishery he is not only an important officer in the boat, but under certain circumstances (night watches on a whaling ground) the command of the ship’s deck is also his; therefore the grand political maxim of the sea demands, that he should nominally live apart from the men before the mast, and be in some way distinguished as their professional superior; though always, by them, familiarly regarded as their social equal.
Now, the grand distinction drawn between officer and man at sea, is this—the first lives aft, the last forward. Hence, in whale-ships and merchantmen alike, the mates have their quarters with the captain; and so, too, in most of the American whalers the harpooneers are lodged in the after part of the ship. That is to say, they take their meals in the captain’s cabin, and sleep in a place indirectly communicating with it.

text:
The rubbish heap was adorned, for the first time, with jam and fish tins from the table in the new hut. It seemed to be understood that neither woman nor dog in the old hut required them.

Squeaker’s dog sniffed and barked joyfully around them till his licking efforts to bottom a salmon tin sent him careering in a muzzled frenzy, that caused the younger woman’s thick lips to part grinningly till he came too close.

The remaining sheep were regularly yarded. His old mate heard him whistle as he did it. Squeaker began to work about a little burning off. So that now, added to the other bush voices, was the call from some untimely falling giant. There is no sound so human as that from the riven souls of these tree people, or the trembling sighs of their upright neighbours whose hands in time will meet over the victim’s fallen body.

There was no bunk on the side of the hut to which her eyes turned, but her dog filled that space, and the flash that passed between this back-broken woman and her dog might have been the spirit of these slain tree folk, it was so wondrous ghostly. Still, at times, the practical in her would be dominant, for in a mind so free of fancies, backed by bodily strength, hope died slowly, and forgetful of self she would almost call to Squeaker her fears that certain bees’ nests were in danger.

He went into town one day and returned, as he had promised, long before sundown, and next day a clothes line bridged the space between two trees near the back of the old hut; and—an equally rare occurrence—Squeaker placed across his shoulders the yoke that his old mate had fashioned for herself, with two kerosene tins attached, and brought them filled with water from the distant creek; but both only partly filled the tub, a new purchase. With utter disregard of the heat and Squeaker’s sweating brow, his new mate said, even after another trip, two more now for the blue water. Under her commands he brought them, though sullenly, perhaps contrasting the old mate’s methods with the new.

His old mate had periodically carried their washing to the creek, and his mole skins had been as white as snow without aid of blue.

Towards noon, on the clothes line many strange garments fluttered, suggestive of a taunt to the barren woman.

A week later it was suggested to Andrey Yefimitch that he should have a rest—that is, send in his resignation—a suggestion he received with indifference, and a week later still, Mihail Averyanitch and he were sitting in a posting carriage driving to the nearest railway station. The days were cool and bright, with a blue sky and a transparent distance. They were two days driving the hundred and fifty miles to the railway station, and stayed two nights on the way. When at the posting station the glasses given them for their tea had not been properly washed, or the drivers were slow in harnessing the horses, Mihail Averyanitch would turn crimson, and quivering all over would shout:
“Hold your tongue! Don’t argue!”
And in the carriage he talked without ceasing for a moment, describing his campaigns in the Caucasus and in Poland. What adventures he had had, what meetings! He talked loudly and opened his eyes so wide with wonder that he might well be thought to be lying. Moreover, as he talked he breathed in Andrey Yefimitch’s face and laughed into his ear. This bothered the doctor and prevented him from thinking or concentrating his mind.
In the train they travelled, from motives of economy, third-class in a non-smoking compartment. Half the passengers were decent people. Mihail Averyanitch soon made friends with everyone, and moving from one seat to another, kept saying loudly that they ought not to travel by these appalling lines. It was a regular swindle! A very different thing riding on a good horse: one could do over seventy miles a day and feel fresh and well after it. And our bad harvests were due to the draining of the Pinsk marshes; altogether, the way things were done was dreadful. He got excited, talked loudly, and would not let others speak. This endless chatter to the accompaniment of loud laughter and expressive gestures wearied Andrey Yefimitch.
